questions.explanation: If the machine in the field must be assumed hostile, the authority to move money has to live somewhere else: in a thin-client model the dispenser acts only on instructions signed by the host, so a compromised core can request cash but can no longer conjure an approval (C). A places the decision inside the very component being distrusted, since local rules are the attacker's rules once the core falls; client-side checks are the right answer only for usability feedback, never for enforcement. B relocates trust sideways rather than upward: peer ATMs share the same hardware, software, and exposure, so cryptographic vouching only proves a peer signed, and a fleet-wide flaw compromises the voters along with the voter being checked. D is detective by construction. An immutable record proves afterwards that cash left, which supports reconciliation and fraud analytics, but the money is already gone; it would be the right answer to an audit-trail question. Put authorization authority on the most trustworthy tier and make the exposed tier a mere executor of signed instructions.
questions.recallLine: Engineers want a terminal fleet in which even a fully compromised core cannot dispense cash on its own. Which architecture BEST delivers that guarantee?

optionsShort.A: Core checks withdrawals against locally stored rules
optionsShort.B: Neighbouring ATMs cryptographically vouch for each other
optionsShort.C: Thin client; host signs every dispense authorization
optionsShort.D: Distributed ledger recording dispenses for later reconciliation

A.label: not the decision-maker's
A.wouldAnswer: Which check belongs on the terminal itself, to give a customer immediate feedback before the request ever reaches the bank?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which mechanism proves a transaction was endorsed by other nodes, where those nodes genuinely fail independently of each other?

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Which design gives auditors an immutable fleet-wide record of every dispense for later reconciliation?

questions.question: Which architectural concept does concentrating PIN handling in a small sealed module BEST illustrate?

options.A: Concentrating security functions in a minimal trusted computing base, isolated from untrusted components.
options.B: Sandboxing, which confines a single untrusted application inside a restricted, monitored runtime environment.
options.C: Virtualization, which runs the sensitive workload inside a hypervisor-managed guest machine.
options.D: Network segmentation, which divides the system into zones separated by filtering devices.

questions.explanation: The design shrinks the set of components that must be trusted for PIN security down to one small, verifiable, physically hardened element. That is the classic trusted computing base argument: a small TCB is easier to protect and evaluate than a sprawling one (A). B inverts the relationship: sandboxing contains something untrusted inside restrictions, whereas here the trusted element is being isolated from everything else; a sandbox is the right answer for running risky code such as a browser plugin. C names a technology, not the principle. Hypervisors could implement this isolation, but nothing in the design requires virtual machines, and a guest still depends on the hypervisor's own trustworthiness. D applies the right instinct at the wrong layer: zones and filtering describe network topology, not the intra-device boundary between a crypto module and its host. Minimizing and isolating the TCB is the architectural move; sandboxes, hypervisors, and network zones are merely tools that can implement it.
questions.recallLine: Calderwood's design runs all PIN handling inside one small sealed module. Which architectural concept does that concentration BEST illustrate?

optionsShort.A: Minimal trusted computing base, isolated from untrusted parts
optionsShort.B: Sandboxing: untrusted code confined in a restricted runtime
optionsShort.C: Virtualization: sensitive workload inside a hypervisor guest
optionsShort.D: Network segmentation into zones separated by filters

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which technique confines risky code such as a browser plugin so it cannot reach the rest of the system?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Which technology could implement this isolation on a general-purpose server that has no dedicated sealed hardware?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Which technique separates a payment estate into zones so a breach in one does not reach another?

questions.question: Which selection BEST aligns with where the payment standards are heading as legacy algorithms are retired?

options.A: RC4, because a fast stream cipher minimizes latency on the slow serial links.
options.B: AES, which the standards bodies are adopting as legacy triple-DES is phased out.
options.C: SHA-256, providing a stronger one-way transformation of each PIN block.
options.D: Single DES with unique per-transaction keys derived under the DUKPT scheme.

questions.explanation: PIN blocks must be encrypted with a strong, standards-approved block cipher that host security modules can translate, and the industry direction is explicit: PCI PIN requirements and the ISO 9564 format-4 PIN block move the ecosystem from triple-DES to AES (B). A fails on both counts. RC4 has well-known keystream biases and has been withdrawn from security protocols generally; no payment standard permits it. C is the wrong primitive entirely: a hash is one-way, and the acquiring host must be able to translate and verify the PIN block, which requires reversible encryption under controlled keys. Hashing is the right answer for storing passwords, not for transporting PINs. D wraps a genuinely good key-management scheme around a dead cipher. DUKPT's per-transaction keys are current practice, but a 56-bit DES key is brute-forceable regardless of how often it changes; DUKPT with triple-DES or AES would be the defensible version. Check both the algorithm and its key management against the current standard, since a strong scheme cannot rescue a retired cipher.
questions.recallLine: Calderwood is replacing PIN-block encryption across the estate. Which choice BEST aligns with where payment standards are heading as legacy algorithms retire?

optionsShort.A: RC4 stream cipher chosen for low latency
optionsShort.B: AES, as triple-DES is phased out
optionsShort.C: SHA-256 hashing of each PIN block
optionsShort.D: Single DES with DUKPT per-transaction keys

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which cipher family minimizes per-byte latency on a slow serial link, once a currently approved algorithm is chosen?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which primitive suits storing a credential that must be verified later but never recovered?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Which key-management scheme gives every transaction a unique key derived from the device's initial key?

questions.question: Which factor MOST determines how long the offline recovery attempt needs before it succeeds?

options.A: The effective key space of the encryption algorithm protecting the blocks.
options.B: The account lockout threshold configured at the card issuer's host.
options.C: The entropy of the four-digit PIN values the customers selected.
options.D: The collision resistance of the hash function used by the terminals.

questions.explanation: Exhaustive key search runs at the attacker's own pace against captured ciphertext, so its expected duration is governed by how many keys must be tried: the effective key space, which is why 56-bit DES falls in hours while 128-bit AES remains beyond feasible computation (A). B is the classic online/offline confusion: lockout thresholds throttle guesses submitted to a live host, and an attacker holding the ciphertext never talks to the issuer; lockout is the right answer when the scenario is PIN guessing at the terminal. C misidentifies the search target. The thieves are trying keys, not PINs, and once the key is found every PIN in the batch falls at once; PIN entropy would dominate if the attack were guessing PINs through the protocol. D names a property of a primitive the scheme does not use for this purpose, since PIN blocks are reversibly encrypted for translation between hosts; nothing in the scheme hashes them. For any brute-force question, first fix what is being enumerated and where. Offline key search answers only to key space, and no online control touches it.
questions.recallLine: Thieves captured encrypted PIN blocks and are trying every possible key offline. Which factor MOST determines how long that recovery attempt takes to succeed?

optionsShort.A: Effective key space of the encryption algorithm
optionsShort.B: Account lockout threshold at the issuer's host
optionsShort.C: Entropy of the customers' four-digit PINs
optionsShort.D: Collision resistance of the terminals' hash function

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which setting limits an attacker who is guessing PINs at a live terminal against the issuer's host?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Which factor governs how long guessing takes when the attack works through the protocol against the PINs themselves?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which hash property matters when an attacker needs two different inputs to produce the same digest?

questions.question: Which security service makes that demonstration to the regulator possible after the fact?

options.A: Confidentiality, because the order traveled through an encrypted channel end to end.
options.B: Integrity, because any alteration of the order after signing would break the signature.
options.C: Authentication, because the session verified her identity when she first logged in.
options.D: Non-repudiation, because the signature is provable to a third party after the fact.

questions.explanation: What the bank needed was evidence that stands up in front of someone else, a regulator, against the signer's own denial, and that is the specific service called non-repudiation: a digital signature binds the order to the sole holder of the private key, so origin cannot be plausibly disclaimed later (D). B is true but answers a narrower claim: the signature does prove the order was not altered, yet the administrator is denying authorship, not alleging tampering; integrity would be the winning service if the dispute were about modification in transit. C also genuinely occurred, but session authentication is evidence between the two communicating parties at that moment. It convinces the server, not a third party reviewing events afterwards, and shared-credential logins can be disputed. A is orthogonal: encryption hides the order from outsiders and proves nothing about who created it. Authentication convinces the counterparty now; non-repudiation convinces a third party later. The private-key signature is what upgrades the first into the second.
questions.recallLine: An administrator denies sending a transfer order that only her smart card's private key could have signed. Which security service lets the bank demonstrate that to a regulator?

optionsShort.A: Confidentiality from the end-to-end encrypted channel
optionsShort.B: Integrity: alteration after signing breaks verification
optionsShort.C: Authentication verified her identity at login
optionsShort.D: Non-repudiation: provable to a third party

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which service keeps the transfer order hidden from anyone watching the network in between?

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Which service settles a dispute about whether the order was altered somewhere between sender and receiver?

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Which service convinces the server, at the moment of connection, that the person logging in is who she claims?

questions.question: Which property is missing from the proprietary cipher, and why does its absence matter MOST?

options.A: Collision resistance; two distinct inputs could be found that produce the same output.
options.B: The avalanche effect; localized changes let analysts map ciphertext structure back to plaintext.
options.C: Forward secrecy; a stolen long-term key would expose previously recorded traffic.
options.D: Key-generation entropy; predictable keys would narrow an attacker's search space.

questions.explanation: A strong cipher must exhibit the avalanche effect, a one-bit input change flipping roughly half the output bits, because it is the visible evidence of diffusion; when a change stays localized, ciphertext regions correspond to plaintext regions, and an analyst can recover structure, spot repeated fields, and mount statistical attacks without the key (B). A imports a hash-function requirement: collision resistance matters where distinct inputs must never share an output, as in signatures over digests, and its absence there enables forgery, a different primitive's failure. C concerns key-management architecture rather than cipher internals; it is the property to demand of a protocol whose recorded traffic must survive later key theft, and no block cipher provides it by itself. D is a real and fatal weakness when present, but the test performed here held the key fixed and varied plaintext, so it measured the cipher's mixing, not the randomness of key generation. Diffusion failures show up exactly this way in testing; treat a missing avalanche as proof the cipher leaks structure, and reject it.
questions.recallLine: Flipping one plaintext bit changes only the corresponding ciphertext byte in a vendor's proprietary cipher. Which property is missing, and why does its absence matter MOST?

optionsShort.A: Collision resistance; distinct inputs share one output
optionsShort.B: Avalanche effect; localized change exposes plaintext structure
optionsShort.C: Forward secrecy; stolen long-term key exposes recordings
optionsShort.D: Key-generation entropy; predictable keys narrow the search

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which property must a digest have before signatures over it can be trusted, so no two inputs share a value?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Which property must a protocol provide if recorded traffic has to survive the later theft of a long-term key?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which weakness would a test of the vendor's random number generation, rather than its mixing, be hunting for?

questions.question: Which security model BEST fits the requirement that access history dynamically bars a consultant from the competitor's files?

options.A: Brewer-Nash, enforcing dynamic conflict-of-interest classes over datasets.
options.B: Bell-LaPadula, enforcing hierarchical confidentiality labels and clearances.
options.C: Clark-Wilson, enforcing well-formed transactions with separation of duties.
options.D: Biba, preventing lower-integrity information from contaminating higher levels.

questions.explanation: The distinguishing feature in the stem is that permissions change as a consequence of the subject's own past reads: access to one competitor's data walls off the other's. That history-dependent, conflict-of-interest behavior is exactly what Brewer-Nash, the Chinese Wall model, was built to formalize (A). B is static by comparison: Bell-LaPadula grants access from fixed clearances and labels, and a Secret-cleared consultant would keep whatever the lattice allows regardless of what they read yesterday; it is the right model for classified hierarchies. C protects how data is modified (certified procedures, duty separation, reconciliations) and has no notion of one dataset excluding another; it fits the question 'how do we keep ledger updates trustworthy?'. D governs the direction of information flow for integrity and likewise never consults access history. When a scenario says permissions depend on what the subject already accessed, the words 'conflict of interest' and 'dynamic' should trigger Brewer-Nash before any of the classic static models.
questions.recallLine: A consultant who opens one bank's engagement files must be barred from its competitor's, on the strength of that access history. Which security model BEST fits?

optionsShort.A: Brewer-Nash: dynamic conflict-of-interest classes over datasets
optionsShort.B: Bell-LaPadula: hierarchical confidentiality labels and clearances
optionsShort.C: Clark-Wilson: well-formed transactions and duty separation
optionsShort.D: Biba: keep low-integrity data out of high

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which model decides access from fixed clearances and labels in a classified hierarchy?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which model keeps ledger updates trustworthy by forcing them through certified procedures and separated duties?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which model stops information at a lower integrity level contaminating data trusted at a higher one?

questions.question: Under the cloud shared-responsibility model, which duty remains MOST squarely with the firm?

options.A: Testing and applying patches to the application platform and middleware serving the management console.
options.B: Hardening the host operating systems running in the vendor's data centers.
options.C: Governing its user accounts, their entitlements, and the data it places in the service.
options.D: Maintaining the hypervisor layer that isolates tenants from one another.

questions.explanation: The arrangement described, consuming a finished application over the network with no visibility into its stack, is SaaS, the model in which the customer's retained duties compress to the two things no provider can own: who may access the tenant, with what privileges, and the classification and handling of the data entrusted to it (C). A sits on the provider's side of the SaaS line, since the customer cannot even see the middleware; platform patching becomes a customer duty only down at IaaS, where the customer builds atop rented infrastructure. B fails the same test one layer lower. OS hardening belongs to the customer in IaaS, but here the vendor runs the operating systems. D is provider territory in every service model; no cloud tenant administers the hypervisor, which is exactly why tenant-isolation assurance is sought through the provider's audits and certifications instead. As the service model climbs from IaaS to SaaS the provider absorbs layer after layer, but identity governance and data accountability never transfer; those stay with the customer in every model.
questions.recallLine: The firm subscribes to a vendor-hosted fleet application in which the vendor runs the servers, operating systems and code. Which duty remains MOST squarely with the firm?

optionsShort.A: Patch the application platform and middleware
optionsShort.B: Harden host operating systems in vendor data centers
optionsShort.C: Govern its accounts, entitlements and data
optionsShort.D: Maintain the tenant-isolating hypervisor layer

A.label: not the decision-maker's
A.wouldAnswer: Which patching duty falls to the customer under IaaS, where it builds its own platform on rented infrastructure?

B.label: not the decision-maker's
B.wouldAnswer: Which hardening duty belongs to the customer under IaaS, where it runs the operating systems itself?

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: Which layer can a tenant only gain assurance over through the provider's audits and certifications?

questions.question: Which property of a well-designed biometric system should the team cite to the regulator?

options.A: Raw scans are retained, but encrypted under keys lodged with an independent escrow agent.
options.B: Mathematical templates are stored instead of images, and the original fingerprint is not recoverable.
options.C: Fingerprint images are hashed with SHA-256 at enrollment and compared by digest thereafter.
options.D: Scans are held solely at the central host rather than on the individual ATM units.

questions.explanation: Well-designed biometric systems never keep the picture: enrollment extracts a template, a mathematical summary of minutiae features, and matching compares fresh templates against it, so a stolen database yields feature vectors rather than reproducible fingerprint images, which is exactly the assurance the regulator asked for (B). A keeps the dangerous artifact and bets everything on key custody. Escrowed keys can be compelled, leaked, or stolen, and the moment they are, full images spill; escrow answers a lawful-recovery requirement, not a data-minimization one. C misapplies a password technique to fuzzy data: two scans of the same finger never match bit-for-bit, so cryptographic digests of images can never be compared successfully; the scheme simply does not function. D changes where the images sit, not whether they exist, and centralization may even raise the stakes by pooling every customer's biometric in one breachable place. Biometric privacy comes from storing derived, non-reversible templates; controls that merely encrypt or relocate raw images leave the irrevocable secret intact.
questions.recallLine: Regulators want assurance about what a breach of the planned fingerprint enrollment database would expose. Which property of a well-designed biometric system should the team cite?

optionsShort.A: Raw scans kept, encrypted under escrowed keys
optionsShort.B: Templates stored instead of images, not reversible
optionsShort.C: Images hashed with SHA-256 and compared by digest
optionsShort.D: Scans held centrally rather than on each unit

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Which design suits material that must stay recoverable in full by an authorized custodian?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which storage technique fits secrets that are compared exactly, bit for bit, such as passwords?

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Which change reduces the number of places from which enrollment data could be stolen?

questions.question: Holiday photos emailed to a personal account carried fragments of a key database in their pixel data. Which technique was used, and which gateway countermeasure would MOST likely disrupt it?

options.A: Encryption; quarantine outbound messages whose attachments show abnormally high entropy.
options.B: A covert timing channel; normalize the transmission intervals of outbound messages.
options.C: Digital watermarking; strip identifying metadata from images at the mail gateway.
options.D: Steganography; recompress or transform outbound images so hidden payloads are destroyed.

questions.explanation: Concealing data inside an innocuous carrier file so that the very existence of the message is hidden is steganography, and because pixel-level payloads rarely survive lossy recompression or resizing, transforming every outbound image is the countermeasure that breaks the channel without blocking legitimate mail (D). A misreads the evidence: encryption scrambles content but announces itself. An encrypted blob looks like noise, whereas these files still displayed as valid holiday photos; entropy quarantine is the right response when exfiltration uses encrypted archives. B names the wrong covert medium, since timing channels signal through when packets are sent, not through file contents, so interval normalization would leave the pixels untouched. C inverts the technology: watermarking embeds marks to assert ownership or trace copies, openly or invisibly, and stripping metadata removes EXIF fields rather than payloads woven into image data. Steganography defeats inspection by hiding existence, so effective countermeasures alter the carrier (recompress, resize, transcode) instead of searching the content.
questions.recallLine: Holiday photos emailed to a personal account carried key-database fragments in their pixel data. Which technique was used, and which gateway countermeasure MOST likely disrupts it?

optionsShort.A: Encryption; quarantine high-entropy outbound attachments
optionsShort.B: Covert timing channel; normalize transmission intervals
optionsShort.C: Watermarking; strip image metadata at the gateway
optionsShort.D: Steganography; recompress outbound images to destroy payloads

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which gateway rule catches an insider shipping data out inside an encrypted archive that looks like noise?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which countermeasure disrupts a channel that signals by varying when packets are sent rather than what they contain?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Which gateway step removes the EXIF fields that reveal where and when a photograph was taken?

questions.question: Which recommendation BEST reflects crime prevention through environmental design for the new sites?

options.A: Screen each ATM behind fencing and dense planting so customers enter their PINs shielded from onlookers.
options.B: Move the ATMs into interior corridors reachable only through staffed building entrances.
options.C: Rotate ATM placements every month so criminals cannot learn local traffic patterns.
options.D: Site the ATMs in open, well-lit locations with clear sightlines and steady natural foot traffic.

questions.explanation: CPTED's core levers are natural surveillance, natural access control, and territorial reinforcement: shaping the environment so ordinary people's presence and sightlines make crime feel observable and risky, which is precisely what open, well-lit, well-trafficked siting delivers for both the robber and the skimmer installer who needs unobserved minutes at the fascia (D). A applies a security instinct backwards. Concealment protects PIN privacy at the shoulder-surfing scale, but screening the whole machine creates the hidden workspace attackers want, defeating natural surveillance. B does reduce crime but through staffing and access control by personnel, which the stem explicitly set aside; it is the right answer where a guarded lobby already exists. C confuses environmental design with unpredictability tactics. Moving targets inconvenience customers, break accessibility planning, and offer no surveillance benefit once the new location is found. CPTED asks what the place itself makes easy: design for eyes on the asset, not for hiding it or garrisoning it.
questions.recallLine: City planners must site new walk-up machines to discourage skimmer installation and robbery without paying for guards. Which recommendation BEST reflects crime prevention through environmental design?

optionsShort.A: Fencing and dense planting screening each machine
optionsShort.B: Interior corridors reached through staffed building entrances
optionsShort.C: Rotate placements monthly to defeat pattern learning
optionsShort.D: Open, well-lit sites with sightlines and foot traffic

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which measure protects a customer's PIN entry from onlookers standing immediately behind them?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Where should machines go for an operator that already has a staffed lobby and will pay for personnel?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Which tactic frustrates an adversary who has learned the routine and timing of a fixed target?

questions.question: To stop one lost key exposing the whole estate again, which control should the operator implement FIRST?

options.A: Relocate the ATMs into bank branches where staff can keep the service panels under observation.
options.B: Fit each unit with a uniquely keyed or electronically credentialed lock that records every opening.
options.C: Add camera coverage of every unit and review the recorded footage after each service visit.
options.D: Engrave serialized asset identifiers on the panels so any tampering can be traced to a specific site.

questions.explanation: The root weakness is keying the whole fleet alike, which turns one stolen key into a master credential; the direct correction is per-unit or electronically managed locks (B), which also add the accountability of logged openings. A abandons the business model instead of fixing the control. Subway placement is the product, and relocation merely moves the exposure without removing the shared-key single point of failure; supervised placement is the right answer for a handful of very-high-value assets. C is detective, and the review happens after entry has already occurred; cameras are the right answer for investigating incidents and deterring casual tampering, not for stopping a keyed entry. D neither prevents nor detects an opening. Engraving supports inventory and forensics, and would be the right answer to an asset-tracking question. When a single shared secret protects many assets, diversify the secret before layering monitoring around it.
questions.recallLine: One stolen vendor key opened dozens of machines. Which control should the operator implement FIRST so a single lost key can never expose the estate again?

optionsShort.A: Relocate machines into branches under staff observation
optionsShort.B: Unique or credentialed lock per unit, openings logged
optionsShort.C: Cameras on every unit, footage reviewed afterwards
optionsShort.D: Serialized asset identifiers engraved on the panels

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Where should a handful of very-high-value machines sit when constant staff observation is affordable?

C.label: detective when preventive is asked
C.wouldAnswer: Which control supports investigating an incident and deterring casual tampering at an unattended machine?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which measure lets the operator trace a recovered panel back to the site it was taken from?

questions.question: Which power investment MOST reduces the chance that the claims platform loses supply during a long utility outage?

options.A: Bring in a second utility feed from a different substation on the far side.
options.B: Extend UPS autonomy at full load from ten minutes to thirty by adding batteries.
options.C: Load bank the generator and run automatic transfer switch tests on a fixed schedule.
options.D: Dual-cord each rack to two power distribution units drawing on separate UPS modules.

questions.explanation: The single feed is the visible weakness, but the design already has an answer to it, a generator with fuel under contract, and that answer has never been proven. A transfer switch that has not operated since installation, in front of a generator that has never carried load, is the failure a site discovers at minute eleven of an outage, so commissioning and periodic testing buys more availability per pound here than any new hardware. A removes the single point of failure at the utility and is the right spend where the outage history is long and the second substation is genuinely independent, yet it changes nothing if the transfer itself fails. B lengthens the bridge the UPS provides, which matters when outages are measured in minutes, but a longer bridge to a generator that will not start is still a bridge to nothing. D protects against a failed cord, breaker or distribution unit inside the hall, a different failure from loss of supply to the building. Test the link in the chain that has never run; untested redundancy is a plan, not a control.
questions.recallLine: A data hall has one utility feed and a 750 kVA generator never transfer-tested. Which power investment MOST reduces the chance of losing supply?

optionsShort.A: Second utility feed from another substation
optionsShort.B: Extend UPS autonomy to thirty minutes
optionsShort.C: Load bank and transfer-test the generator
optionsShort.D: Dual-cord racks to separate UPS modules

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: Which investment BEST protects a site whose sole substation feed fails repeatedly and whose generator is already commissioned and routinely tested?

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Which change BEST covers a site whose outages run under twenty minutes and which has no standby generator at all?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which arrangement BEST keeps a rack running when one power distribution unit or breaker inside the hall fails?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | PE-11 Emergency Power
NFPA 110 Standard for Emergency and Standby Power Systems | routine maintenance and operational testing
Uptime Institute Tier Standard: Topology | engine generator commissioning

questions.question: Which change MOST directly closes the path the testers used from one clinical workstation to another?

options.A: Give every workstation a unique local administrator password, rotated automatically by a managed solution.
options.B: Set a sixteen-character minimum on the shared local administrator password and rotate it quarterly.
options.C: Stop help desk staff from signing in to workstations with domain administrator credentials.
options.D: Deploy endpoint detection that alerts when a process reads credentials out of LSASS memory.

questions.explanation: Reuse is the mechanism. A hash lifted from the first machine authenticates to every other machine that shares the secret, so the change that ends the technique is to make the secret different everywhere and rotate it without a human touching it. B changes how hard the password is to guess, which is beside the point here: nobody guessed anything, the hash was replayed, and a sixteen-character shared secret replays exactly as well as an eight-character one; length matters when the attack is offline cracking. C is genuinely necessary and belongs in the same remediation plan, but it closes the escalation route from workstation to domain rather than the lateral route from workstation to workstation, and without it the testers would still hold eleven laboratories worth of endpoints. D would have shown the credential theft as it happened and is the right investment when the question is dwell time rather than reachability; detection does not remove the reachability that made one memory dump worth 4,200 machines. When a credential works in more than one place, the number of places it works is the control.
questions.recallLine: One local administrator password is shared by 4,200 workstations. Which change MOST directly closes the lateral path between those workstations?

optionsShort.A: Unique rotating local administrator password per workstation
optionsShort.B: Longer shared local administrator password, rotated quarterly
optionsShort.C: Stop domain admin logons on workstations
optionsShort.D: Alert on credential dumping from LSASS

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which change BEST protects a local administrator account whose password hash has been captured and is being cracked offline?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Which change BEST stops a hash stolen from a workstation from also being a domain administrator hash?

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Which control BEST shortens the time between an attacker dumping credentials on an endpoint and the security team noticing?

sources: MITRE ATT&CK | T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash
Microsoft | Mitigating Pass-the-Hash and Other Credential Theft, version 2
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 Authenticator Management

domains.title: Communication and Network Security
domains.caseStudy:
Domain 4 covers the design and protection of networks: the OSI and TCP/IP layers, secure protocols, VPNs, wireless and cellular links, and the components that carry data between systems that do not trust each other.

Case Study: The "AirLink" Cellular Intercept (IMSI Catcher Attack)

### Context

CityBank deployed portable "AirLink" ATMs to a major music festival. The machines reached the bank's processing center over 4G/LTE modems on a private APN. The network engineers judged the carrier's link encryption and the private APN sufficient, and did not configure an IPsec tunnel or application-layer TLS. The transaction messages travelled in clear text above the cellular layer.

### What went wrong

Criminals parked a rogue base station, an IMSI catcher, near the festival grounds and broadcast a stronger signal than the legitimate towers. The modems attached to it. The rogue station forced a downgrade from 4G, where the network and the device authenticate each other, to 2G GSM, where only the device authenticates. Now the attackers were the tower. They decrypted the 2G A5/1 stream, which has been practically broken for years, and read the application traffic underneath: customer track data and PIN blocks, captured in real time.

The white paper's section on network attacks covers this family: interception by a rogue device on the line, eavesdropping when the payload is not independently encrypted, and, one step further, modifying a host's "declined" into "approved" or impersonating the host outright, which is jackpotting by another route. It makes the same point the AirLink engineers missed: the value of sniffing depends entirely on whether TLS and a VPN are in place above the transport.

### What a practitioner does differently

Assume the carrier is hostile. Encrypt at the layer you control: an IPsec tunnel from modem to bank, and TLS 1.2 or later between the ATM application and the host with mutual certificate validation, so a spoofed host fails the handshake. Add a message authentication code to each transaction message; a forged approval then fails verification even if the tunnel is somehow breached. The white paper lists all three, TLS with mutual validation, VPN, and MACing, among its network controls.

Configure the modems for LTE only and disable 2G and 3G fallback. The default "stay connected at any cost" chose availability over integrity; for a cash dispenser, dropping the link is the safe failure. Monitor the modems for downgrade events and the host for response anomalies, and segment the festival fleet from the rest of the ATM network so a compromised unit is not a path inward, a risk the white paper calls out for any ATM connection.

### Outcome

The captured track data went to fraud. CityBank pulled the AirLink units, reissued the cards, and rebuilt the mobile ATM design with a tunnel, application TLS and LTE-only modems before the next event.

### What the exam tests

Expect questions on where encryption sits in the stack and why link encryption is not end-to-end encryption, on downgrade attacks and mutual authentication, on IPsec modes versus TLS, on wireless and cellular authentication, and on defense in depth as a network design principle rather than a slogan.

### Related reading

The bank in this scenario is a composite. The attack and the controls are documented in:

- [Technical Risks and Attack Vectors Targeting ATMs](https://portfolio.atmavailability.com/atm-technical-risks-white-paper.pdf), the sections on network attacks and on network security controls.
- [ATM Security Capability Maturity Worksheet](https://portfolio.atmavailability.com/atm-capability-maturity-worksheet.pdf), Domain 2, logical and network controls.
- [The four-part ATM security series on the ATM Availability blog](https://atmavailability.com/blog/).

stimuli.title: A tower that was not the carrier's
stimuli.text: CityBank deploys portable cash machines that reach its processing center over 4G modems. The network team relied on the carrier's link encryption and a private access point name, and configured neither IPsec nor TLS. At a music festival an attacker's rogue base station forced the modems down to 2G, broke the older link encryption and read cardholder track data in clear. The TLS-inspection and firewall infrastructure at the processing center observed nothing unusual throughout. Voice traffic on the same site links has separately become choppy every evening while bulk transfers run.

profile.environment: Machines on 4G modems · carrier link encryption only · no IPsec, no TLS
profile.state: Cardholder track data read in clear at a festival

stimuli.title: What the interception actually yielded
stimuli.text: CityBank's incident commander must classify an event for the regulator. During it a rogue base station relayed every transaction between the machines and the carrier network while silently recording cardholder data, and machine service was never interrupted. Privacy counsel wants to know what the attackers could have learned from subscriber identity captures alone, before any traffic was decrypted. An engineer on the review board claims an IPsec tunnel to the processing center would have prevented the incident entirely. Staff handhelds at the same site were separately found to have had contact lists retrieved over Bluetooth.

profile.environment: Rogue base station relaying live transactions · service never interrupted
profile.state: Event being classified for the regulator

stimuli.title: Reading the design file afterwards
stimuli.text: An auditor reopening CityBank's design file finds the original justification: the carrier's private access point name 'keeps the traffic private', so no further transit protection was configured. The bank also leases dark fiber between its two data centers, and the wide-area team argues that because the bank lights and operates that fiber itself, replication traffic across it can run unencrypted. A separate proposal would terminate an IPsec tunnel from each machine to the processing center. The mobile team must also cut the risk of further Bluetooth data theft from handhelds that still need Bluetooth for card sleds.

profile.environment: Private access point name relied on for confidentiality · dark fiber between data centers
profile.state: Original design justification under audit

stimuli.title: Naming the attack, and the ones like it
stimuli.text: Meridian Transit Authority is agreeing a threat taxonomy for its fare payment network before it reports to the board. In one event an interposed device sat between two endpoints, read live traffic and injected its own. Architects separately worry that a compromised public certificate authority could issue attackers a valid certificate for the processing center's hostname, letting a future rogue network impersonate it. A flat operations network of 500 devices suffers periodic slowdowns from legitimate broadcast traffic reaching every host. Mall security has reported someone parked outside a station for hours with a laptop and a roof antenna.

profile.organization: Meridian Transit Authority · fare payment network
profile.environment: Public concourse machines · certificate authorities outside the authority's control
profile.state: Threat taxonomy being agreed with the board

stimuli.title: What a switch changed
stimuli.text: A workshop at Meridian Transit Authority still connects its five diagnostic machines through an old Ethernet hub. Technicians complain transfers slow sharply when several are busy, and a consultant has shown that a sniffer on any hub port captures every station's traffic. When a technician patched a second uplink through a third switch to give the workshop a backup path, the same broadcast frames began circulating endlessly and the segment slowed to a crawl. Tap-to-pay readers are being added to the fare machines, and a risk workshop is weighing how much protection the short operating range gives.

profile.organization: Meridian Transit Authority · station equipment workshop
profile.environment: Old Ethernet hub still in service · access ports in meeting rooms · tap-to-pay readers planned
profile.state: Workshop upgrade being justified

stimuli.title: Loops, leases and broadcast
stimuli.text: A technician at Northfield Health patched a second uplink between two access switches through a third, creating a physical ring, and within seconds the campus network was unusable: switch processors pinned, the same broadcast frames circulating endlessly. The hospital centralizes its address assignment at headquarters, and when a newly routed ward segment came online its machines received no addresses at all, though the same laptops obtain leases immediately at headquarters and the link between the sites tests clean. Warehouse barcode scanners supporting only an obsolete wireless standard are still attached to a network that also carries clinical traffic.

profile.environment: Flat operations segment · DHCP centralized at headquarters · redundant uplinks patched by hand
profile.state: Outage during a change window

stimuli.title: Keeping the front door open under load
stimuli.text: Northfield Health's public web tier is under a flood of connection attempts from constantly shifting spoofed addresses: connection tables fill with half-open sessions and real patients time out. The team needs a mitigation that keeps accepting legitimate connections while the flood continues. An audit has separately found that a visitor can plug a laptop into any lobby network jack and receive an address on the corporate network, and a penetration test showed a laptop in a meeting room announcing itself as the default gateway and silently proxying other hosts' traffic. Access points in branches run a deprecated cipher for compatibility.

profile.environment: Public portal behind a perimeter firewall · access ports in public waiting areas
profile.state: SYN flood in progress

stimuli.title: Two ends of a tunnel
stimuli.text: Redcliff Bank is specifying two encrypted paths at once. The first joins a temporary operations trailer to the processing center: compliance requires that internal host addresses never appear on the carrier network, and a gateway at each end will terminate the cryptography for the hosts behind it. The second joins two application servers inside one data center that must exchange settlement files confidentially, terminate the cryptography themselves, and add as little packet overhead as possible. Branch wireless is moving to 802.1X with no client certificate infrastructure and none budgeted.

profile.environment: Festival operations trailer · data center application servers · branch wireless on 802.1X
profile.state: Two tunnels being specified at once

stimuli.title: Letting outsiders in, carefully
stimuli.text: Redcliff Bank must give external auditors access to three internal web applications. The auditors work from their own firms' locked-down laptops, on which no client software may be installed, and from office networks that commonly allow only web ports outbound. Separately, the bank's own administrators need to manage servers inside the card-processing enclave from the corporate network, and the architect requires every administrative session to pass through a single hardened, fully logged entry point protected by a second authentication factor. Two application servers must also exchange settlement files with minimal added overhead.

profile.environment: Auditors on their own locked-down laptops · card enclave management interfaces
profile.state: Access designs being approved

stimuli.title: Answers that were not the bank's
stimuli.text: Customers of Colville Savings are reporting certificate warnings on the online portal, and an analyst finds their queries for the portal's hostname returning an address in an attacker's netblock. The records on the bank's own authoritative name servers are verified unchanged and the registrar's delegation is intact. Elsewhere, the bank's internet gateway is being saturated by echo replies from hundreds of hosts inside a university network the bank never contacted, and the university reports its hosts each received requests appearing to come from the bank. A lobby audit found unauthenticated devices receiving corporate addresses.

profile.environment: Authoritative name servers verified unchanged · registrar delegation intact
profile.state: Customers seeing certificate warnings

stimuli.title: Proving an answer is genuine
stimuli.text: Colville Savings' architect must recommend a control that lets resolvers verify answers for the bank's zone are genuine and unmodified, wherever those answers were obtained. A marketing launch is separately expected to drive a fiftyfold traffic spike, plus probable volumetric attack attention, to a promotional site currently served from one origin data center, and the infrastructure team must keep it available without re-platforming that origin. At a small branch with no certificate infrastructure, staff have been attaching unmanaged mini-switches under desks to fan single wall jacks out to personal devices.

profile.environment: Zone signing under consideration · promotional site on one origin · unmanaged switches under desks
profile.state: Controls being recommended after the poisoning incident

stimuli.title: Handshakes worth capturing
stimuli.text: Fenwick Events is specifying the wireless build for its festival season. A prior assessment showed attackers in the crowd capturing the four-way handshakes of its shared-passphrase network and running offline dictionary attacks against the passphrase at leisure. In a lab reconstruction of a separate incident, testers captured a valid, fully encrypted withdrawal authorization and retransmitted it an hour later; the processing center accepted it and dispensed cash again. Administrators manage the site's routers and switches over an unencrypted protocol, with individual accounts on a central server.

profile.environment: Staff handhelds on a shared passphrase · crowd within radio range · replayed authorizations tested
profile.state: Wireless build being specified for the season

stimuli.title: Convenience features with a cost
stimuli.text: A wireless assessment of Fenwick Events' permanent offices finds consumer-grade access points with push-button setup enabled to make onboarding easier, and the assessor must state the risk accurately so the finding survives challenge. A configuration audit separately finds the routers and switches managed over an unencrypted terminal protocol, with a central server giving each administrator an individual account; the network team argues the per-administrator accounts make that acceptable. A red-team capture from one site showed telephony call-setup traffic readable in clear: dialled numbers, extensions and negotiated session parameters.

profile.organization: Fenwick Events · branch and site equipment
profile.environment: Consumer access points with push-button setup · voice on the site network · administrators on Telnet
profile.state: Assessment findings being written up

stimuli.title: A stronger transmitter in the crowd
stimuli.text: Fenwick Events' staff handhelds automatically join any network broadcasting the staff network name, and last season an attacker exploited exactly that with a stronger transmitter. Staff reported handhelds briefly dropping off, reconnecting by themselves, then showing certificate warnings, while a spectrum survey found a second network broadcasting the same name at higher power from the crowd area. A survey inside headquarters separately found an unlabeled consumer access point plugged into a wall jack behind a printer, broadcasting an open network bridged onto the corporate network. Recorded call audio was reassembled from a mirrored port.

profile.environment: Handhelds auto-joining any network with the staff name · unlabeled access point found on a jack
profile.state: Post-season review of wireless incidents

stimuli.title: Carrier promises and what they cover
stimuli.text: A carrier has assured Ravensworth Group that its label-switched service is 'a private network' on which encryption 'is unnecessary', and the group's architect must characterize what the service actually provides before anyone signs. The group runs 200 branches over a mixture of transports, each configured locally, and successive audits keep finding branch firewall and routing policies that have drifted from the corporate standard. A customer portal compromised through a plugin was contained by the design around it. Auditors need read access to firewall configurations for six weeks.

profile.environment: Label-switched carrier service on offer · voice and data sharing links · branch policies drifting
profile.state: Contract under review before signature

stimuli.title: Getting data out through the one open port
stimuli.text: Ravensworth Group's egress firewall permits outbound traffic only on the standard encrypted web port, and the security operations team had assumed this made bulk data theft impractical. A red team nonetheless exfiltrated a large test dataset in a single afternoon without raising any alert, and the team must explain the result. A wireless design document has separately come back from the architect with a note asking the author to specify which authentication method will actually be deployed rather than naming the framework. Domain machines have also begun failing authentication after a hypervisor migration left clocks drifting.

profile.environment: Egress firewall permitting outbound web only · directory-integrated wireless planned
profile.state: Red-team result under discussion

questions.question: Which statement BEST explains why controls higher in the stack had no visibility of the downgrade?

options.A: The radio negotiation happens at the data link and network layers of the cellular stack, below anything the center's application-layer controls can observe.
options.B: The downgrade messages were encrypted with the 2G A5/1 stream cipher, which the center's inspection devices could not decrypt quickly enough to raise an alarm.
options.C: The rogue base station silently discarded the ATMs' logging traffic before it could ever reach the processing center's collectors.
options.D: The modems' TLS sessions renegotiated automatically as the bearer changed, and the monitoring stack treated the renegotiation as a routine handshake rather than an alarm.

questions.explanation: Visibility follows the layer at which a control operates: the forced fallback was negotiated between modem and tower in the lower layers of the cellular stack, and nothing about it is ever presented to equipment inspecting application traffic at the far end. A explains the blindness structurally and would hold for any similar radio-layer attack. (B) misplaces the mechanism: A5/1 encrypts user traffic after the downgrade, and radio signaling between modem and tower never transits the center's inspection path at all; it would be a fair answer if the question were why over-the-air captures were unreadable to bystanders. (C) invents an action the attacker did not need; a relay that quietly forwards traffic is precisely why MITM interception is hard to spot. (D) fails on the facts of the case: the fleet had no TLS configured, which is what made the cleartext capture possible. An attack at layer N is invisible to controls that only see layer N+1's payloads, so monitoring must exist at the layer where the trust decision is made.
questions.recallLine: CityBank's TLS-inspection and firewall gear at the processing center saw nothing while the modems were forced onto 2G. Which statement BEST explains that blindness?

optionsShort.A: Radio negotiation sits below application-layer controls
optionsShort.B: A5/1 ciphertext outran the inspection devices
optionsShort.C: Rogue tower discarded the machines' logging traffic
optionsShort.D: Monitoring read TLS renegotiation as routine

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Why would a bystander capturing festival radio traffic off the air have found the user data unreadable at first?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Which attacker action would explain one machine's own log stream never arriving at the central collector?

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: What can hide a genuine bearer change on a fleet whose sessions really are wrapped in TLS?

questions.question: Which change would MOST directly restore call quality on the shared links?

options.A: Increasing the TCP window size on the replication servers so the nightly transfers complete sooner each evening.
options.B: Re-encoding the branch calls with a noticeably higher-bitrate audio codec to improve their perceived sound fidelity.
options.C: Enabling compression on the WAN links to reduce the total volume of traffic they must carry.
options.D: Applying quality-of-service policies so voice packets are queued and forwarded ahead of bulk transfer traffic.

questions.explanation: The symptom pair is diagnostic: bulk TCP transfers ride out congestion by retransmitting and reordering, so they 'complete without error', while real-time voice cannot wait for retransmission; every delayed or jittered packet is a gap the listener hears. The fix is therefore not more capacity arithmetic but scheduling: QoS classifies voice into a priority queue so it crosses the congested link with bounded delay and jitter while the replication absorbs the slack it tolerates so well; that is D. (A) does the opposite of helping: a larger window lets the transfers fill the path more aggressively, deepening the queues that voice is stuck behind; window tuning answers a throughput problem. (B) raises fidelity per packet while making the stream heavier and just as delayed: garbling here is loss and jitter, not codec quality. (C) buys some headroom at the cost of processing delay, and an already-compressed replication stream yields little, and nothing about compression protects voice at the moment of contention. Real-time traffic fails on latency and jitter, elastic traffic on throughput; when they share a link, priority queueing reconciles them.
questions.recallLine: Voice on CityBank's shared site links turns choppy every evening while bulk replication runs. Which change would MOST directly restore call quality?

optionsShort.A: Raise TCP window size on replication servers
optionsShort.B: Re-encode calls with a higher-bitrate codec
optionsShort.C: Compress the WAN links to cut volume
optionsShort.D: Queue voice ahead of bulk transfers

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which tuning change raises throughput for a long-haul bulk transfer that is not filling the bandwidth available to it?

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Which change improves how a call sounds when listeners describe the audio as thin on an uncongested link?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Which change stretches a link that is simply too small for the total volume of compressible traffic it carries?

questions.question: What is the MOST accurate account of what the attackers learned from the subscriber identity captures alone?

options.A: The cardholder PIN blocks queued up for onward transmission by each of the affected festival ATMs.
options.B: The contents of calls and data sessions that passed through the rogue base station while it operated.
options.C: The unique subscriber identity of each nearby SIM, letting individual devices be identified and tracked.
options.D: The street-level home addresses registered by the carrier against each captured subscriber account in its own records.

questions.explanation: An IMSI is the identifier a SIM presents to the network, and an IMSI catcher harvests exactly that: which subscriber identities are present, when, and where. That alone supports identification and movement tracking of everyone near the rogue tower, a privacy harm independent of any decryption, which is what counsel needs stated, so C. (A) confuses the identifier layer with the payload: PIN blocks are application data, obtainable only after the traffic itself was captured and read. It describes the later data-capture stage of this incident, not the IMSI harvest. (B) likewise requires interception and decryption of session content; capturing identities does not open the sessions. (D) reaches into the carrier's subscriber database, which the radio interface never transmits; an attacker would need a separate compromise of carrier records to get it. Identifiers leak presence and movement; metadata is a privacy breach in its own right, even when every payload stays sealed.
questions.recallLine: Privacy counsel asks what the rogue base station learned from subscriber identity captures alone, before any traffic was decrypted. Which account is MOST accurate?

optionsShort.A: Cardholder PIN blocks queued by festival machines
optionsShort.B: Contents of the calls and data sessions
optionsShort.C: Unique identity of every nearby SIM
optionsShort.D: Home addresses held against each subscriber account

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Which cardholder data became exposed once the relayed festival traffic had been captured and decrypted?

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: What does an interceptor obtain after breaking the link encryption on sessions relayed through a rogue tower?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: What would an attacker learn from compromising the carrier's own subscriber records rather than its radio interface?

questions.question: Which assessment of the engineer's IPsec claim is MOST accurate?

options.A: The tunnel would have stopped the rogue base station from forcing the modems down to 2G in the first place.
options.B: The interception would still have occurred, but the captured traffic would have been unreadable ciphertext instead of cardholder data.
options.C: IPsec's added overhead would have made transactions over a 2G link time out, so the ATMs would simply have gone offline.
options.D: The tunnel would have alerted the SOC as soon as the peer's identity could no longer be cryptographically verified.

questions.explanation: Encryption at a layer the bank controls changes what the attacker obtains, not whether the attacker can sit on the path: the rogue tower would still relay traffic, but every intercepted packet would be ESP ciphertext, so the loss event (cardholder data exposure) is averted even though the attack itself proceeds. That distinction is why B is the accurate assessment and why 'prevented entirely' overstates. (A) puts IPsec at the wrong layer: the downgrade is negotiated in the radio stack beneath the tunnel, which IPsec neither sees nor influences; refusing 2G fallback is a modem configuration, not a VPN feature. (C) is a performance guess, not a security property: IPsec's overhead is modest and 2G, while slow, carries small transaction messages. (D) misunderstands a relay MITM. The attacker forwards the IKE exchange untouched between the true endpoints, so peer authentication succeeds and no alarm exists to raise.
questions.recallLine: A review-board engineer claims an IPsec tunnel to the processing center would have prevented the machine interception entirely. Which assessment of that claim is MOST accurate?

optionsShort.A: Tunnel would have blocked the 2G downgrade
optionsShort.B: Interception proceeds, but yields only ciphertext
optionsShort.C: Overhead would time out 2G transactions
optionsShort.D: Tunnel would alert on peer-verification failure

A.label: not the decision-maker's
A.wouldAnswer: Which change would have kept the fleet off 2G altogether, a decision made in the radio stack beneath any tunnel?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which operational risk should a team weigh before adding tunnel overhead to a narrowband cellular bearer?

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: What would IPsec surface if the attacker terminated the tunnel itself and could not present the peer's authenticated identity?

questions.question: Which evaluation of the dark fiber argument is MOST accurate?

options.A: It holds: traffic on a point-to-point fiber that the bank alone lights is not realistically observable anywhere in transit.
options.B: It holds, provided the fiber's full physical route is inspected on a regular schedule for evidence of splices or taps.
options.C: It fails: dark fiber carries other tenants' wavelengths on the same strand, so their equipment can observe the bank's frames.
options.D: It fails: fiber can be tapped with minimal signal loss along uncontrolled ground, so traffic in transit still requires encryption.

questions.explanation: Leasing dark fiber buys exclusivity of the strand, not custody of the path: the glass runs through ducts, vaults and rights-of-way the bank neither owns nor watches, and optical taps (a bend coupler leaking a fraction of the light) extract traffic with losses small enough to hide in normal attenuation. Exclusive use therefore does not equal confidentiality, and encryption of data in transit remains required; D states why the argument fails. (A) mistakes a commercial arrangement for a physical guarantee: 'we light it' says who transmits, not who can listen along kilometres of accessible cable. (B) converts a preventive requirement into detective comfort: route inspections are periodic and taps are built to be unobtrusive, so the exposure window between visits is exactly what an attacker uses; inspection supplements encryption, it cannot substitute. (C) reaches the right verdict through the wrong facts. Sharing one strand via multiple wavelengths describes a lit/wavelength service; dark fiber is precisely the product where the strand is yours alone, so the stated reason is refutable and would sink the finding. Control of the endpoints is not control of the ground between them. Data crossing territory you cannot secure gets encrypted, whatever the contract says about the medium.
questions.recallLine: The wide-area team argues replication needs no encryption because the bank lights and operates the leased dark fiber itself. Which evaluation of that argument is MOST accurate?

optionsShort.A: Holds: nobody can observe fiber we light
optionsShort.B: Holds if the route is inspected regularly
optionsShort.C: Fails: other tenants share the strand's wavelengths
optionsShort.D: Fails: taps draw light with negligible loss

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: What does leasing a dark strand actually guarantee the bank about who else transmits over that glass?

B.label: detective when preventive is asked
B.wouldAnswer: Which practice raises the chance of eventually discovering a physical splice along a leased fiber route?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which exposure applies to a lit wavelength service where several tenants' channels ride the same strand?

questions.question: Which classification BEST fits what the interposed device did during that event?

options.A: A denial-of-service attack, because the ATMs were forced away from the legitimate 4G network they should have used.
options.B: A replay attack, because the transactions captured by the rogue station could be resubmitted at a later time.
options.C: An on-path (man-in-the-middle) attack, because the adversary sat between the endpoints and observed live traffic in transit.
options.D: An injection attack, because the rogue station inserted itself into the carrier's trusted infrastructure.

questions.explanation: Classification should follow the mechanism that caused the loss: an adversary interposed between two communicating parties, relaying their traffic while reading it, is the definition of an on-path/MITM attack, and the stem's details (full relay, silent recording, uninterrupted service) match it exactly, so C. (A) fixes on the forced network change but draws the wrong conclusion: availability was preserved throughout (deliberately, to keep victims transacting), so denial of service misstates the impact; it would fit if the rogue tower had attached the ATMs and then black-holed them. (B) names a real follow-on risk of holding captured transactions, but nothing was resubmitted during the event — replay is what the regulator would be told if duplicate withdrawals had been executed. (D) stretches 'injection', which denotes inserting crafted data into an application or protocol stream, not positioning a device in a path. A MITM's hallmark is service that keeps working while confidentiality quietly fails.
questions.recallLine: An interposed device relayed live traffic between the machines and the carrier while recording it, and service never faltered. Which classification BEST fits that event?

optionsShort.A: Denial of service: forced off legitimate 4G
optionsShort.B: Replay: captured transactions could be resubmitted
optionsShort.C: On-path: adversary sat between the endpoints
optionsShort.D: Injection: device inserted into trusted infrastructure

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: How would the event be classified if the rogue tower had attached the machines and then black-holed their traffic?

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: What would the regulator be told if the captured transactions had later been resubmitted as duplicate withdrawals?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Which term covers crafted data pushed into an application or protocol stream, rather than a device placed in a path?

questions.question: Which upgrade MOST directly addresses both the slowdowns and the sniffing, and why?

options.A: Replace the hub with a switch, giving each port its own collision domain and forwarding unicast frames to the destination port.
options.B: Replace the hub with a small router, so that every PC is placed into a separate IP subnet of its own.
options.C: Cascade a second hub off the first and split the PCs between the two devices, halving the shared load.
options.D: Upgrade to a faster hub, so the shared medium offers more headroom to every attached station.

questions.explanation: Both complaints have one cause: a hub is a shared medium that repeats every bit out of every port, so contention throttles throughput and every NIC in promiscuous mode hears everything. A switch fixes both with one change: per-port collision domains end the contention, and MAC-learned forwarding delivers unicast frames only where they belong, so a sniffer on another port sees broadcasts and its own traffic, no more; A resolves the cause itself. (B) would also isolate traffic, but at the wrong layer and cost: per-PC subnets add addressing and gateway complexity a five-PC workshop does not need. It is the right shape of answer when policy boundaries between segments are required, not connectivity. (C) misunderstands cascading; hubs joined to hubs still form one collision domain and one listening zone, so both problems survive intact. (D) buys speed for a medium that stays shared: contention scales down but persists, and the confidentiality exposure is untouched at any speed. Shared-medium problems, collisions and universal sniffing alike, are solved by switching to per-port forwarding, not by making the shared medium faster or more numerous.
questions.recallLine: A workshop's five diagnostic machines share an old Ethernet hub: transfers crawl when several are busy, and one port sniffs everyone. Which upgrade MOST directly fixes both?

optionsShort.A: Switch: per-port collisions, unicast forwarding
optionsShort.B: Small router, each PC its own subnet
optionsShort.C: Cascade a second hub, splitting the machines
optionsShort.D: Faster hub, more headroom for everyone

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Which design fits a workshop that needs enforced policy boundaries between segments, not merely private connectivity?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Which change adds ports for more workshop machines without altering how the shared medium behaves?

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Which upgrade raises raw throughput on a shared segment where confidentiality between stations does not matter?

questions.question: Which explanation BEST fits the ward segment receiving no addresses, and points to the standard fix?

options.A: The DHCP scope is exhausted, so the server has no addresses left to offer the branch clients; extend the pool.
options.B: The WAN provider is filtering the lease traffic somewhere in transit; request an exception for those flows.
options.C: The branch clients' requests carry addressing the server does not recognize; renumber the branch to match the server's scopes.
options.D: DHCP discovery is broadcast, and routers do not forward broadcasts; configure a relay agent on the branch router.

questions.explanation: The evidence isolates the variable: same clients, same server, success on the local LAN, failure across a routed boundary, healthy link. What changes across that boundary is broadcast reach: a client's DHCPDISCOVER is broadcast because the client has no address yet, and routers terminate broadcasts at the segment edge, so the plea for an address dies on the branch wire. The standard cure is a relay agent (IP helper) on the branch router, which converts the broadcast to a unicast aimed at the headquarters server; D explains the failure and names the fix, which is why relays exist in every centralized-DHCP design. (A) cannot survive the control case. An exhausted scope would refuse the same laptops at headquarters too, and exhaustion is a fault that appears under load, not precisely at a new segment's turn-up. (B) contradicts the clean bidirectional link test and, more basically, the traffic pattern: without a relay, no lease traffic enters the WAN to be filtered. (C) reverses DHCP's premise: clients request precisely because they have no addressing, and scope selection is driven by the relay's tagged source information. Protocols that begin from nothing must broadcast, and broadcasts stop at routers, so centralized services for such protocols work only through per-segment relays.
questions.recallLine: Machines on a newly routed ward segment get no addresses, though the same laptops lease instantly at headquarters and the link tests clean. Which explanation and fix BEST fit?

optionsShort.A: Scope exhausted; extend the address pool
optionsShort.B: Provider filters the traffic; request an exception
optionsShort.C: Client addressing unrecognized; renumber the ward
optionsShort.D: Routers drop broadcasts; add a relay agent

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Why would clients across the whole hospital start being refused leases during a busy morning?

B.label: not the decision-maker's
B.wouldAnswer: Which step fits a fault that transit filtering by the carrier has actually been shown to cause?

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Which fix applies when a segment's existing addressing falls outside every scope the server is configured to serve?

questions.question: A web server compromised through a plugin probed for a week without reaching the database. Which design property MOST directly accounts for the containment?

options.A: The inner screen permitted the web server one database port inward, so every other probe from it was dropped.
options.B: Address translation at the perimeter hid the internal numbering plan, leaving the attacker unable to identify any internal targets worth probing.
options.C: The portal host's hardening baseline had already removed the scanning and enumeration tooling an intruder would need to probe internal ranges.
options.D: The outer firewall's alerting brought the SOC in early, and its containment actions cut the probing short.

questions.explanation: The screened subnet earned its keep on the inward side: the architecture's premise is that exposed hosts will eventually fall, so the inner screen restricts what a fallen host may initiate (here, one database port to one destination), and a week of probing becomes a week of drops at a policy boundary the attacker cannot alter from the web server. That least-privilege egress from the DMZ is the property doing the containing; A. (B) overrates obscurity: translation hides numbering from the outside, but the attacker was inside the DMZ, learning real reachable addresses from the server's own configuration and its permitted database path. Concealment, unlike filtering, ends at first compromise. (C) is worthwhile friction that cannot carry the outcome: attackers bring or fetch tooling, and hardening the host does not constrain where its packets may go; the firewall does. (D) is contradicted by the timeline: a week of unimpeded probing is the opposite of early detection, and the stem credits design, not response. Measure a DMZ by its inner rules; the design succeeds when a compromised exposed host discovers that almost nothing inward will answer it.
questions.recallLine: A web server compromised through a plugin probed for a week without ever reaching the database. Which design property MOST directly accounts for the containment?

optionsShort.A: Inner screen permitted one port inward
optionsShort.B: Translation hid the internal numbering plan
optionsShort.C: Hardening had removed the enumeration tooling
optionsShort.D: Firewall alerting brought responders in early

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Which measure keeps an outside scanner from learning the internal addressing before any host has been compromised?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Which measure slows an intruder who would otherwise use whatever enumeration tooling the host already carries?

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: Which capability shortens an intrusion by pulling responders in while an exposed host is still being probed?

questions.question: A partner campus eighteen router hops away must reroute within seconds. Which limitation of the proposed distance-vector protocol MOST justifies rejecting it?

options.A: RIP carries its routing updates in cleartext, so route advertisements can be captured and read off the wire by listeners.
options.B: RIP treats 16 hops as unreachable and converges slowly, so both the 18-hop path and the recovery target fail.
options.C: RIP requires a backbone-area hierarchy to scale, which a merged campus network would struggle to support.
options.D: RIP floods complete topology maps on every change, consuming bandwidth on the WAN links between the merged sites.

questions.explanation: Relevance means the limitation that breaks the stated requirements, and RIP breaks both at once: its metric counts to 15, with 16 meaning unreachable, so an 18-hop destination is administratively nonexistent; and its periodic-update, distance-vector convergence takes minutes (with hold-downs), not the seconds required. B is the direct, two-count rejection. (A) is a real hygiene concern (RIPv2 supports authentication, and updates are observable), but confidentiality of advertisements is not among the requirements the proposal must meet, so it cannot carry the rejection. (C) belongs to the wrong protocol: the backbone-area design (area 0) is OSPF's architecture; RIP has no areas at all, and citing this hands the partner an easy rebuttal. (D) also describes the other family: flooding link-state advertisements to build topology maps is OSPF/IS-IS behavior, whereas RIP sends distance vectors, not maps. Reject a protocol on the requirements it measurably fails, for RIP its diameter (15 hops) and convergence time, and keep the failings of one protocol family from being pinned on the other.
questions.recallLine: A merged network must reach a segment eighteen router hops away and reroute within seconds. Which distance-vector limitation MOST justifies rejecting RIP?

optionsShort.A: Cleartext updates can be read off-wire
optionsShort.B: Sixteen means unreachable, and convergence crawls
optionsShort.C: Needs a backbone-area hierarchy to scale
optionsShort.D: Floods full topology maps on every change

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Which routing concern would matter if an eavesdropper on the WAN link were among the requirements to be met?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which scaling constraint would a reviewer raise against OSPF, whose design rests on a backbone area?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which behavior characterises the link-state family, which shares maps rather than distance vectors?
