questions.question: Users will authenticate with directory passwords that must stay protected over the air. Which method BEST fits?

options.A: EAP-TLS, mutually authenticating the client and the server with X.509 certificates issued to each side.
options.B: EAP-MD5, hashing the password exchange so the credential itself is not transmitted over the air.
options.C: LEAP, using a lightweight proprietary vendor challenge-response protocol designed specifically for early wireless deployments.
options.D: PEAP, opening a server-authenticated TLS tunnel and passing the password exchange inside it.

questions.explanation: The constraints are explicit (password authentication, no client PKI, credentials protected over the air), and PEAP is the method shaped to them: the client first validates the server's certificate and builds a TLS tunnel (one server-side certificate is the entire PKI bill), then runs the password exchange inside that encrypted, server-authenticated channel, so credentials neither travel exposed nor get offered to an impostor AP; D satisfies every stated condition. (A) is the stronger method and the wrong fit: mutual certificate authentication presupposes issuing and lifecycle-managing a certificate per client, exactly the PKI the stem rules out; it is the right answer the day that budget exists. (B) fails the transit requirement it pretends to meet: an unprotected challenge-response hash invites offline guessing, the method authenticates no server, and it yields no keying material for the wireless session. (C) is a broken legacy proprietary method whose challenge-response fell to practical cracking tools years ago, and choosing it re-imports the problem. When passwords must cross wireless, wrap them in a server-authenticated tunnel. Read constraints as hard requirements: the technically strongest method is wrong when it needs infrastructure the design cannot have.
questions.recallLine: Branch wireless is moving to 802.1X with directory passwords, no client certificate infrastructure and none budgeted. Which authentication method BEST protects those credentials over the air?

optionsShort.A: EAP-TLS: certificates issued to both sides
optionsShort.B: EAP-MD5: hashed challenge instead of password
optionsShort.C: LEAP: proprietary lightweight challenge-response
optionsShort.D: PEAP: password inside a server-authenticated tunnel

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: Which method becomes the strongest choice the day the bank can issue and manage a certificate per client?

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Which method merely keeps the literal password off the wire, with no server proof and no session keys?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which method did a vendor offer as a lightweight answer for early wireless, before tunneled standards existed?

questions.question: Which design BEST implements the single hardened entry point for enclave administration?

options.A: Firewall rules permitting SSH and RDP only from administrators' registered workstations to the enclave hosts.
options.B: A bastion (jump) host in a controlled segment, the only source permitted to reach enclave management interfaces.
options.C: Individual VPN profiles on administrator laptops, each terminating inside the enclave's server network.
options.D: A dedicated management VLAN trunked from the administrators' desk switches into the enclave switches.

questions.explanation: The architecture asked for is a choke point: one hardened system that every management session must traverse, where MFA is enforced once and session logging is complete. That is the definition of a bastion or jump host, made effective by firewall policy that admits management traffic from it alone; B implements the requirement rather than approximating it. (A) creates as many entry points as there are administrators: each workstation becomes an attack path into the enclave, MFA and logging must be replicated everywhere, and one compromised desktop reaches the servers directly. It is the pattern the requirement exists to eliminate. (C) also multiplies entry points, just tunneled: per-laptop VPNs terminate inside the enclave, so a stolen laptop carries the enclave with it, and sessions bypass any central recording. It suits remote access to a general network, not privileged access to an enclave. (D) extends Layer 2 adjacency across the boundary: a trunked VLAN is connectivity, not control, and offers no authentication or session capture at all. Privileged access wants concentration, one heavily instrumented door, because every additional path into a sensitive zone is a full copy of the risk.
questions.recallLine: Every administrative session into the card-processing enclave must cross one hardened, fully logged entry point behind a second factor. Which design BEST implements that requirement?

optionsShort.A: Firewall rules from administrators' registered workstations
optionsShort.B: Jump host, the only source permitted inward
optionsShort.C: Per-laptop VPN profiles terminating inside the enclave
optionsShort.D: Management VLAN trunked from desk switches inward

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Which approach suits an environment willing to treat every administrator's own desktop as a trusted entry path?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which control gives staff remote access to the general corporate network from laptops away from the office?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Which change simply gives the administrators' desks network reachability to the enclave's switches?

questions.question: Audits keep finding branch firewall and routing policies drifting from the corporate standard. Which capability MOST directly addresses that?

options.A: It replaces the branches' broadband and LTE circuits with uniformly provisioned MPLS.
options.B: It raises each branch's usable bandwidth by bonding whatever links the site has available.
options.C: It applies centrally defined policy to every branch edge device, independent of each site's underlying transport.
options.D: It encrypts traffic between branches using keys that each site's edge device manages for itself.

questions.explanation: The finding is configuration drift, 200 hand-tended devices diverging from standard, and the SD-WAN property that answers it is the separation of control plane from transport: policy is authored once in the orchestrator and pushed to every edge, so the architecture itself enforces the standard, with no reliance on 200 acts of local discipline, and an audit compares sites against one source of truth; that is C, and 'independent of transport' is what lets one policy span MPLS, broadband and LTE alike. (A) reverses SD-WAN's economics: the technology exists to use cheap heterogeneous links safely, not to standardize on the expensive one, and uniform circuits would not stop local config drift anyway. (B) is a genuine SD-WAN benefit aimed at a different complaint; more bandwidth fixes congestion findings, not policy findings. (D) undercuts itself in the second clause: SD-WAN does encrypt its overlay, but per-site self-managed keying is the decentralization the finding indicts; the value lies in central orchestration of the crypto too. Recurring drift across many sites is a management-plane problem; buy centralization of control, not more capacity or faster links.
questions.recallLine: Audits keep finding branch firewall and routing policies drifting from the corporate standard across 200 hand-tended edge devices. Which SD-WAN capability MOST directly addresses that finding?

optionsShort.A: Replace branch circuits with uniformly provisioned MPLS
optionsShort.B: Bond the site's links to raise bandwidth
optionsShort.C: Central policy to every edge, any transport
optionsShort.D: Encrypt between branches with locally managed keys

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Which change would give every branch an identically provisioned carrier circuit, whatever their configurations then say?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which SD-WAN benefit answers an audit finding about branch links running out of capacity at peak?

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: Which SD-WAN property protects branch-to-branch traffic as it crosses public broadband links?

questions.question: Which measure BEST keeps the promotional site available through the spike and the attack traffic?

options.A: Double the origin's web servers behind the existing load balancer ahead of the launch window.
options.B: Add a second internet circuit at the origin data center, roughly doubling the total ingress bandwidth available for the launch.
options.C: Set aggressive browser-caching headers, so returning visitors render the promotional pages from their own local caches.
options.D: Front the site with a content delivery network, serving cached content from edge locations near the traffic's sources.

questions.explanation: Fifty-fold plus a flood is a scale problem that a single origin cannot meet at the origin: a CDN answers it by moving the serving edge outward: promotional content is cached across many distributed points, each visitor is served nearby, and both the legitimate spike and volumetric attack traffic are spread across the provider's aggregate capacity instead of converging on one building. The origin keeps its architecture and sees a trickle of cache fills; D meets the availability goal within the no-re-platforming constraint, and static promotional content is the ideal cacheable workload. (A) buys 2x against 50x, and compute was never the choke point a volumetric flood aims at; the pipe is. (B) widens that pipe finitely while leaving every packet converging on one location; volumetric attacks are sized in multiples of any circuit pair. (C) helps only visitors who have already been served once, and launch traffic is first visits by definition, and attackers' tools ignore cache headers entirely. Availability at internet scale comes from distributing where demand is absorbed; capacity added at a single point is spent the moment the internet aims at it.
questions.recallLine: A fiftyfold spike plus probable volumetric attack is heading for a promotional site served from one origin that cannot be re-platformed. Which measure BEST keeps it available?

optionsShort.A: Double the origin's web servers before launch
optionsShort.B: Add a second circuit at the origin
optionsShort.C: Aggressive browser caching for returning visitors
optionsShort.D: Serve cached copies from edge locations nearby

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which change helps when the origin's own compute, not its connection, is what buckles under a launch?

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Which change helps a site whose peak demand slightly exceeds its present pipe and converges nowhere else?

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Which measure trims repeat load from visitors who have already fetched the promotional pages once?

questions.question: Packets shuttled between two misconfigured routers until a header field reached zero and an error returned. Which mechanism limited the damage?

options.A: The TCP retransmission timer, which bounds how long any unacknowledged segment stays in flight before the sending host finally gives up.
options.B: The fragmentation offset field, which forces malformed or oversized packets to be discarded at each hop along the forwarding path they traverse.
options.C: The IP time-to-live field, decremented at each router so that packets caught in forwarding loops are eventually discarded.
options.D: The Ethernet frame check sequence, which discards any frame whose contents were corrupted somewhere in transit between two directly adjacent devices.

questions.explanation: The capture narrates the mechanism: a field decreasing at each router, a discard when it runs out, and 'time exceeded' notifications. That is the IP TTL (hop limit in IPv6), a per-packet self-destruct decremented by every forwarding hop precisely so that a routing loop degrades into discarded packets and error messages instead of a link-saturating storm of immortal traffic. The mutual default routes made the loop; TTL made it survivable, and the same expiry mechanism is what traceroute exploits deliberately. C identifies both mechanism and purpose. (A) lives in the endpoints, not the path: retransmission timers govern when a sender tries again and cannot expire a packet already circling between routers; arguably they add traffic while the loop persists. (B) is a reassembly bookkeeping field; nothing about fragmentation offsets counts hops or expires looping datagrams. (D) checks integrity per link: the shuttling packets were perfectly intact, and corruption detection has no opinion about forwarding sanity. Networks assume routing will sometimes be wrong, so packets carry a hop budget. Recognize TTL expiry and 'time exceeded' backscatter as the visible signature of a loop being safely bled off.
questions.recallLine: Packets shuttled between two misconfigured routers until a header field reached zero and an error was returned to the sender. Which mechanism limited the damage?

optionsShort.A: TCP retransmission timer bounding unacknowledged segments
optionsShort.B: Fragmentation offset field discarding malformed packets
optionsShort.C: IP time-to-live, decremented at every hop
optionsShort.D: Ethernet frame check sequence catching corruption

A.label: not the decision-maker's
A.wouldAnswer: Which timer decides how long a sending host keeps waiting before it gives up on an unacknowledged segment?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which header field tells a receiver where each piece belongs when it rebuilds a fragmented datagram?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Which check catches a frame whose bits were corrupted on the wire between two directly adjacent devices?

questions.question: Which statement of the push-button setup risk is MOST accurate?

options.A: It weakens the encryption in use, forcing access points to fall back from AES to TKIP for all clients.
options.B: It broadcasts the network passphrase in cleartext during every new client association handshake, so anyone capturing the exchange can read it directly.
options.C: Its PIN can be brute-forced in hours because each half is validated separately, after which the passphrase is recoverable.
options.D: It lets joining clients bypass captive-portal authentication on nearby guest wireless networks that gate access through a web page.

questions.explanation: Findings survive challenge only when the mechanism is stated correctly: WPS's external-PIN design confirms the two halves of its eight-digit PIN independently, collapsing the search space to a few thousand tries per half, so an online brute force completes in hours and the protocol then hands over the network passphrase. C is the defensible statement and the reason 'disable WPS' is standard remediation. (A) invents a cipher interaction: WPS automates enrollment and has no effect on the AES/TKIP suite the AP negotiates; a reviewer who knows this discards the finding, the credibility failure the stem warns about. (B) also misstates the mechanism: the passphrase is delivered inside the WPS protocol exchange after PIN authentication, not broadcast in cleartext at each association; close enough to sound right, wrong enough to be challenged. (D) connects WPS to captive portals, which are unrelated web-layer gating on open networks.
questions.recallLine: Consumer access points in the offices have push-button setup enabled, and the finding must survive a vendor's challenge. Which statement of that risk is MOST accurate?

optionsShort.A: Forces a fallback from AES to TKIP
optionsShort.B: Broadcasts the passphrase at every association
optionsShort.C: PIN halves checked separately, passphrase then recoverable
optionsShort.D: Bypasses captive portals on nearby guest networks

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which finding would support a downgrade concern about the cipher suite an access point negotiates with clients?

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: At which point in the enrollment exchange is the network secret actually handed to the joining device?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Which weakness concerns open guest networks that gate access through a web login page?

questions.question: Which control MOST directly prevents an eavesdropper recovering conversation content from captured streams?

options.A: SIP over TLS, encrypting the call-setup channel between the handsets and the call servers.
options.B: SRTP, encrypting and authenticating the media streams that actually carry the audio.
options.C: Disabling port mirroring on branch switches except during approved troubleshooting windows.
options.D: Transcoding calls with a proprietary audio codec so captured streams resist casual decoding.

questions.explanation: The recovered artefact is audio, and audio travels in the media stream (RTP), separate from signaling; the control that makes a captured stream unplayable is SRTP, which encrypts and integrity-protects the media packets themselves, so a mirrored copy yields ciphertext wherever it was collected. B addresses the exact loss demonstrated. (A) is the complement, not the fix: TLS on SIP hides call metadata and protects key negotiation, but the audio packets it sets up still travel unencrypted if SRTP is off; it is the right answer to the previous finding, about readable signaling. (C) attacks one collection method rather than the exposure: mirroring is merely how this red team listened; taps, compromised switches, or any on-path position hear the same cleartext, and the control evaporates the moment an attacker can configure a switch. (D) is obscurity with a shelf life: codecs are identified from RTP headers and decoders are public or reversible; 'harder to decode' is not a confidentiality property. Protect the data, not the vantage point: if content is cleartext on the wire, somewhere to stand and listen will always exist.
questions.recallLine: Recorded call audio was reassembled from a mirrored switch port. Which control MOST directly prevents an eavesdropper recovering conversation content from captured streams?

optionsShort.A: SIP over TLS protecting the setup channel
optionsShort.B: SRTP encrypting and authenticating the media packets
optionsShort.C: Disable port mirroring outside approved windows
optionsShort.D: Transcode calls with a proprietary codec

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which control hides dialled numbers and extensions when a capture shows call setup in clear?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Which measure removes the particular vantage point this red team used to collect the packets?

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Which choice marginally raises the effort for a listener with no knowledge of the protocol in use?

questions.question: Which characterization of the label-switched service is MOST accurate?

options.A: MPLS encrypts each labeled packet between the provider's edge routers using carrier-managed keys.
options.B: MPLS separates customers' traffic using labels but applies no encryption, so confidentiality rests on trust in the provider.
options.C: MPLS wraps traffic in IPsec automatically whenever a label-switched path crosses the provider's shared core.
options.D: MPLS varies each packet's path through the core unpredictably, which makes interception impractical in the first place.

questions.explanation: MPLS is a forwarding technology: labels steer each customer's packets down its own label-switched paths and keep tenants' traffic logically separated across a shared core, but the payload rides exactly as submitted, cleartext in and cleartext through. 'Private' therefore means separated, and confidentiality reduces to trusting the provider's staff, equipment and interconnects; B gives the architect the accurate characterization, and the standard consequence follows: run IPsec or TLS over the MPLS service for data that matters. (A) asserts a cryptographic service that plain MPLS has no mechanism to perform; label operations are header manipulation, and no carrier keys touch the payload. (C) imagines a default that does not exist; IPsec over MPLS is precisely the customer-side overlay the accurate characterization leads to, never an automatic property of the carrier's LSPs. (D) inverts MPLS's behavior to manufacture comfort: traffic engineering makes paths deterministic along established LSPs, and in any case an observer at one traversed point reads everything regardless of route variety. Like the private APN before it, a carrier's 'private network' is a separation claim. Test it by asking who could read the payload, and encrypt at a layer you control when the answer includes anyone but you.
questions.recallLine: A carrier calls its label-switched service a private network on which encryption is unnecessary. Which characterization of what that service actually provides is MOST accurate?

optionsShort.A: Encrypts labeled packets with carrier-managed keys
optionsShort.B: Labels separate tenants; confidentiality rests on trust
optionsShort.C: Wraps traffic in IPsec across the core automatically
optionsShort.D: Unpredictable paths make interception impractical

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Which property would a carrier have to add above its label operations for the payload itself to be protected?

C.label: not the decision-maker's
C.wouldAnswer: Which overlay should the group itself run over the carrier service for traffic that matters?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Which comfort would varied routing give, if an interceptor genuinely had to sit on every possible path?

questions.question: Which explanation of the red team's result is MOST accurate?

options.A: The red team tunneled the data out inside TLS on the permitted port, indistinguishable at the firewall from ordinary encrypted web traffic.
options.B: The rule set must also have been permitting a second port, since one allowed port would not carry both browsing and exfiltration.
options.C: The red team split the dataset into small transfers spaced across many days, staying beneath volume-based alerting thresholds.
options.D: The red team routed the data out through the firewall's own management interface, which egress policy does not evaluate.

questions.explanation: A port-only egress policy asks one question, 'is this TCP to 443?', and an attacker's TLS tunnel answers it identically to a browser: the red team wrapped its exfiltration in encrypted traffic to a server it controlled, and at the firewall's level of inspection there is nothing to distinguish stolen gigabytes from a long video call; no rule was broken, which is why no alert fired. A explains the result and exposes the assumption: port filtering was treated as data-loss control, a job that needs TLS-inspecting proxies, egress destination reputation, or DLP with visibility into the tunnel. (B) misunderstands multiplexing: one permitted port carries unlimited concurrent sessions to unlimited destinations, and that generosity is exactly what the tunnel exploits. (C) proposes a real evasion technique that the stem's facts exclude: a single afternoon session is the opposite of low-and-slow, and no volume thresholds existed to duck. (D) invents a bypass with the wrong direction of risk: management interfaces are an attack surface for reaching the firewall, not a side channel exempting traffic through it. An allowed encrypted port is a tunnel anyone may use. Egress control by port number decides where traffic may go, and says nothing about what leaves inside it.
questions.recallLine: A red team moved a large dataset out through an egress firewall permitting only the standard encrypted web port, and nothing alerted. Which explanation is MOST accurate?

optionsShort.A: Tunneled inside TLS, indistinguishable from ordinary browsing
optionsShort.B: A second port must also have been permitted
optionsShort.C: Split into small transfers spread across days
optionsShort.D: Routed out through the firewall's management interface

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: What would have to be true for one permitted port to be unable to carry browsing and a bulk transfer together?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which technique defeats an egress monitor that alerts on unusual transfer volume rather than on ports?

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: Which interface is itself worth attacking as a way of reaching the firewall's own configuration?

questions.question: Which explanation BEST connects the clock drift to the authentication failures?

options.A: Kerberos rejects authenticators whose timestamps fall outside the permitted clock skew, a freshness check that keeps captured tickets from being replayed.
options.B: Kerberos derives its session keys from the current clock value, so drifted machines compute mismatched keys.
options.C: Ticket lifetimes are measured by the client alone, so a drifted client discards its own still-valid tickets before they have truly expired.
options.D: The domain controllers sign tickets with time-based one-time codes that drifted servers can no longer generate.

questions.explanation: Kerberos builds replay resistance out of time: each request carries an encrypted authenticator whose timestamp the verifier checks against its own clock, and anything outside the allowed skew (five minutes by convention) is refused as possibly re-sent. Twenty minutes of drift puts every honest authenticator outside that window, so authentication fails wholesale until the clocks agree. A ties the symptom to the mechanism and names the security purpose the check serves. (B) misplaces time in the cryptography: session keys come from the KDC's key distribution, encrypted under principal and service keys; the clock gates validity decisions, it is not key material. (C) has the arbiter wrong: lifetimes are stamped into the ticket by the KDC and enforced at validation; clients do not adjudicate their own tickets, and early self-discard would not produce server-side rejections. (D) imports TOTP, a different authentication family, into a protocol that uses plain timestamps within encrypted structures, not generated one-time codes. When authentication breaks in step with clock drift, you are watching an anti-replay freshness check do its job, which is why time synchronization is a security dependency, not an operational nicety.
questions.recallLine: Domain machines began failing authentication after a hypervisor migration left clocks drifting. Which explanation BEST connects the drift to the failures?

optionsShort.A: Authenticators outside the permitted skew are refused
optionsShort.B: Session keys are derived from the current clock
optionsShort.C: Clients judge their own tickets' lifetimes
optionsShort.D: Controllers sign tickets with time-based codes

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which part of the exchange would break if the clock really were an input to the cryptography rather than a check?

C.label: not the decision-maker's
C.wouldAnswer: Which party stamps a ticket's lifetime and enforces it, given that the holder does not adjudicate its own?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Which authentication family really does depend on both ends generating the same time-based code?

domains.title: Identity & Access Management (IAM)
domains.caseStudy:
Domain 5 is identification, authentication, authorization and accountability, applied to people, devices and services. It covers access control models, the identity lifecycle, federation, and privileged access.

Case Study: The "Omni-Key" Insider Threat

### Context

QuickCash Inc. operates 300 ATMs. To save time, the regional manager created one administrative account, "SuperAdmin", password "Welcome123!", and shared it among the five field technicians. The account had unrestricted rights on the ATM management console, including PIN resets and account limits. The physical master keys for the ATM safes lived in an unlocked desk drawer in the regional office, in an envelope labelled "ATM Keys".

### What went wrong

A technician who knew he was about to be dismissed logged in as SuperAdmin from home. There was no MFA. He created ten customer accounts with high withdrawal limits, took the master keys from the drawer, drove to five ATMs, put each into service mode with the shared key, and withdrew $200,000 in cash using the accounts he had made.

The logs showed SuperAdmin logging in and SuperAdmin creating accounts. Five people could have been SuperAdmin. QuickCash could not prove which one until the cash was gone.

The white paper's access-management controls read like a list of what QuickCash lacked: MFA for technicians, administrators and any remote access; role-based access limiting each user to the minimum their job needs; default and shared passwords replaced. Its physical controls add key management and unique locks, and it notes that attackers installing malware may pose as technicians precisely because a technician's access is rarely questioned.

### What a practitioner does differently

One identity per person, always. Privileged access goes through a PAM system: the technician checks out a time-limited credential for a named task, the session is recorded, and the credential expires. MFA on every remote and privileged path. Roles split by job: a field technician gets service-mode rights on assigned machines, not console administration; account creation and limit changes belong to a separate role, and setting a limit above a threshold needs a second approver. That is separation of duties, and it would have stopped the fake accounts on the first day.

The leaver process starts when the decision to dismiss is made, before the employee is told. Access ends with the decision, not with the exit interview.

Physical keys are credentials. They live in a key cabinet with a log, under dual control, and a machine entering service mode outside a scheduled ticket raises an alert. The white paper's monitoring section lists exactly the transaction signals that would have fired here: rapid maximum withdrawals and unusual frequency from a single card.

### Outcome

The technician was identified from the ATM's camera, not from the logs. QuickCash retired the shared account, issued individual credentials with MFA, moved the keys into a controlled cabinet, and rewrote its termination procedure so revocation precedes notification.

### What the exam tests

Scenarios like this test IAAA and non-repudiation (shared accounts destroy accountability), least privilege and separation of duties, the account lifecycle and why deprovisioning is time-critical, the access control models and where RBAC fits, the factor types behind MFA, and the idea that physical access is part of identity management, not a separate concern.

### Related reading

The company in this scenario is a composite. The controls are documented in:

- [Technical Risks and Attack Vectors Targeting ATMs](https://portfolio.atmavailability.com/atm-technical-risks-white-paper.pdf), the sections on access management, on physical security controls (key management), and on monitoring.
- [ATM Security Capability Maturity Worksheet](https://portfolio.atmavailability.com/atm-capability-maturity-worksheet.pdf), Domain 1 (physical) and Domain 4 (process and governance) controls.

stimuli.title: QuickCash: after SuperAdmin
stimuli.text: QuickCash Inc runs 300 ATMs with five field technicians who once shared a single 'SuperAdmin' account, until one of them used it from home to create fake customer accounts. The shared account is gone, every technician now has a named identity, and the company is rebuilding around that. Its directory runs on two domain controllers in the regional office, and the ATM management console authenticates against them. The board has bought a cloud service desk and a cloud expense tool, and both want their own logins. The five field technicians need administrative rights on the console, but only while a work order is open. The regional manager who created SuperAdmin still signs off every access request. The next audit closes in eight weeks.

profile.organization: QuickCash Inc · 300 ATMs, five field technicians
profile.environment: Two on-premises domain controllers · ATM management console · two new cloud applications
profile.state: Eight weeks to audit, access model half rebuilt

stimuli.title: One account, five people
stimuli.text: QuickCash Inc's five field technicians share a single administrative account on the machine management console. One of them used it from a home computer to create fake customer records and withdraw $200,000. The logs show only that the shared account logged in from a residential address, and no individual can be tied to any transaction. The security manager has budget for one change this quarter and must choose. The console accepted the login on the shared password alone, from a machine nobody had ever seen before, at a time nobody was rostered.

profile.regime: PCI DSS · state money transmitter license
profile.environment: Five field technicians sharing one console account · remote access permitted from anywhere
profile.state: $200,000 taken, nobody can be charged

stimuli.title: Why a shared superuser was wrong before anyone misused it
stimuli.text: Presenting a post-mortem to QuickCash Inc's board, the chief information security officer is asked why a single shared administrative design was dangerous even before anyone misused it. The board also wants to know why nobody noticed that an employee who had transferred departments three times in five years could approve invoices, modify vendor master records and view payroll, a combination no current duty requires. Elsewhere the company has rolled out app-generated time-based codes as a second factor on webmail, after employees typed passwords into lookalike login pages, and wants to know what still gets through.

profile.organization: QuickCash Inc · board and audit committee
profile.environment: Shared administrative credential retired · entitlements never recertified
profile.state: Post-mortem presented to the board

stimuli.title: What actually counts as two factors
stimuli.text: An auditor at Ardleigh Bank is reviewing a proposed console login upgrade, which the bank's own standard requires to be genuine multi-factor authentication, and several of the combinations offered are not. The bank is separately comparing three fingerprint products whose vendors each quote impressive numbers measured at different threshold settings, one boasting the fewest false accepts and another the fewest rejects. Its help desk currently resets any password for a caller who can state the employee's birthday and manager's name, details attackers routinely harvest. Forty applications have just been consolidated behind one sign-on portal.

profile.environment: Console login upgrade under audit · three fingerprint products shortlisted
profile.state: Auditor reviewing the proposal

stimuli.title: Forging tickets and stealing hashes
stimuli.text: A red team at Ardleigh Bank has demonstrated that compromising one component of its Kerberos realm would let them forge ticket-granting tickets for any principal and impersonate anyone to any service. An earlier incident report describes an attacker who gained administrator rights on one workstation, extracted the local administrator hash and authenticated to two hundred other workstations with it directly, cracking nothing. Field staff in areas with unreliable mobile coverage need a second factor, and company policy bars personal phones from work use. Attackers published ninety percent of a stolen password table within hours.

profile.organization: Ardleigh Bank · directory and endpoint security
profile.environment: Kerberos realm across three sites · local administrator password identical estate-wide
profile.state: Red team engagement in progress

stimuli.title: Choosing how the machine decides
stimuli.text: Brackley Retail Group has heavy seasonal turnover and wants store associates' access created and removed automatically from HR job codes, so every cashier receives an identical, pre-approved bundle of permissions on day one. A review of the outgoing platform found that store managers had accumulated rights far beyond their duties, because every technician on the old console held full administrative powers regardless of what the job required. Millions of login attempts are arriving daily across thousands of usernames, one or two password tries each, from a rotating botnet, and many pairs match a recent third-party breach dump.

profile.environment: Heavy seasonal turnover · store associate accounts created from HR job codes
profile.state: Access model being selected for the new platform

stimuli.title: Letting a partner in without a password
stimuli.text: Brackley Retail Group wants employees to open a partner-hosted benefits portal from their browsers using their existing corporate directory logins, with the partner receiving no corporate passwords at any point, and the architecture board must pick the standard designed for exactly that. Its own directory is centralized for network access, and an engineer must centralize wireless and remote-access authentication so every connection attempt is validated against it with per-session accounting captured for chargeback. Employee representatives have objected to a proposed eye-based biometric on the grounds that scans could reveal medical conditions to the employer.

profile.environment: Partner-hosted benefits portal · corporate directory as identity provider
profile.state: Federation design being chosen

stimuli.title: Tokens, clocks and what a token proves
stimuli.text: Help-desk tickets at Kelvin Mutual spiked after a hypervisor migration: every six-digit code from users' authenticator apps is rejected by one of the two authentication servers while the same codes validate against its peer. The platform team must also settle how device administration is authenticated, wanting every typed command individually authorized against the operator's profile with the whole exchange encrypted. A consumer web application has separately been found treating possession of a bare access token as proof of identity: any valid token presented to the interface logs that bearer in as the user.

profile.environment: Two authentication servers behind a load balancer · one migrated to a new hypervisor
profile.state: Help-desk tickets spiking after a migration

stimuli.title: Labels, owners and rules
stimuli.text: Thorne Defense Systems is implementing a document system that must enforce government classification markings, with the operating system imposing every access decision so that no file owner can override or reclassify on their own authority. An auditor has separately found that spreadsheets holding cardholder data on a Windows file share were readable company-wide because their creators granted everyone read access on their own initiative. A shoulder-surfing concern has been raised about which of two token types leaves a glimpsed code useful for the shortest time, and a portal locks accounts after three failed logins.

profile.environment: Operating system enforces classification markings · file shares with owner-set permissions
profile.state: Two access models being compared

stimuli.title: Deciding on more than who you are
stimuli.text: Thorne Defense Systems wants console sessions permitted only when a technician connects from the corporate network, during a scheduled maintenance window, from a managed laptop that passes a patch-level check, and the policy engine must evaluate all of those together. The company is also moving domain logons to smart cards so that initial authentication uses certificate-based public key cryptography rather than a password-derived key. A consumer site already enforcing a second factor is receiving millions of automated credential-stuffing attempts daily from rotating residential proxies, and genuine login latency is degrading.

profile.environment: Console sessions restricted by network, time window and device posture
profile.state: Policy engine being specified

stimuli.title: Keys, cabinets and standing privilege
stimuli.text: Dunmore Cash Services keeps its safe master keys in an unlocked drawer that any office visitor could reach, and must bring physical key handling into line with the way it now controls logical access. It is evaluating privileged access management platforms, having found that anonymous use of a shared administrative account destroyed accountability. Its service desk provisions new hires by copying the account of a colleague on the same team, including group memberships that colleague accumulated over years. A benefits portal is separately being federated to a partner using browser-based assertions.

profile.organization: Dunmore Cash Services · vault and console operations
profile.environment: Safe master keys in an unlocked drawer · privileged access platform being evaluated
profile.state: Physical and logical key handling under review

stimuli.title: Two people, two halves
stimuli.text: Dunmore Cash Services requires that its safes open only under dual control, and the redesign has to satisfy that principle genuinely rather than in name. A separate vault combination is split so that each of two senior officers memorises only half, and policy forbids either from ever learning the other. An application security review has found a portal authenticating users by simple bind to the corporate directory over an unprotected port, sending every username and password across the data-center network in clear. A bookkeeper has declined leave for four years.

profile.state: Dual control being formalised

stimuli.title: One person who knows how it works
stimuli.text: An operations review at Dunmore Cash Services finds that a single administrator is the only person who understands the payment batch system, and auditors add that this concentration has let unexplained adjustments go unchallenged for years. A review of the monitoring software's service account separately finds it holds domain administrator rights, with login records showing technicians signing in with it interactively for day-to-day troubleshooting. The company is migrating workforce authentication to a cloud identity provider, and investigators have reconstructed how fabricated customer records with inflated limits were entered before any withdrawal was made.

stimuli.title: Oakhaven and the fall intake
stimuli.text: Oakhaven Claims Services settles auto claims for eleven insurers and hires 400 seasonal adjusters each fall, most of whom never visit an office. Recruiting collects a scanned driver's license by email and a manager's word that the person exists; a directory account and a laptop follow within a day. Adjusters sign in to the claims platform through Oakhaven's own identity provider, and three of the eleven insurers accept that assertion to open their portals. Team membership is copied from whichever adjuster the new hire is said to resemble. Two adjusters promoted to fraud review in March still hold the payment-release right they carried as adjusters. The fall intake starts in five weeks.

stimuli.title: Saltmarsh turns on the access gateway
stimuli.text: Saltmarsh Securities runs an online brokerage for 90,000 retail customers and 340 staff. stimuli.title: Kentmere and the identities that are not people
stimuli.text: Kentmere Utilities meters 210,000 homes and equips 900 field crew with rugged tablets that read meters over Bluetooth and sync to the billing platform each evening. Any tablet presenting a valid crew password syncs, whether or not it is one of the 900. The customer mobile app authenticates to the same billing API with a key compiled into the app, and that key has been unchanged for three years. Overnight, a meter-data service pulls consumption records using a static API key held in a scheduled task, and the account behind that key has full read and write access to the billing database. Nobody at Kentmere can say which team owns the account.

questions.question: The console is reachable from any office workstation and from the technicians' home connections. Which change BEST treats the console itself, rather than its accounts, as the protected asset?

options.A: Requiring a second authentication factor from every technician who signs in to the console.
options.B: Reviewing the console's account list each quarter and removing accounts no longer needed.
options.C: Admitting console sessions through one managed access point that mediates and records them.
options.D: Encrypting console session traffic so credentials stay unreadable on the office network.

questions.explanation: Accounts and systems are different asset classes and they fail differently. Everything in options A, B and D improves who may hold a credential or what happens to it in flight, and none of them changes the fact that the console answers from anywhere. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-17(3) Remote Access | Managed Access Control Points requires remote access to be routed through a defined number of managed network access control points, and AC-3 Access Enforcement puts the enforcement in the system rather than at its edge. A single mediated path is also the only arrangement that produces one place to watch. A is the right control for a different problem, strengthening the authentication event the stem deliberately sets aside. B is detective when preventive is asked, finding a stale account a quarter after it stopped being needed. D is wrong scope, protecting the traffic rather than the set of places the system will answer. Ask what the asset is before choosing the control.
questions.recallLine: An administration console answers from anywhere. What treats the console, not its accounts, as the asset?

optionsShort.A: Second factor for technicians
optionsShort.B: Quarterly account list review
optionsShort.C: One managed access point for sessions
optionsShort.D: Encrypt console session traffic

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: What raises the cost of using a technician's stolen password?

B.label: detective when preventive is asked
B.wouldAnswer: How does QuickCash find accounts that outlived the person or the job?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: What stops someone on the office network reading a console session in transit?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-17(3) Remote Access | Managed Access Control Points
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 Access Enforcement

questions.question: QuickCash wants staff to sign in to the two cloud applications with their existing directory accounts, and the directory will stay in the regional office. Which element MOST determines whether that federation is trustworthy?

options.A: Whether the identity provider runs on the firm's own hardware or on a hosted platform.
options.B: Whether the assertion travels over a channel encrypted end to end between the parties.
options.C: Whether each application can read the full set of attributes held in the directory.
options.D: Whether the terms each party is trusted for are agreed and documented before the first sign-in.

questions.explanation: Federation is a transfer of belief, and what makes it safe is that both sides have written down what they are believing. NIST SP 800-63C-4 Section 3.5 Trust Agreements states that all federation transactions shall be governed by the terms of one or more trust agreements between the applicable parties, and it enumerates the relationships those terms cover, including what the relying party trusts the identity provider to represent and what the identity provider trusts the relying party to do with the attributes released. Section 3.2 defines the roles the agreement binds. One useful caution: SP 800-63C-4's own two models are general-purpose identity providers and subscriber-controlled wallets, at Section 3.1. The on-premise, cloud and hybrid split is the exam outline's deployment framing, and the trust-agreement obligation is identical wherever the provider runs. A is symptom not cause, because location decides who operates the provider, not whether the trust was ever established. B is the right control for a different problem: a well-protected assertion from an untrusted issuer is still untrusted. C is wrong scope, one clause inside the agreement and, released in full, a bad one. Write down what you are trusting.
questions.recallLine: Staff will sign in to cloud applications using an on-premises directory. What most determines trustworthiness?

optionsShort.A: Own hardware or hosted platform
optionsShort.B: End-to-end encrypted assertion channel
optionsShort.C: Applications read all directory attributes
optionsShort.D: Documented trust agreement terms first

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: What changes about operational responsibility when an identity provider moves to a hosted platform?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: What protects an assertion from disclosure or tampering while it is in transit?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: What should a trust agreement say about which attributes may be released to which relying party?

sources: NIST SP 800-63C-4 | Section 3.5 Trust Agreements; Section 3.2 Roles; Section 3.1 Federation Models
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-8 Identification and Authentication (Non-Organizational Users); SA-9 External System Services

questions.question: QuickCash's card-data extract is copied nightly from the console to an analyst's laptop, then into a spreadsheet on a shared drive. Access is controlled separately on each of the three systems. Which control BEST protects the information itself as it moves?

options.A: Requiring the same group membership on all three systems before access is granted.
options.B: Encrypting each system's storage so the extract is unreadable if a disk is removed.
options.C: Labeling the extract and enforcing flow rules that follow the label between systems.
options.D: Reviewing the three systems' access lists on the same quarterly cycle.

questions.explanation: Three well-controlled systems can still add up to an uncontrolled dataset, because the extract loses its protection at every boundary and reacquires whatever the next system happens to grant. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-4 Information Flow Enforcement requires approved authorizations to be enforced for controlling the flow of information within the system and between connected systems, and AC-16 Security and Privacy Attributes provides the binding that makes it possible, associating attributes with information and enforcing decisions on the basis of them. Together they are the catalog's answer to information as an access-control asset class, distinct from the system-by-system enforcement in AC-3. A is wrong scope, harmonizing three per-system decisions while the data still crosses unattended. B is the right control for a different problem, protecting media at rest rather than a copy in motion. D is detective when preventive is asked, and it looks at who may reach each system rather than where the data went. Control the data, not only the doors.
questions.recallLine: A card-data extract crosses three separately controlled systems. What protects the information itself?

optionsShort.A: Same groups on all three systems
optionsShort.B: Encrypt storage on each system
optionsShort.C: Label the data, enforce flow rules
optionsShort.D: Aligned quarterly access reviews

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: How does the firm keep one person's entitlements consistent across three systems?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: What protects the extract if a laptop or a drive leaves the building?

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: How does the firm confirm periodically that only the right people can reach each system?
