NIST SP 800-115 | Chapter 8 Post-Testing Activities

questions.question: Which gap in the testing program MOST directly allowed the flaw to reach production?

options.A: The team skipped regression testing, so a previously fixed defect returned unnoticed.
options.B: The team skipped unit testing, so individual functions went unverified in isolation.
options.C: The team performed happy-path tests and left invalid or hostile input untried.
options.D: The team skipped load testing, so behavior under peak transaction volume was unknown.

questions.explanation: Valid deposits were tested and worked; what no one exercised was invalid input: an amount outside the legitimate range. That is negative (edge-case) testing, and its absence is what C identifies. A is wrong because regression testing guards previously working behavior against new changes; this flaw existed from the first release, so nothing regressed. B is wrong because unit tests verify the behavior developers specified. The specification itself omitted invalid amounts, so unit tests written to it would have passed the flaw too. D is wrong because load testing addresses volume and concurrency, and this defect appears at any transaction rate. Happy-path success says nothing about how software treats input it was never meant to receive.
questions.recallLine: FinCorp's deposit feature accepted a check amount of minus one hundred. Which testing-program gap MOST directly allowed that flaw to reach production?

optionsShort.A: Skipped regression testing, a fixed defect returned
optionsShort.B: Skipped unit testing, functions unverified in isolation
optionsShort.C: Happy-path tests, hostile input untried
optionsShort.D: Skipped load testing, peak-volume behavior unknown

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which testing practice catches a previously fixed defect that a later code change quietly reintroduces?

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Which testing level verifies that one function behaves as its developers specified, isolated from the rest of the application?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which testing practice reveals how the deposit feature behaves once transaction volume reaches its peak?

questions.question: Which term BEST describes the portal engagement as directed?

options.A: A white-box engagement, since testers can observe every response the portal returns.
options.B: A black-box engagement, since testers start with no internal knowledge of the target.
options.C: A gray-box engagement, since the public URL constitutes a grant of partial internal knowledge.
options.D: A design review, since the portal's exposed interface reveals its architecture.

questions.explanation: The testers begin with zero internal knowledge, public URL only, which is what the classification turns on: black-box, option B, chosen precisely to reproduce an uninformed external attacker's view. A is wrong because white-box means testers are given internals such as source code and architecture; observable responses are available to any attacker and confer no inside knowledge. C is wrong because gray-box implies deliberately granted partial internals, such as a user account or diagrams; a public URL is available to everyone and grants nothing. D is wrong because a design review evaluates documentation, not a live target, and no documentation was provided. Classify tests by what the testers are given, never by what they manage to discover.
questions.recallLine: Testers of Kingsmere's customer portal receive only the public address, with no credentials, diagrams or code. Which term BEST describes the engagement?

optionsShort.A: White-box, since every response is observable
optionsShort.B: Black-box, since testers begin with nothing internal
optionsShort.C: Gray-box, since a public URL grants partial knowledge
optionsShort.D: Design review, since the interface reveals architecture

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: What is the term for an engagement in which testers are handed source code and architecture diagrams?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: What describes a test where the insurer deliberately gives testers a user account or a network diagram?

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Which assessment evaluates documented architecture rather than probing a live system for exploitable weaknesses?

questions.question: What issue does that server sitting unassessed for months illustrate?

options.A: A false positive: the scanner reported findings that did not actually exist.
options.B: A false negative: the scanner examined the server but failed to recognize the flaws present.
options.C: A true negative: the scanner correctly determined the server was not vulnerable.
options.D: A coverage gap: the server was outside scan scope, so no result exists for it.

questions.explanation: A result can only be true or false if the control actually examined the target. This server was removed from scope, so the scanner produced no result about it at all: a coverage gap, option D, which clean-looking reports then concealed. A is wrong because a false positive is a reported finding that turns out to be untrue; nothing was reported here. B is wrong because a false negative requires the scanner to have tested the server and missed the flaw. It never tested it. C is wrong because a true negative is a correct determination of no vulnerability, and no determination occurred. Scope errors are silent: validate what a scan covered before trusting what it concluded.
questions.recallLine: A firewall change dropped a new application server's subnet from the scanner's target list for months. What issue does the episode illustrate?

optionsShort.A: False positive: findings reported that did not exist
optionsShort.B: False negative: server tested, its flaws missed
optionsShort.C: True negative: server correctly judged not vulnerable
optionsShort.D: Coverage gap: server unscanned, so no result

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: What term applies when a scanner flags a critical injection flaw the application team proves cannot be triggered?

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: What term fits a real flaw sitting in a function the assessment did exercise and still declared clean?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: What describes a scan that examined a host and correctly concluded the weakness was not present?

questions.question: How should the injection finding be classified, given the retest?

options.A: A true positive that must remain open until the vendor confirms the patch.
options.B: A false negative that indicates the scanner's plugins are out of date.
options.C: A false positive: the scanner alerted on a vulnerability that is not present.
options.D: A true negative, reflecting the parameter's correct, safe, and verified implementation.

questions.explanation: The tool asserted a vulnerability; independent verification, specifically the parameterized code plus a failed manual proof-of-concept, shows the assertion was wrong. An alert on a condition that is absent is a false positive, option C. A is wrong because a true positive requires the flaw to actually exist, and the retest demonstrates it does not. B is wrong because a false negative is the mirror image: a real flaw the tool missed. Plugin currency has nothing to do with over-reporting. D is wrong because a true negative would mean the scanner correctly reported the parameter clean; it reported the opposite. Classify results on two axes: what the tool said, and what is actually true.
questions.recallLine: A scanner flagged a critical injection flaw that parameterised code and a failed manual proof-of-concept both refute. How should the finding be classified?

optionsShort.A: True positive, open until the vendor patches
optionsShort.B: False negative, showing plugins are out of date
optionsShort.C: False positive: alerted on an absent vulnerability
optionsShort.D: True negative, reflecting a safe verified implementation

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: What is the term for a tool alert that manual verification confirms is a genuine, exploitable weakness?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which classification fits a real flaw the tool examined and passed because its feed carried no check for it?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: What term applies when the tool examines a safe parameter and correctly reports nothing wrong with it?

questions.question: How should the weekly log review be categorized in the framework?

options.A: Detective, because it identifies security events after they have taken place.
options.B: Preventive, because publicizing the review deters would-be insiders from attempting fraudulent transactions.
options.C: Corrective, because reviewers restore the accounts affected by fraudulent activity.
options.D: Compensating, because it substitutes for transaction controls Ravenscar Building Society lacks.

questions.explanation: The review identifies fraud after the transactions complete: it changes knowledge, not outcomes, which places it squarely in the detective category, option A. B is wrong because discouragement through publicity is a deterrent effect, a different category from prevention. The review itself blocks nothing; a preventive control would stop the transaction from completing. C is wrong because correction is what happens in response to what the review finds; restoring accounts is a separate corrective activity, not the review itself. D is wrong because a compensating control stands in for a primary control that cannot be implemented, and nothing in the stem says transaction controls are absent. Categorize a control by what it does by itself: detect, prevent, or correct. Do not classify by what its output later enables.
questions.recallLine: A regulator asked Ravenscar to place its weekly application-log review, which spots fraud after transactions complete and halts none, within a control framework. Which category fits?

optionsShort.A: Detective, identifying events once they have occurred
optionsShort.B: Preventive, since publicity deters would-be insiders
optionsShort.C: Corrective, since reviewers restore affected accounts
optionsShort.D: Compensating, standing in for missing transaction controls

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Which control category stops the fraudulent transaction from completing in the first place?

C.label: correct but not first
C.wouldAnswer: Which category covers reversing the transactions and restoring the accounts once fraud has been identified?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which category describes a control adopted because the primary transaction control cannot be implemented here?

questions.question: Which measure BEST addresses counsel's requirement on the audit trail?

options.A: Encrypting the log archive so its contents stay confidential while in storage.
options.B: Writing logs to write-once storage with integrity verification outside admin control.
options.C: Replicating the logs to a second data center so they survive a site failure.
options.D: Restricting log queries to the investigation team for the duration of the case.

questions.explanation: For evidence to survive challenge, the bank must show tamper-resistance against every actor, including its own administrators. Write-once storage with integrity verification held outside admin control, option B, makes post-write alteration technically infeasible and independently checkable. A is wrong because encryption protects confidentiality; an administrator with the keys can still decrypt, alter, and re-encrypt, leaving no integrity guarantee. C is wrong because replication protects availability. It faithfully copies tampered records to the second site. D is wrong because query restrictions limit who reads the logs and do nothing about privileged writes or deletions underneath. Map the requirement to the property it names: counsel asked for integrity, so the control must make modification impossible or detectable, not merely limit access.
questions.recallLine: Counsel needs the audit trail shown to be unaltered after writing, including by the administrators who run the logging platform. Which measure BEST meets that?

optionsShort.A: Encrypt the archive so contents stay confidential
optionsShort.B: Write-once storage, integrity checks outside admin control
optionsShort.C: Replicate the logs to a second data center
optionsShort.D: Restrict log queries to the investigation team

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which control keeps archived log contents unreadable to anyone who gets hold of the storage media?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which measure keeps the fraud investigation's records available if the primary data center is lost?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Which measure limits who can read sensitive log records while an investigation is under way?

questions.question: Which monitoring approach BEST meets the overnight end-to-end requirement?

options.A: Scripted synthetic transactions that exercise the deposit workflow on a fixed schedule.
options.B: Real user monitoring that measures the sessions of actual customers as they occur.
options.C: A weekly credentialed vulnerability scan of the servers behind the deposit service.
options.D: Quarterly regression testing of the deposit code in the staging environment.

questions.explanation: Detecting a failure at 3 a.m., before customers do, requires traffic that exists at 3 a.m. Synthetic transactions, option A, run scripted deposit journeys on a schedule and alert the moment one fails. B is wrong because real user monitoring is passive: with no users active it has nothing to measure, and when users do arrive they become the victims the team wanted to spare. C is wrong because vulnerability scans assess security posture on a weekly cadence and reveal nothing about transaction health in the moment. D is wrong because staging regression tests validate code changes, not the availability of the production service tonight. Active monitoring answers whether it works right now; passive monitoring answers what users experienced.
questions.recallLine: Operations want proof the deposit service works end to end at three in the morning, before a customer meets an error. Which monitoring approach BEST fits?

optionsShort.A: Scripted journeys run on a fixed schedule
optionsShort.B: Real user monitoring of live customer sessions
optionsShort.C: Weekly credentialed vulnerability scan of the servers
optionsShort.D: Quarterly regression testing in the staging environment

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Which approach measures the latency and errors that actual customers met during their own sessions?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which weekly check reports missing patches and unsafe settings on the servers behind the deposit service?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: How does Colebrook confirm a code change did not break deposit behavior before that build is released?

questions.question: Which report BEST meets the need for twelve months of operating effectiveness?

options.A: A SOC 1 Type II report on the controls relevant to financial reporting.
options.B: A SOC 2 Type I report on the design of security controls at year-end.
options.C: A SOC 3 report, which is intended for unrestricted general distribution.
options.D: A SOC 2 Type II report covering control operation over the review period.

questions.explanation: Three requirements decide it: security and availability point to the Trust Services Criteria, so a SOC 2 rather than SOC 1; operating effectiveness across twelve months requires testing over a period, making Type II the right choice over Type I; and auditor-level detail requires the full restricted report, not a stripped summary. Option D satisfies all three. A is wrong because SOC 1 addresses controls relevant to a customer's financial reporting, not security operations. B is wrong because a Type I opines on control design at a single date and says nothing about how controls operated over the year. C is wrong because SOC 3 is a general-use summary stripped of the testing detail Colebrook Payments's auditors need. Map the subject matter to the SOC series, and the time dimension to the type.
questions.recallLine: Colebrook wants third-party assurance that a provider's security and availability controls worked across twelve months, detailed enough for its own auditors. Which report BEST meets that?

optionsShort.A: SOC 1 Type II on financial-reporting controls
optionsShort.B: SOC 2 Type I on control design at year-end
optionsShort.C: SOC 3, a general-distribution summary
optionsShort.D: SOC 2 Type II covering operation over the period

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which report tells a customer's financial auditors whether a provider's processing could misstate their accounts?

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Which report opines on whether a provider's controls were suitably designed as at one single date?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Which report can a provider publish openly to reassure prospects without exposing its testing detail?

questions.question: A single executive was able to waive security review to protect a launch date. Which control should the CISO recommend?

options.A: Scheduling an independent penetration test of each new release soon after it reaches production.
options.B: An enforced SDLC gate whose security criteria and waiver authority sit outside the project.
options.C: A larger regression suite covering the security defects discovered in each previous release.
options.D: Real-time monitoring dashboards giving executives immediate visibility of security incidents in production.

questions.explanation: The control failure was governance, so the fix must relocate authority: a gate whose pass criteria are defined in advance and whose waiver requires formal risk acceptance outside the project, option B, makes skipping security a decision the project cannot take alone. A is wrong because a post-production penetration test, however independent, happens after exposure begins. The VP could still ship unreviewed. C is wrong because regression suites re-check known defects; this flaw was unknown, and no test suite constrains an executive's waiver power. D is wrong because dashboards inform after release; visibility is not authority. When a control can be waived by the person it constrains, the defect is the waiver path, and the correction is separation of authority.
questions.recallLine: A single executive was able to waive security review to protect a launch date. Which control should the CISO recommend?

optionsShort.A: Independent penetration test soon after each release
optionsShort.B: Enforced SDLC gate, waiver authority outside the project
optionsShort.C: Bigger regression suite covering past security defects
optionsShort.D: Real-time dashboards showing executives production incidents

A.label: detective when preventive is asked
A.wouldAnswer: How would Colebrook find the flaws in a release that has already shipped without any security review?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which measure keeps security defects fixed in earlier releases from quietly reappearing in later builds?

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: How can executives see production security incidents as they happen rather than in a monthly summary?

questions.question: Which change BEST implements shifting security work earlier in practice?

options.A: Adding threat modeling and static analysis to the earliest development phases.
options.B: Increasing the frequency of production penetration tests from yearly to quarterly.
options.C: Moving the security team's reviews to the final gate before each release.
options.D: Expanding post-launch monitoring so exploitation is detected within minutes.

questions.explanation: Shifting left means moving security activity toward the early phases, where the review found fixes cost minutes instead of millions. The implementing change is threat modeling and static analysis at design and coding time, option A. B is wrong because production penetration testing, however frequent, still finds flaws after they are built and shipped: the expensive end of the timeline. C is wrong because a final pre-release gate is the rightmost point before launch, the position whose waiver started this story. D is wrong because faster detection of exploitation accepts the flaw's arrival in production and merely optimizes the response to it. The economics in the stem are the whole argument: each phase earlier multiplies the fix-cost advantage, so put the effort where the defect is cheapest to kill.
questions.recallLine: A defect at Ellesmere would have cost minutes at design, days at code review and millions after launch. Which change BEST implements shifting security work earlier?

optionsShort.A: Threat modeling and static analysis in early phases
optionsShort.B: Production penetration tests quarterly instead of yearly
optionsShort.C: Security review moved to the final release gate
optionsShort.D: Expanded post-launch monitoring detecting exploitation within minutes

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: How does the trust find exploitable weaknesses in systems already running in production more often than yearly?

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Which arrangement gives the security team one last look at a release just before it goes live?

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: How can the trust shorten the gap between a flaw being exploited in production and anyone noticing?

questions.question: Which procedure provides the MOST direct evidence that role separation holds?

options.A: Logging in as a technician and attempting each administrator function in a controlled test.
options.B: Reading the role-assignment policy and confirming it defines the separation correctly.
options.C: Interviewing the console administrators about whether technicians have ever exceeded their assigned role.
options.D: Confirming that the console vendor's SOC 2 report covers logical access controls in scope.

questions.explanation: Documents and testimony describe how access control is supposed to work; only exercising the system shows how it does work. Logging in as a technician and attempting each restricted function in a controlled test, option A, produces direct, first-hand evidence that the separation holds or fails. B is wrong because reading the policy verifies design intent, and the auditor's question is about operation. C is wrong because interviews collect assertions, the weakest evidence class, useful mainly for corroboration. D is wrong because a vendor's SOC 2 report, whatever its stated scope, attests to the vendor's own organization and generic product controls, never to how Ellesmere Trust configured its roles. Audit evidence has a hierarchy: testing above inspection, inspection above inquiry. Reach for the highest class the engagement allows.
questions.recallLine: An auditor must verify that a field-technician login cannot invoke the restricted administrator functions on the machine management console. Which procedure gives the MOST direct evidence?

optionsShort.A: Log in as a technician and attempt each admin function
optionsShort.B: Read the role-assignment policy and confirm it defines separation
optionsShort.C: Interview administrators about technicians exceeding their role
optionsShort.D: Check the vendor's SOC 2 covers logical access

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: How does the auditor confirm the trust has properly defined which functions each console role may invoke?

C.label: correct but not first
C.wouldAnswer: Which procedure gathers the console team's own account of how the role restrictions work in practice?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Which evidence covers the security of the console vendor's own organization and its generic product controls?

questions.question: Which approach BEST supports a defensible conclusion within the audit window?

options.A: Reviewing the records from the department where problems surfaced before.
options.B: Reviewing the most recent month's records and extrapolating to the full year.
options.C: Selecting a statistically representative sample of records across the whole population.
options.D: Asking each manager to self-certify their own reviews and tallying the responses.

questions.explanation: A defensible conclusion about 12,000 records in limited time is exactly what statistical sampling provides: a representative selection across the population, option C, supports an inference about the whole with quantifiable confidence. A is wrong because sampling only where problems already surfaced biases the result and supports no conclusion about the rest of the population. B is wrong because one month is a convenience sample; sign-off discipline in December says little about March. D is wrong because manager self-certification replaces independent verification with the auditee's own assertion, the conflict of interest audits exist to avoid. When full-population testing is impossible, the defensibility of the conclusion comes from how the sample was drawn, not from how many records were checked.
questions.recallLine: An internal auditor must verify 12,000 access-review sign-offs in a window too short to check every record. Which approach BEST supports a defensible conclusion?

optionsShort.A: Review the department where problems surfaced before
optionsShort.B: Review the latest month and extrapolate to the year
optionsShort.C: Statistically representative sample across the whole population
optionsShort.D: Ask each manager to self-certify their own reviews

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: How would the auditor concentrate testing on the one department where sign-off problems have already appeared?

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: How can the auditor judge whether sign-off discipline held during the most recent month of the year?

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: How can managers state to the trust that they completed the access reviews assigned to them?

questions.question: What is the MOST likely basis for the customers rejecting the internal assessment?

options.A: The internal report is confidential and may not lawfully be shared outside Ellesmere Trust.
options.B: The internal team used sampling, and the customers require full-population testing.
options.C: An assessment by Ellesmere Trust's own staff lacks the independence third parties require.
options.D: The internal audit examined control design but could not test operating effectiveness.

questions.explanation: Third parties discount even excellent internal work for a structural reason: the assessor is employed by the organization being assessed, so the independence external assurance requires is absent. That is option C, and no thoroughness of working papers cures the relationship. A is wrong because internal reports can be shared under agreement; confidentiality is a choice, not a legal bar, and not the customers' objection. B is wrong because external auditors rely on sampling too. Sampling methodology is standard practice, not the disqualifier. D is wrong because internal audit can and does test operating effectiveness; the customers doubt the reporter, not the technique. Internal audit's independence is organizational, reporting inside the company, ideally to the audit committee. For assurance that must cross company boundaries, only an independent third party's opinion travels.
questions.recallLine: Payment-processor customers reject the trust's internal assessments even though the working papers are thorough and the findings candid. What MOST likely explains the rejection?

optionsShort.A: The report is confidential and may not be shared
optionsShort.B: The team sampled; customers require full-population testing
optionsShort.C: Own staff assessing themselves lacks the required independence
optionsShort.D: Internal audit tested design, not operating effectiveness

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Why might the trust choose not to hand a detailed internal audit report to an outside customer?

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Which objection would apply to an assessment whose sample was drawn too narrowly to represent the population?

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Which objection applies to a report opining only on how controls were designed, never on how they ran?

questions.question: Which exercise should run FIRST to find gaps at minimal cost and zero production risk?

options.A: A full interruption test, failing the live production deposit service over to standby.
options.B: A parallel test, processing mirrored ATM transactions at the standby recovery site.
options.C: A structured walkthrough, stepping through the plan with all stakeholders at a table.
options.D: An unannounced red-team exercise measuring how the team responds under realistic pressure.

questions.explanation: An unexercised plan fails first on paper problems: wrong names, dead phone numbers, unclear authority. A structured walkthrough, option C, finds those at a table at near-zero cost and no production risk, which is why it comes before every other exercise type. A is wrong because a full interruption test is the riskiest and most expensive exercise, indefensible for a plan that has yet to survive a read-through. B is wrong because a parallel test validates recovery processing capacity, a different objective, and still presumes the procedural basics work. D is wrong because an unannounced red-team run measures live response maturity; run against an unrehearsed team it mostly documents predictable chaos. Test maturity is a ladder: read, discuss, simulate, then interrupt. Each rung earns the next.
questions.recallLine: Marlow's incident response plan has never been exercised, and the CISO wants gaps found at minimal cost and zero production risk. Which exercise should run FIRST?

optionsShort.A: Full interruption test failing production over to standby
optionsShort.B: Parallel test processing mirrored transactions at the recovery site
optionsShort.C: Structured walkthrough of the plan around a table
optionsShort.D: Unannounced red-team exercise under realistic pressure

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: Which exercise proves processing genuinely moves to standby, once the bank accepts the risk and books a window?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which test shows the recovery site can carry the transaction load while the primary keeps serving customers?

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: Which exercise measures how a well-rehearsed team performs when an incident arrives with no warning?

questions.question: Which test BEST satisfies the regulator's demand for the highest attainable assurance?

options.A: A tabletop walkthrough of the failover runbook with senior operations staff.
options.B: A simulation of the failover decision chain using a scripted outage scenario.
options.C: A parallel test validating recovery-site transaction processing while the primary keeps running live.
options.D: A full interruption test shutting down primary processing to run live from recovery.

questions.explanation: Only one test type demonstrates actual failover: shutting down primary processing and running live from the recovery site, option D. The stem grants the two preconditions that normally rule it out, accepted risk and a scheduled window, so the highest-assurance option becomes the required one. A is wrong because a walkthrough shows the runbook reads correctly, not that failover works. B is wrong because a simulation exercises the decision chain against a script while production never actually moves. C is wrong because a parallel test proves the recovery site can process load but never severs the primary, so the failover mechanism itself goes untested. That is the regulator's actual question. Assurance scales with realism and risk together; when proof is demanded and the risk is accepted, interruption is the answer.
questions.recallLine: A regulator demands the highest attainable assurance that Marlow's processing genuinely fails over, with risk accepted and a maintenance window approved. Which test BEST satisfies that?

optionsShort.A: Tabletop walkthrough of the failover runbook with operations
optionsShort.B: Simulation of the failover decision chain from a script
optionsShort.C: Parallel test validating recovery processing while primary runs
optionsShort.D: Full interruption test running live from the recovery site

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Which exercise checks the failover runbook is complete and understood before anything is actually switched?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which exercise tests whether the right people make the right failover calls without touching production?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Which test evidences recovery-site capacity when the bank cannot take its primary out of service?

questions.question: Which weakness in the draft plan is the MOST serious, given where Wrenfield's claims data physically resides?

options.A: Scanning the Kubernetes tenant repeats work the cloud provider's own platform testing already performs each quarter
options.B: The colocation servers hold in-scope claims records, and no planned activity examines that hardware at all
options.C: The self-assessment tests how controls are designed, stopping short of whether they operated all year
options.D: The provider's attestation covers platform controls rather than how Wrenfield configured its own tenant

questions.explanation: Scope follows the data, not the org chart or the hosting model. Claims records on the two Columbus servers are in scope for the client's contract and for HIPAA, yet the plan tests neither those hosts nor the people who run them, and an assessment that omits a location holding regulated data cannot support a conclusion about the environment as a whole. A is a real inefficiency, but duplicated effort wastes money rather than leaving records unexamined. C is a genuine defect, since design without operating effectiveness supports no annual conclusion, though a self-assessment at least looks at controls that exist. D is the sharpest of the three losers, because shared responsibility does leave tenant configuration unassessed; even so, the SOC 2 and the tenant scan together touch that platform, while nothing touches the cage. Rank scope gaps first by the data they leave out, then by the depth of what remains.
questions.recallLine: A claims processor funds one assessment cycle across a cloud tenant, a provider attestation, and two colocation servers. Which weakness in the plan is MOST serious?

optionsShort.A: Scanning duplicates the provider's own platform testing
optionsShort.B: No activity examines the colocation servers
optionsShort.C: Tests control design, not operation over time
optionsShort.D: Attestation covers the platform, not tenant configuration

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which critique of the plan would MOST reduce the cost of the cycle without changing what the assessment covers?

C.label: correct but not first
C.wouldAnswer: Which defect leaves a committee unable to say whether controls worked all year rather than on review day?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Which limitation of a cloud provider's SOC 2 report MOST affects assurance over a customer's own settings?

NIST SP 800-53A Rev 5 | Assessing Security and Privacy Controls, determining assessment scope
NIST SP 800-37 Rev 2 | authorization boundary determination

questions.question: Which change to the backup metric would do the MOST to keep the committee from being misled again?

options.A: Break the 99.6 percent figure out by system rather than reporting one fleet-wide rate
options.B: Report the number of jobs that failed overnight and were re-run inside the window
options.C: Report retention of backup media against the schedule set in the records policy
options.D: Report the share of systems whose data was restored and verified during the period

questions.explanation: A backup job reports on itself. It says the software finished writing, not that anything readable came back, which is why eleven weeks of writes into a decommissioned share scored 99.6 percent. Restoring a sample of systems and checking the recovered data against expected content closes that loop, and it would have failed on the first night rather than at a tabletop in March. A improves granularity and would narrow the search once a failure is known, but a per-system success rate still measures the same wrong event. B counts recoveries of the job itself, which is hygiene for the backup team and says nothing about recoverability to the committee. C belongs to records retention; media kept for exactly the right period can still be unreadable. Measure the outcome a control exists to produce, not the completion of the task meant to produce it.
questions.recallLine: Nightly backup jobs report a 99.6 percent success rate, yet a tabletop restore failed. Which change to the backup metric helps the committee MOST?

optionsShort.A: Break the success rate out per system
optionsShort.B: Count failed jobs re-run inside the window
optionsShort.C: Track media retention against the records schedule
optionsShort.D: Report systems whose restores were verified

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Once a restore has failed somewhere in the fleet, which reporting change narrows down which systems to investigate first?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which measure tells a backup team whether overnight failures are being cleared inside the operational window?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which backup measure shows an auditor that copies are kept for the period the records policy requires?

sources: ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 6.3.4 Collect security process data — Backup verification data
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CP-9(1) System Backup — Testing for Reliability and Integrity
NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 | Contingency Planning Guide, backup and restoration testing

questions.question: The committee also asked who verifies the pack. Which change to the internal assurance strategy adds the GREATEST credibility to the numbers?

options.A: Have internal audit re-perform a sample of the evidence behind each metric before publication
options.B: Engage an external assurance firm to re-perform the whole metrics pack every quarter
options.C: Rotate the engineers who compile each metric onto different systems every quarter
options.D: Require the chief information officer to countersign the pack before the committee sees it

questions.explanation: Numbers become credible when somebody outside the reporting line can reproduce them from the underlying evidence. Sampling the restore logs and the personnel extract and recalculating what the pack claims is the check that catches a metric counting the wrong event, which is precisely how a 99.6 percent figure survived eleven weeks of unusable backups. B buys the same assurance from further away, but re-performing an entire pack quarterly costs more than the insurer's whole assessment budget, and the committee asked about its own process. C separates duties among the people producing the numbers, limiting collusion and single-person error while leaving the method unexamined; a rotated engineer computing the wrong metric gets the same wrong answer. D adds executive accountability, and management review has its own value, but the CIO owns the systems being reported on, and signing is not verifying. Put independence where the evidence is checked.
questions.recallLine: An insurer's control owners compile their own quarterly security metrics. Which change to the internal assurance strategy adds the GREATEST credibility?

optionsShort.A: Internal audit re-performs a sample of evidence
optionsShort.B: External firm re-performs the pack quarterly
optionsShort.C: Rotate engineers who compile each metric
optionsShort.D: CIO countersigns the pack before publication

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: When a regulator will not accept management's own figures, who should re-perform the security metrics an insurer reports?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which staffing change reduces the chance that one engineer can quietly shape a metric in their own favor?

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: Which step records executive accountability for the security numbers a risk committee receives each quarter?

NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CA-2(1) Control Assessments — Independent Assessors, CA-7 Continuous Monitoring

domains.title: Security Operations
domains.caseStudy:
Domain 7 is the daily running of a security program: monitoring, incident response, patch and change management, backups, disaster recovery and business continuity, and the physical operations that keep systems available.

Case Study: The "Patch Tuesday" Fleet Outage

### Context

Global ATM Corp runs 5,000 ATMs. On the second Tuesday of the month its IT operations team approved a critical Windows security patch. To reach compliance quickly, the lead engineer pushed it to the entire fleet at once through SCCM, at 2:00 PM.

### What went wrong

The patch conflicted with the cash dispenser driver used on 80% of the fleet. Within thirty minutes 4,000 ATMs had crashed to a blue screen. The team triggered an automated uninstall, but 4,000 machines rebooting and checking in at once saturated the network, and the rollback command never reached them. Technicians drove to each ATM, booted it into safe mode and removed the patch by hand. The network was down for eighteen hours.

The white paper puts patching at the top of its logical controls, rated High against malware and exploit vectors, and it is equally clear about the other side of the trade: an ATM is a multi-vendor stack of operating system, application, XFS middleware and peripheral drivers, and a weakness in any one link affects the whole chain. Service availability is one of its named impact categories. A patch that takes 80% of the fleet offline is an availability incident with a security label on it.

### What a practitioner does differently

Change management does the work here. Every change to production carries a tested backout plan, and "tested" means run in a lab that holds every hardware and driver variant in the fleet, including the dispenser population that failed. The vendor's certification of the patch against the ATM application and driver stack is a gate, not a courtesy.

Deploy in rings: lab, then a 1% canary, then a 10% pilot, then the rest, with a soak period long enough to cover a business cycle and a halt trigger in monitoring (a failure rate, not a feeling). Windows are chosen off-peak; 2:00 PM on a weekday is peak. Throttle the deployment so the network can carry a rollback if it comes to that, and keep the recovery runbook current so a site visit takes minutes rather than an afternoon.

Then the continuity side: what is the maximum tolerable downtime for the ATM channel, and what did customers use during the eighteen hours? If the answer is "the branches", the business continuity plan should say so, and the branches should have known.

### Outcome

Eighteen hours of fleet downtime, a technician visit to 4,000 sites, and a change advisory board that now refuses any fleet-wide push without a pilot ring and a demonstrated rollback. The patch went out again, ring by ring, without incident.

### What the exam tests

Scenarios like this test the change management process end to end, patch management as a lifecycle, configuration baselines, availability as a pillar of the CIA triad, and business continuity terms: maximum tolerable downtime, recovery time objective, and how an eighteen-hour outage measures against them. Expect a question on why the rollback failed and which control would have prevented it.

### Related reading

The operator in this scenario is a composite. The controls are documented in:

- [Technical Risks and Attack Vectors Targeting ATMs](https://portfolio.atmavailability.com/atm-technical-risks-white-paper.pdf), the sections on inherent vulnerabilities (the multi-vendor stack), on software integrity and patching, and on monitoring and incident response.
- [ATM Security Capability Maturity Worksheet](https://portfolio.atmavailability.com/atm-capability-maturity-worksheet.pdf), Domain 2 (platform) and Domain 4 (process) controls.
- [ATM Availability on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC_2uToOyDBvrHoqBfN3RobA), for how the self-service channel is run day to day.

stimuli.title: Global ATM: the Toledo prompt
stimuli.text: Global ATM Corp operates 5,000 ATMs. Its service desk logs a report from a branch: an ATM in Toledo displayed a command prompt for a few seconds during a maintenance visit. The fleet runs a standard Windows build with anti-malware and a monthly patch cycle. Each machine writes its own event log locally and keeps thirty days of it. There is no rule about which programs may run. The maintenance vendor's technician says he ran a diagnostic tool he downloaded that morning. By the time an analyst calls back, the machine has been rebooted twice.

profile.environment: Standard Windows build · local event logs, 30 days · outsourced maintenance
profile.state: One reported command prompt, machine already rebooted twice

stimuli.title: Global ATM: two exercises
stimuli.text: Global ATM Corp has a written disaster recovery plan for the transaction switch behind its 5,000 ATMs, and has run one tabletop against it. The plan names a recovery team of eleven people across three time zones, lists a call tree, and assumes the switch can be brought up at the Columbus site within four hours. Nobody has yet performed any of the steps. The board has approved two exercises this year and will not accept an outage of production. The operations director has asked what the two exercises should be and what evidence each will produce.

profile.regime: State banking examination · card brand availability requirements
profile.environment: Transaction switch · alternate site at Columbus · eleven-person recovery team, three time zones
profile.state: Plan written, one tabletop run, no procedure yet performed

stimuli.title: A patch that took the fleet down
stimuli.text: A security patch put every one of Global ATM Corp's 5,000 machines into a reboot loop, and customers could not withdraw cash for eighteen hours. No card data was exposed and no transaction record was altered. The test lab cannot replicate every dispenser hardware variant in the field, and the vendor certifies patches only against a reference build. Business impact analysis sets a four-hour recovery time objective and a twenty-four-hour maximum tolerable downtime for the fleet. An engineer has found a registry fix that would stop the loop, but the change board does not meet for three days.

profile.environment: Test lab cannot replicate every dispenser variant · vendor certifies against a reference build
profile.state: 18-hour outage, no data exposed

stimuli.title: Who may change what, and who checks
stimuli.text: Global ATM Corp's change board is reviewing four backout plans submitted with a proposed dispenser firmware change, and only one of them is a plan at all. An outage review has separately noted that the lead engineer who wrote a deployment change request also approved it in the tracking system and then executed the deployment. A fleet audit found machines running inconsistent settings: some hardened, others with services re-enabled by field technicians, and no record of what any machine is supposed to look like. Operations also want to compare the reliability of two dispenser models over the coming year.

profile.organization: Global ATM Corp · change and configuration management
profile.environment: Firmware changes submitted with backout plans · machines running inconsistent settings
profile.state: Change process being rebuilt after an outage

stimuli.title: Objectives, and whether they were met
stimuli.text: Trentham Payments restored its transaction switch to working order three hours into a recovery test, after which data validation and reconciliation took another three hours before the business could resume processing. The recovery objective is four hours and the maximum tolerable downtime is eight. The business has separately determined the switch database can lose at most fifteen minutes of committed transactions in a disaster, and the architect must pick a data-protection design that meets that without overspending. A monitoring server was down for a day when its single disk failed.

profile.environment: Four-hour recovery objective, eight-hour maximum tolerable downtime · reconciliation after restore
profile.state: Recovery test results being assessed

stimuli.title: Copies, mirrors and what each protects
stimuli.text: An administrator at Trentham Payments proposes mirrored disks after a monitoring server was lost to a single disk failure, and asks whether nightly backups can then be retired. The same review found that an operator had accidentally deleted a week of alert history months earlier. An engineer is separately configuring local storage for a log-collection server with four drive bays, needing to tolerate any single drive failing while keeping as much usable capacity as possible. An archived-records system consulted a few times a month carries a two-week recovery objective on a tight budget, and leased machines are being returned.

profile.environment: Four drive bays in the log collector · nightly backups and a proposed mirror · archived records rarely consulted
profile.state: Backup design being revisited

stimuli.title: Full, differential, incremental
stimuli.text: An administrator at Ashcombe Mutual runs a full backup of the log server every Sunday night and a differential every other night, and the server's disk has failed on a Thursday morning. The nightly jobs have separately begun overrunning their window near the end of each week, because every night re-copies all changes since Sunday; the administrator must shorten them and accepts that restores may take longer. When a midday incremental was added to the existing scheme, the nightly differentials were afterwards found to be missing files changed during the mornings.

profile.environment: Sunday full backups · nightly differentials overrunning · a midday incremental added
profile.state: Restore and window problems together

stimuli.title: Rehearsing a plan nobody has run
stimuli.text: Ashcombe Mutual has just finished writing its first disaster recovery plan for the transaction switch. Nothing in it has been validated and management will accept no disruption to production while confidence remains low. A flood exercise at another firm is being studied as a warning: every system was restored within its objective, yet the business stalled for days because the call center had no workspace, cash-in-transit contracts held no fallback instructions and nobody held authority to relocate staff. The mutual's own analysis concludes settlement can survive at most twenty-four hours of downtime.

profile.regime: State insurance regulation · board risk appetite
profile.environment: First disaster recovery plan written · nothing validated · flood exposure at head office
profile.state: Confidence low, no disruption acceptable

stimuli.title: An objective that does not fit inside the tolerance
stimuli.text: Ashcombe Mutual's analysis concludes that its settlement function can survive a maximum of twenty-four hours of downtime before regulatory penalties and unrecoverable losses begin. The information technology recovery proposal for the supporting systems specifies a thirty-six-hour recovery objective, because faster options exceed this year's budget, and the continuity coordinator must respond. The mutual is separately outsourcing overnight monitoring of its machine estate and wants the provider's response to outages to be enforceable with defined consequences. An earlier midday incremental broke the nightly differentials.

profile.environment: 24-hour maximum tolerable downtime · 36-hour recovery proposal · service level agreement being drafted
profile.state: Proposal awaiting the coordinator's response

stimuli.title: A command prompt on a machine in Toledo
stimuli.text: A branch has reported to Halloway Cash Systems that one of its machines displayed a command prompt for a few seconds during a maintenance visit. The fleet runs a standard build with anti-malware and a monthly patch cycle, each machine writes its own event log locally and keeps thirty days of it, and there is no rule about which programs may run. The maintenance technician says he ran a diagnostic tool he downloaded that morning. By the time an analyst called back the machine had been rebooted twice. A USB stick with an unknown executable was found in another machine's port.

profile.environment: Standard build with anti-malware · thirty days of local event log · no rule on which programs may run
profile.state: Machine rebooted twice before an analyst called back

stimuli.title: Evidence that will survive a challenge
stimuli.text: Prosecutors reviewing Halloway Cash Systems' skimming case are weighing four items of evidence for trial and must pick the one most likely to survive challenge. An incident responder has separately reached a compromised machine that is still running and believed to hold the attacker's injected code in memory, and management wants it analyzed with as little evidence lost as possible. The security operations center wants visibility into attacks against the transaction network, but the network team refuses any inline device that could delay or drop legitimate transactions. Egress rules were written years ago.

profile.environment: Skimming case heading to trial · memory-resident code on a running machine
profile.state: Prosecutors weighing four items of evidence

stimuli.title: Blocking what has no patch yet
stimuli.text: A critical vulnerability in Halloway Cash Systems' transaction switch is being actively exploited across the industry, the exploit's network signature is well documented, and the vendor's corrected patch is three weeks away. After an earlier patching disaster the change board insists any patch must first complete full staging tests. The internet-facing gateway is separately being flooded with packets whose source addresses belong to the company's own internal ranges, arriving from outside. Peer firms have been breached by a group whose tooling evades signature detection, with dwell times of months.

profile.environment: Exploit signature published, vendor patch three weeks away · spoofed internal addresses at the border
profile.state: Change board insisting on full staging tests

stimuli.title: Too many alerts, too few people
stimuli.text: Cranfield Bank's security operations center receives hundreds of phishing-report alerts each week, and for every one analysts manually extract the indicators, check them against threat intelligence, search mailboxes for related messages and quarantine the hits: identical steps every time, consuming most of each shift. Alert quality is good; the volume is the problem. A fraud investigation separately needed four days to assemble a timeline because each machine keeps logs locally with inconsistent clocks and nothing can search across them. An audit found maintenance laptops trusted unconditionally once on the internal network.

profile.environment: Hundreds of phishing reports weekly · machine logs local with inconsistent clocks · maintenance laptops trusted once inside
profile.state: Analysts consumed by identical manual steps

stimuli.title: Least privilege, and the people problem
stimuli.text: A fraud investigator at Cranfield Bank assigned to a case involving twelve customer accounts turns out to be able to read the records of every customer in the bank, and his database account also carries administrative rights he has never used. Internal audit separately warns that only one engineer understands the settlement reconciliation jobs and could conceal an ongoing fraud indefinitely because nobody else touches the process. A further audit finds four operations staff sharing one domain administrator password, using it for routine work such as email and browsing, unchanged for two years.

profile.environment: Investigator able to read every customer record · one engineer owns settlement reconciliation · four staff sharing a domain administrator password
profile.state: Audit findings requiring response

stimuli.title: A transformer fire at the valve works
stimuli.text: Kestrel Valve Works machines industrial valves at a single plant in Sandusky, Ohio, and books ninety per cent of its revenue through one ERP order-entry system. A transformer fire on a Saturday night cuts plant power and fills the ground-floor server room with suppression foam. All 340 staff are out of the building and accounted for by 23:40. The disaster recovery plan names the chief operating officer as the sole declaring authority, sets a four-hour recovery time objective for order entry, and holds a warm site in Toledo loaded nightly from a 22:00 backup. By 01:15 the plant manager, the DR coordinator and the property insurance broker are all on a bridge call, each pressing a different next move.

profile.organization: Kestrel Valve Works · industrial valve manufacturing
profile.environment: single plant, warm site ninety miles away
profile.state: disaster in progress, plan not yet declared

stimuli.title: Forty engineers, a storm zone and a two in the morning approval
stimuli.text: Halcyon Grid Partners is a 600-person power-transmission engineering firm whose only office sits four blocks from Tampa Bay, inside a mandatory storm evacuation zone. Forty of its engineers are about to spend twelve weeks on a substation joint venture in a country carrying a Level 3 travel advisory, taking the firm's proprietary relay-protection drawings with them. In March a night-shift engineer approved an authentication push at 02:10 after eleven consecutive prompts, and an attacker held VPN access for six hours. The firm runs an annual security-awareness course with a 98 per cent completion rate and a fire drill every October that nobody has ever timed, and its emergency action plan was last revised in 2019.

profile.regime: client NERC CIP obligations; OSHA emergency action plan rules
profile.environment: single Tampa office; forty engineers deploying overseas
profile.state: pre-deployment, hurricane season, one MFA compromise on record

questions.question: Management asks which change would have stopped the technician's downloaded tool from running at all. Which control BEST meets that description?

options.A: Anti-malware configured to submit unknown executables to the vendor for analysis.
options.B: A policy forbidding technicians from downloading software to fleet machines.
options.C: Blocking the fleet's outbound web access to sites known to host hacking tools.
options.D: A deny-by-default policy admitting software the organization has explicitly authorized to execute.

questions.explanation: Every option except D starts from a list of things known to be bad, and a diagnostic tool downloaded that morning is on nobody's list. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-7(5) Least Functionality | Authorized Software - Allow-by-Exception is the precise control: identify the software authorized to execute, employ a deny-all permit-by-exception policy to allow it, and review and update the list on a defined frequency. Its sibling CM-7(4) Unauthorized Software - Deny-by-Exception is the weaker direction, and the catalog says so by structure. Note the vocabulary: Rev 5 uses allow-list and deny-list where older material says whitelisting and blacklisting. A is detective when preventive is asked, and it acts on an executable that is unknown by definition. B is the right control for a different problem, a rule aimed at a person rather than a condition enforced on the machine. C is wrong scope, applying deny-by-exception to the network, where the list can never be complete and the tool arrived on a technician's own laptop anyway. Enumerate the good, not the bad.
questions.recallLine: What would have stopped an unapproved downloaded tool from executing on a fleet machine?

optionsShort.A: Submit unknown executables to the vendor
optionsShort.B: Policy forbidding downloads
optionsShort.C: Block known hacking-tool sites
optionsShort.D: Deny all, permit authorized software

A.label: detective when preventive is asked
A.wouldAnswer: How does the fleet get coverage for a variant the anti-malware vendor has not yet seen?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: What belongs in the maintenance contract about technician conduct on the bank's machines?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: What reduces casual access to tooling sites from machines that have no need to browse?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7(5) Authorized Software - Allow-by-Exception
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7(4) Unauthorized Software - Deny-by-Exception; CM-10 Software Usage Restrictions

questions.question: Three weeks later the incident is closed. Which outcome BEST shows that the lessons-learned step actually worked?

options.A: The software policy, the maintenance contract and the response playbook were each changed.
options.B: A report was circulated describing the timeline and the root cause in full detail.
options.C: The analysts who handled the incident briefed the wider team on what they had seen.
options.D: A follow-up meeting was scheduled once recovery of the four machines was complete.

questions.explanation: The test of a lessons-learned step is whether anything is different afterwards, and only A names artefacts that changed. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IR-4 Incident Handling states the obligation directly: incorporate lessons learned from ongoing incident handling into response procedures, training and testing, and implement the resulting changes accordingly, with IR-8 Incident Response Plan requiring the plan itself to be reviewed and updated. NIST CSF 2.0 puts the same idea in ID.IM-01 through ID.IM-04, where improvements are identified from evaluations, from tests and exercises, from operational processes, and are then reflected in the plans. NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 adds a change of emphasis worth knowing: lessons should often be shared as soon as they are identified rather than held until recovery concludes. B is symptom not cause, documenting the incident while nothing changed. C is the right control for a different problem, moving knowledge between people rather than into procedure. D is wrong phase, and it is the habit Revision 3 argues against. Look for the diff, not the deck.
questions.recallLine: An incident closes. Which outcome shows the lessons-learned step actually worked?

optionsShort.A: Policy, contract and playbook all changed
optionsShort.B: Detailed timeline report circulated
optionsShort.C: Analysts briefed the wider team
optionsShort.D: Follow-up meeting scheduled after recovery

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: What record does the organization need in order to answer an examiner about this incident?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: How does a response team spread hard-won knowledge to analysts who were not on the incident?

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: What is the traditional four-phase model's final step, before Revision 3 moved improvement into a continuous layer?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | IR-4 Incident Handling; IR-8 Incident Response Plan
NIST CSF 2.0 (NIST CSWP 29) | ID.IM-01 to ID.IM-04
NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 | Sections 1 and 3.1, lessons shared as identified

questions.question: The tabletop found the plan readable. The operations director wants the next exercise to confirm that each named person can state their own steps. Which test type BEST fits?

options.A: A walkthrough in which each role reads and talks through its own procedures in sequence.
options.B: A simulation in which the team responds to an injected scenario under time pressure.
options.C: A parallel test bringing the alternate switch up beside production and comparing output.
options.D: A full interruption test failing production over to the alternate site and back.

questions.explanation: The ladder the exam tests runs read-through and tabletop, then walkthrough, then simulation, then parallel, then full interruption, and each rung adds one thing. A walkthrough is the rung where the plan stops being a document the team has read and becomes procedures individuals can state for their own role. Be careful with the sourcing here: this five-type ladder is CISSP-canon vocabulary and is not NIST's taxonomy. NIST SP 800-84 uses training sessions, tabletop exercises, functional exercises and tests, and NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Section 3.5.3 defines a tabletop as discussion-based only, with no equipment deployed. The control obligation is NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CP-4 Contingency Plan Testing. B is wrong phase, the next rung up, and it measures reaction rather than knowledge of the steps. C is a correct action but not the first one, committing real recovery infrastructure to procedures nobody has yet performed. D is not the decision-maker's, since the board has ruled out an outage of production. Climb one rung at a time.
questions.recallLine: The plan reads well. Which test type confirms each named person can state their own steps?

optionsShort.A: Walkthrough of procedures by role
optionsShort.B: Simulation under time pressure
optionsShort.C: Parallel test beside production
optionsShort.D: Full interruption failover

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: What test measures whether the team decides well when information arrives out of order?

C.label: correct but not first
C.wouldAnswer: What test proves the alternate switch produces the same output as production?

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: What test would the board have to approve an outage for, and what does it finally prove?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CP-4 Contingency Plan Testing
NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 | Section 3.5.3 Exercises (tabletop is discussion-based only)
NIST SP 800-84 | Chapters 3 to 6 (NIST taxonomy differs from the CISSP five-type ladder)

questions.question: The simulation stalls for fifty minutes because the only person who can authorize the failover is on a flight. Which change to the plan MOST directly addresses that?

options.A: Adding a second alternate site so the failover has more than one destination.
options.B: Naming a deputy for every plan role, with the authority each deputy may exercise.
options.C: Recording the exercise so the delay can be reviewed with the recovery team afterwards.
options.D: Moving the call tree from a printed sheet to an automated notification service.

questions.explanation: A recovery plan that depends on one reachable human has a single point of failure made of flesh, and eleven people across three time zones guarantees that somebody is always unreachable. The fix is delegation recorded in advance: who stands in, and what they may decide. NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Section 4.2.2 Notification Procedures requires the plan to document how recovery personnel are notified during business and non-business hours, and the plan structure the document specifies carries delegation of authority alongside the team rosters. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CP-2 Contingency Plan requires roles, responsibilities and contact information for key personnel, with CP-3 Contingency Training behind it. A is the right control for a different problem, adding destinations when the failure was authority. C is symptom not cause, capturing the delay rather than removing it. D is a correct action but not the first one, since a faster call reaches the same absent person. Name the deputy before the flight.
questions.recallLine: A recovery exercise stalls waiting for the one person who can authorize failover. What fixes it?

optionsShort.A: Add a second alternate site
optionsShort.B: Name deputies and their authority
optionsShort.C: Record the exercise for review
optionsShort.D: Automate the call tree

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: What addresses the risk that the alternate site is itself unavailable when needed?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: How does the team gather accurate evidence about what happened during an exercise?

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: How does the company shorten the time between an outage and the team knowing about it?

sources: NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 | Section 4.2.2 Notification Procedures; plan structure and delegation of authority
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CP-2 Contingency Plan; CP-3 Contingency Training

questions.question: An analyst investigating a suspected insider at Global ATM Corp needs to establish which technician was physically at the Toledo machine on the night in question. The suspect is the administrator of the badge system, holds the account that exports its records, and has not yet been told that he is under investigation. Which step should the analyst take FIRST?

options.A: Interview the suspect's supervisor about the technician's assignment for that week.
options.B: Query the badge system directly for the day's entries and export them to a report.
options.C: Compare the badge records with the ATM's local event log on the machine itself.
options.D: Preserve the badge records from a source beyond the suspect's reach, then compare.

questions.explanation: An investigation into the person who administers the evidence has one problem before it has any others, and that is custody. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-9 Protection of Audit Information requires audit information and tooling to be protected from unauthorized access, modification and deletion, and its enhancements say how: AU-9(2) Store on Separate Physical Systems or Components, and AU-9(4) Access by Subset of Privileged Users, which limits management of audit functionality to a defined subset of privileged users. Those controls exist precisely so that the administrator of a system is not the custodian of the record about them. IR-4(12) Incident Handling | Malicious Code and Forensic Analysis covers the analysis that follows. NIST SP 800-86 is the guide that covers forensic technique itself. A is a correct action but not the first one, part of the investigation and no protection for an alterable record. B is symptom not cause, producing an answer from a system the suspect controls, so the answer cannot be defended later. C is wrong phase, correlating before preserving and touching the live machine to do it. Secure the record before you read it.
questions.recallLine: The suspect administers the system holding the evidence. What should the analyst do first?

optionsShort.A: Interview the supervisor
optionsShort.B: Query and export the badge records
optionsShort.C: Compare against the ATM's local log
optionsShort.D: Preserve from a source beyond his reach

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: How does the analyst establish what the technician was supposed to be doing that week?

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: How does an analyst pull entries quickly when the system owner is not a subject of the investigation?

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: What does the analyst do once both records are preserved and the timeline has to be built?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-9 Protection of Audit Information; AU-9(2); AU-9(4) Access by Subset of Privileged Users
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | IR-4(12) Malicious Code and Forensic Analysis
NIST SP 800-86 named as the dedicated forensic-technique source

questions.question: Which change to the deployment process would MOST reduce the impact of a future patch that conflicts with fleet hardware?

options.A: Schedule fleet deployments for the overnight low-transaction window with support staff on standby.
options.B: Obtain written vendor certification of compatibility for each patch before it is approved.
options.C: Release each patch to a small canary group, then a pilot ring, then the wider fleet.
options.D: Prepare a scripted, tested uninstall routine that can be triggered remotely after deployment.

questions.explanation: No amount of pre-release checking can rule out a conflict with hardware the test lab does not contain, so the winning control is the one that limits how many machines a bad patch can reach: a canary-and-pilot rollout caps the damage at the first ring regardless of the failure's cause. A is wrong because timing is the wrong variable - an overnight window changes when 4,000 machines crash, not whether they do. B is wrong because vendor certification against a reference build is exactly the assurance that failed here; it cannot cover hardware variants the vendor has never tested. D is wrong because the outage proved a fleet-wide failure can saturate the network and block remote rollback; an uninstall script is worth having, but it works reliably only when the deployment is already staged. Limit exposure first; prediction and rollback are supplements, not substitutes.
questions.recallLine: Which change to Global ATM Corp's patch deployment process would MOST reduce the impact of a future patch that conflicts with dispenser hardware?

optionsShort.A: Deploy overnight with support staff standing by
optionsShort.B: Require written vendor compatibility certification first
optionsShort.C: Canary group, then pilot ring, then fleet
optionsShort.D: Prepare a remotely triggered uninstall script

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which deployment practice limits how many customers are inconvenienced while a planned change is being applied?

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Which supplier requirement gives the bank contractual assurance that a patch works on the vendor's own certified reference build?

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: Once patches roll out in rings, what mechanism reverses a bad patch on machines that already received it?

questions.question: When the report classifies the security impact of the outage, which conclusion is MOST accurate?

options.A: Integrity was the primary impact, because the patch modified system files on every machine.
options.B: Confidentiality was the primary impact, because cardholder data resided on the crashed ATMs.
options.C: Non-repudiation was the primary impact, because interrupted sessions could no longer be attributed.
options.D: Availability was the primary impact, because authorized customers were denied use of the service.

questions.explanation: The harm the business actually suffered was denial of a legitimate service to authorized users - the definition of an availability impact - so D classifies the incident correctly. A misreads the event: integrity concerns unauthorized or incorrect modification of data, and the investigation confirmed no records were altered; system files changing through an approved patch process is not an integrity compromise, even when the patch is faulty. B is wrong because confidentiality fails only when data is disclosed to unauthorized parties, and none was exposed; sensitive data merely residing on a crashed machine is not a disclosure. C is wrong because non-repudiation concerns a party denying an action they performed, and no completed transactions were in dispute. Classify impact by what the business lost, not by which component happened to break.
questions.recallLine: The patch outage left 5,000 ATMs unusable for eighteen hours. Which classification of the incident's security impact is MOST accurate?

optionsShort.A: Integrity, because the patch modified system files
optionsShort.B: Confidentiality, because cardholder data resided there
optionsShort.C: Non-repudiation, because interrupted sessions lost attribution
optionsShort.D: Availability, because authorized customers were denied service

A.label: true of a different thing
A.wouldAnswer: Which impact classification applies when an attacker alters transaction records on a machine without taking it out of service?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which impact classification applies if the crashed ATMs had spilled cardholder data to an unauthorized party?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which impact classification applies when a customer denies making a transaction the bank cannot attribute to them?

questions.question: Which submission should the board accept as a valid backout plan?

options.A: Restore every affected ATM from the previous month's full system backup if problems appear.
options.B: An uninstall script validated in the staging environment, with defined criteria for when to invoke it.
options.C: Keep the firmware vendor's support line on standby to advise the team if the change fails.
options.D: Re-image affected machines on site as technicians can be dispatched to each location.

questions.explanation: A backout plan is judged on whether it returns systems to a known-good state quickly and whether that has been demonstrated rather than assumed - only one submission was exercised in staging and defines the trigger conditions for invoking it, which is what B provides. A is wrong because restoring month-old full backups rolls every machine back past weeks of legitimate changes and has not been rehearsed at fleet scale; it is a disaster-recovery action, not a change backout. C is wrong because a support line on standby is advice, not a reversal mechanism - nothing in it returns the fleet to its prior state. D is wrong because dispatching technicians to every site is the uncontrolled worst case this incident already demonstrated; a plan whose mechanism is manual site visits concedes the outage without reversing it. Untested recovery is hope, not a plan.
questions.recallLine: The change board is judging four backout plans filed with a dispenser firmware change. Which submission should it accept as a valid backout plan?

optionsShort.A: Restore from last month's full system backup
optionsShort.B: Staging-validated uninstall script with defined trigger criteria
optionsShort.C: Vendor support line on standby for advice
optionsShort.D: Dispatch technicians to re-image machines on site

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: How is an ATM rebuilt after a disaster destroys its entire configuration, not merely one bad change?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Who does the team call for diagnostic help when a firmware change misbehaves in ways the runbook never covered?

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: What remains once a remote backout has failed and individual ATMs must still be returned to a known-good build?

questions.question: Which data-protection design is MOST appropriate for the fifteen-minute requirement?

options.A: Nightly full backups shipped to the recovery site, with weekly restore verification.
options.B: Synchronous replication in which both sites commit every transaction together.
options.C: Transaction-log shipping to the recovery site every ten minutes.
options.D: Hourly incremental backups retained on site and copied to the recovery site.

questions.explanation: A 15-minute recovery point objective bounds acceptable data loss at 15 minutes of committed transactions, and shipping transaction logs every ten minutes meets that bound with margin at modest cost. A is wrong because nightly backups expose up to a full day of transactions - a recovery point roughly a hundred times looser than the requirement.
