B is wrong for the opposite reason: synchronous replication delivers a near-zero RPO the business never asked for, at the price of dedicated bandwidth and added write latency on every transaction, which fails the stem's cost constraint. D is wrong because hourly incrementals still permit four times the tolerated loss. Match the control to the stated objective - undershooting the RPO loses data the business said it cannot lose, and overshooting it spends money the business said it will not spend.
questions.recallLine: Trentham's switch database may lose at most fifteen minutes of committed transactions, without overspending. Which data-protection design is MOST appropriate?

optionsShort.A: Nightly full backups shipped off site
optionsShort.B: Synchronous replication committing at both sites
optionsShort.C: Transaction-log shipping every ten minutes
optionsShort.D: Hourly incrementals copied to the recovery site

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Which backup design suits an archive whose owners can accept losing a day of updates?

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Which replication design fits a switch that can tolerate no measurable transaction loss whatever the bandwidth bill?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Which backup cadence fits a system whose owners accept losing up to an hour of work?

questions.question: Which configuration BEST meets the single-drive-failure requirement while keeping capacity?

options.A: RAID 5 across the four disks, striping data with distributed parity.
options.B: RAID 1 on one mirrored pair, keeping the other two disks as hot spares.
options.C: RAID 0 across the four disks, striping data for the fastest throughput.
options.D: RAID 10, striping data across two mirrored pairs of disks.

questions.explanation: With four disks, striping with distributed parity survives any single-drive failure while leaving three disks of usable capacity - the best ratio of any fault-tolerant option offered. B is wrong because one mirrored pair plus two spares yields only a single disk of usable space, sacrificing most of the capacity for standby redundancy the requirement did not ask for. C is wrong because striping alone has no redundancy at all: one failed drive destroys the entire set, so it fails the core requirement outright. D is wrong on the capacity clause rather than the tolerance one - RAID 10 also survives a single drive failure, but returns only two disks of usable space. When two options both satisfy the fault-tolerance requirement, the stem's capacity constraint is the tiebreaker that separates them.
questions.recallLine: A log-collection server has four drive bays and must survive any single drive failure with as much usable capacity as possible. Which RAID configuration is BEST?

optionsShort.A: RAID 5 striping with distributed parity
optionsShort.B: RAID 1 pair plus two hot spares
optionsShort.C: RAID 0 striping for maximum throughput
optionsShort.D: RAID 10 across two mirrored pairs

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Which layout maximizes redundancy for a small critical volume where usable capacity hardly matters?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which disk layout gives a scratch volume the fastest throughput when the data can be lost?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which fault-tolerant layout is preferred when write performance matters more than usable capacity?

questions.question: Seven years of transaction logs sat on a compromised machine where operations needed ninety days. Which practice would MOST have limited the exposure?

options.A: Encrypting the local transaction logs, with the decryption keys stored on the ATM.
options.B: A data lifecycle policy purging local logs once their 90-day operational need ends.
options.C: Compressing logs older than 90 days into archives to reduce local disk usage.
options.D: Classifying the transaction logs as sensitive so handling requirements attach to them.

questions.explanation: Data that has been destroyed on schedule cannot be stolen later - lifecycle management exists precisely so that information is disposed of when its business need ends, and here it would have cut the exposed data from seven years to 90 days. A is wrong because encryption whose keys sit on the same compromised device yields the attacker both lock and key; even done properly, it protects the data while leaving seven unnecessary years of it in harm's way. C is wrong because compression changes the format, not the presence - every record remains on the machine for the taking. D is wrong because classification is the input to a lifecycle decision, not the decision itself; a sensitivity label on data that should not exist merely documents the exposure. The cheapest data to defend is the data you no longer hold; minimize before you fortify.
questions.recallLine: Seven years of transaction logs sat on a compromised ATM where operations needed only ninety days. Which practice would MOST have limited the exposure?

optionsShort.A: Encrypt local logs with keys on the ATM
optionsShort.B: Purge local logs once operational need ends
optionsShort.C: Compress logs older than ninety days
optionsShort.D: Classify the logs as sensitive data

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which control protects log contents on an ATM whose disk is physically removed by a thief?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: How does an ATM keep years of logs on local disk without running out of space?

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Which step determines what handling and protection requirements attach to transaction logs before disposal rules are written?

questions.question: Which test type should the team conduct FIRST on the unvalidated plan?

options.A: A parallel test, running recovery systems alongside production and comparing their output.
options.B: A tabletop exercise, walking the recovery team through a disaster scenario against the plan.
options.C: A full interruption test, failing production over to the recovery site and back again.
options.D: An unannounced live drill measuring how staff perform under realistic pressure.

questions.explanation: Testing maturity is a ladder, and an unvalidated plan starts on the bottom rung: a tabletop exercise puts the team around a scenario, exposes missing steps, wrong assumptions, and unclear roles, and costs production nothing - exactly what a first validation is for. A is wrong because a parallel test commits real recovery infrastructure and staff time to executing procedures nobody has yet sanity-checked; it is the right test after paper exercises have wrung out the plan's logic. C is wrong because deliberately failing over production is the highest-risk test in the catalog, directly violating management's constraint, and running it against an unvalidated plan is how DR tests become disasters. D is wrong because surprise measures readiness, not correctness - springing an unrehearsed plan on unbriefed staff tests people with a document that has never been proofread. Validate the plan before you validate the performance.
questions.recallLine: Ashcombe's first disaster recovery plan is written but unvalidated, and management will accept no disruption to production. Which test should the team conduct FIRST?

optionsShort.A: Parallel test running recovery beside production
optionsShort.B: Tabletop walkthrough of a disaster scenario
optionsShort.C: Full interruption failover of production
optionsShort.D: Unannounced live drill under realistic pressure

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: Which test comes next once paper exercises have proven the plan's logic and recovery systems can be exercised safely?

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Which test gives final proof that a mature, repeatedly rehearsed plan really works when production is failed over?

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: Which exercise measures how staff perform under pressure once the plan itself has been proven correct?

questions.question: How should the continuity coordinator respond to the thirty-six-hour proposal?

options.A: Accept the proposal, since budget constraints legitimately override planning targets for a year.
options.B: Raise the documented MTD to 48 hours, since the recovery capability actually available should define the tolerance.
options.C: Accept it if the RPO remains within limits, since data loss outweighs downtime.
options.D: Reject the proposal, because the RTO must fit inside the MTD for the recovery to be viable.

questions.explanation: The maximum tolerable downtime is a statement of business fact - the point at which the organization suffers unrecoverable harm - and every recovery objective is derived beneath it. An RTO of 36 hours against a 24-hour MTD is a plan to recover the systems after the business they support has already been irreparably damaged, so the proposal fails on its face and the gap goes to management as a funding-or-risk decision. Budget pressure does not shrink the harm; A's silent acceptance is risk acceptance without the authority or visibility that decision requires. B is wrong because it reverses the derivation - the MTD comes from impact analysis of penalties and losses, and editing the number does not edit the regulator. C is wrong because the RPO governs data loss, an independent axis; flawless data recovered twelve hours too late still breaches the tolerance. Recovery targets cascade downward from business survival, never upward from this year's budget.
questions.recallLine: Settlement can survive twenty-four hours of downtime, yet the IT proposal specifies a thirty-six-hour recovery objective on budget grounds. How should the continuity coordinator respond?

optionsShort.A: Accept it; budget constraints override planning targets
optionsShort.B: Raise the documented MTD to 48 hours
optionsShort.C: Accept if the RPO stays within limits
optionsShort.D: Reject it; the RTO must fit the MTD

A.label: not the decision-maker's
A.wouldAnswer: Who is entitled to accept the residual risk of recovering settlement later than the business can survive?

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Which figure changes when a fresh impact analysis shows settlement can survive longer than previously believed?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which objective must the proposal still satisfy to guarantee no unacceptable loss of committed settlement data?

questions.question: The team must learn what the executable does without endangering other systems or alerting the attacker. Which approach BEST meets these requirements?

options.A: Scan the executable with several locally installed anti-malware engines and record their verdicts.
options.B: Upload the file to a public multi-engine analysis portal and review the community results.
options.C: Detonate the executable in an isolated internal sandbox instrumented to record its behavior.
options.D: Run the executable on a spare workstation on the office network under monitoring tools.

questions.explanation: Learning what a program does means letting it run somewhere its actions are captured and cannot escape - an instrumented, isolated sandbox delivers the behavioral record while containing the blast and keeping the sample in-house. A is wrong because local scanning is static and signature-bound: a custom ATM implant will likely return clean verdicts, and no scan reveals runtime behavior like C2 addresses or dispense commands. The second requirement eliminates B: public portals share uploaded samples, and attackers routinely watch for their own binaries appearing there; the upload itself announces that the implant was found. It is a fine first move for commodity malware with no secrecy concern. D is wrong because a spare workstation on the office network satisfies neither requirement: the malware can spread or beacon out from a live segment, and the machine lacks the instrumentation to capture what happened. Contain the execution, record everything, tell no one outside.
questions.recallLine: The team must learn what the USB executable does without endangering other systems or alerting the attacker. Which approach BEST meets both requirements?

optionsShort.A: Scan it with local anti-malware engines
optionsShort.B: Upload it to a public analysis portal
optionsShort.C: Detonate it in an instrumented isolated sandbox
optionsShort.D: Run it on a spare networked workstation

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Which check quickly establishes whether the file matches any malware signature the bank's engines already know?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: How does an analyst identify a widespread commodity malware sample fast when secrecy does not matter?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: How is trusted software's behavior checked when the only question is how it runs on a spare machine?

questions.question: The fraud team wants the earliest company-specific warning when its cards surface on criminal marketplaces. Which capability BEST provides this?

options.A: A dark web monitoring service watching criminal markets for the bank's card ranges and branding.
options.B: A subscription feed of malware hashes and hostile IP addresses seen across the financial sector.
options.C: Fraud scoring in the authorization stream that flags anomalous use of individual cards.
options.D: A data loss prevention program inspecting outbound corporate traffic for card numbers.

questions.explanation: The signal the team wants lives where stolen cards are sold, so the capability that watches those marketplaces for this bank's specific card ranges is the one that raises the alarm while the data is being offered - before large-scale fraudulent use begins. B is wrong because a generic indicator feed describes attacker infrastructure and tooling across the sector; it says nothing about whether this bank's cards are in the current dump. C is right in kind but wrong on timing: authorization scoring catches the cards as criminals use them, an inherently later stage - it is the right answer to how losses get limited once cards are in play. D is wrong because DLP polices the corporate egress path, and skimmed or breached card data has already left through channels DLP never saw. Intelligence about your own stolen data comes from watching where it is traded, not from tools pointed inward.
questions.recallLine: The fraud team wants the earliest company-specific warning that its own cards are being sold on criminal marketplaces. Which capability BEST provides it?

optionsShort.A: Dark web monitoring for the bank's card ranges
optionsShort.B: Feed of malware hashes and hostile addresses
optionsShort.C: Fraud scoring in the authorization stream
optionsShort.D: DLP inspecting outbound corporate traffic for cards

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Which source tells the SOC which malware samples and hostile addresses are active across the financial sector?

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Which capability limits losses once stolen cards start being used at merchants and machines?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which control stops card numbers leaving the bank's own network through email or web uploads?

questions.question: Which item of evidence is MOST likely to survive an admissibility challenge?

options.A: An analyst's recollection of a forum rumor naming the suspect as an ATM fraudster.
options.B: A hash-verified image of the ATM's drive, collected under a documented chain of custody.
options.C: A junior technician's personal opinion that the malware appeared to be foreign-made.
options.D: A screenshot of the attacker's marketplace listing, sent in by an anonymous tipster.

questions.explanation: Admissible evidence must be relevant to the case, material to its issues, and competent - lawfully obtained and reliable - and the drive image is the only item that can prove its own reliability: the hash values demonstrate the contents are unchanged, and the custody record accounts for every hand it passed through. The rumor A cites is hearsay layered on hearsay: the analyst cannot testify to facts heard third-hand, and no declarant is available to examine. C is wrong because opinion testimony carries weight only from a qualified expert, and a junior technician's impression about malware origin has no established expertise behind it. D is wrong because authenticity cannot be established: an anonymous source means no one can testify to when, where, or how the screenshot was made, or whether it was fabricated. Evidence wins by provenance, and provenance is built at collection time, not at trial.
questions.recallLine: Prosecutors are weighing four items from the skimming case. Which is MOST likely to survive an admissibility challenge?

optionsShort.A: An analyst's recollection of a forum rumor
optionsShort.B: A hash-verified drive image with custody records
optionsShort.C: A junior technician's opinion on malware origin
optionsShort.D: An anonymous tipster's marketplace screenshot

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Which sort of information usefully points investigators toward a suspect long before anything reaches a courtroom?

C.label: not the decision-maker's
C.wouldAnswer: Whose assessment of a malware sample's origin can a court accept as opinion testimony?

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Which material can start an investigation into a marketplace listing even though nobody can vouch for it?

questions.question: Which improvement BEST addresses the volume of identical manual steps?

options.A: Expand the SOC team so the triage workload spreads across more analysts.
options.B: Tune the SIEM to suppress phishing alerts that score below a severity threshold.
options.C: Outsource the alert triage queue to a managed security service provider.
options.D: Implement SOAR playbooks automating the extraction, lookup, search, and quarantine steps.

questions.explanation: Work that is high-volume, well-understood, and identical every time is the defining use case for security orchestration: a playbook executes the extraction, intelligence lookup, mailbox search, and quarantine in seconds per alert, and analysts touch only the cases that need judgment. A is wrong because hiring scales cost linearly with a volume that will keep growing, and it spends scarce analysts on work that requires none of their skill - the right answer only when the workload genuinely demands human judgment. B is wrong because the stem says alert quality is good: suppression works by ignoring alerts, which converts a workload problem into missed phishing incidents. C is wrong because outsourcing relocates the manual toil without removing it, adds a coordination seam during incidents, and bills for exactly the repetitive steps automation would erase. Automate the repeatable; reserve people for decisions.
questions.recallLine: The SOC repeats the same extraction, lookup, mailbox search and quarantine steps on hundreds of phishing alerts a week. Which improvement BEST addresses that volume?

optionsShort.A: Hire more analysts to spread the triage
optionsShort.B: Suppress phishing alerts below a severity threshold
optionsShort.C: Outsource the triage queue to a provider
optionsShort.D: SOAR playbooks automating the repeated steps

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: What is the right response when the backlog is made of cases that genuinely need analyst judgment?

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: How does a SOC cut its queue when most alerts are low-value noise rather than real reports?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: How does a bank get overnight triage coverage when it cannot staff the hours itself?

questions.question: Which assessment of the investigator's two findings is MOST accurate?

options.A: Reading unrelated customer records breaches need-to-know, while the standing admin rights breach least privilege.
options.B: Both findings are a single defect, because the two principles amount to the same control in practice.
options.C: Least privilege governs which records he may read, and need-to-know limits his system permissions.
options.D: Neither finding is a defect, since investigators require broad reach to follow leads across accounts.

questions.explanation: The two principles constrain different things: need-to-know restricts access to information to what the current task requires - twelve accounts, not every customer - while least privilege restricts system rights and permissions to the minimum the role requires, which unused administrative rights plainly exceed. A maps each finding to the principle it violates. B is wrong because the principles are related but distinct; collapsing them hides the fact that fixing one finding leaves the other open. C is wrong because it swaps the definitions - records are information (need-to-know), permissions are rights (least privilege) - and applying the wrong principle produces the wrong remediation owner. Breadth is granted per investigation on demonstrated need, not as standing access; D overstates the investigator's entitlement, and convenience does not create need. When a question mixes data access with system rights, sort each finding into its own principle first.
questions.recallLine: An investigator assigned twelve accounts can read every customer record and holds unused administrative rights. Which assessment of the two findings is MOST accurate?

optionsShort.A: Need-to-know for records; least privilege for rights
optionsShort.B: One defect; the principles are the same
optionsShort.C: Least privilege for records; need-to-know for permissions
optionsShort.D: No defect; investigators need broad reach

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: What do need-to-know and least privilege have in common as expressions of minimizing access?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which principle names each finding if information access and system rights were assigned to the opposite principles?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: How much reach does a fraud investigator get for a case that genuinely spans every customer account?

questions.question: Which action must happen FIRST on the 01:15 bridge call, before any other recovery step begins?

options.A: Send the damage assessment team into the flooded server room to survey the equipment
options.B: Start restoring order entry at the Toledo warm site from the 22:00 backup
options.C: Have the chief operating officer declare a disaster, activating the plan and its contracts
options.D: Have the property insurance broker photograph and document the flooded equipment for the claim

questions.explanation: Everything else on the call is spending someone else's money until one recorded decision exists. Declaration by the named authority is what releases the Toledo contract, the emergency purchase limits and the overtime authorization, and it starts the four-hour clock the plan is measured against. A is the outage assessment, which the plan does need, but it follows declaration, and sending people into an unpowered room full of suppression foam before an incident commander exists is how a recovery injures someone. B is the recovery work itself: a restore nobody has authorized can be countermanded halfway, and the warm site may not yet be contractually available. D is real work the broker owns, and the photographs matter for the claim, but a claim recovers money rather than service and nothing in it gates order entry. Authority first, assessment second, recovery action third, and the order holds for every plan activation.
questions.recallLine: A transformer fire has taken a valve maker's plant and server room offline. Which action comes FIRST when the recovery bridge call convenes?

optionsShort.A: Send assessors into the flooded server room
optionsShort.B: Start the order-entry restore at Toledo
optionsShort.C: The COO formally declares a disaster
optionsShort.D: Photograph the flooded equipment for the claim

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: Once a disaster has been declared, which step tells the incident commander how long the primary plant will be out of service?

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: What does the recovery team do once the warm site has been formally released and the restore authorized?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which activity protects the firm's ability to recover the cost of the ruined equipment rather than the service it ran?

sources: NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 | §4.2 Activation and Notification Phase — activation criteria and declaration authority
ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 7.11.1 Response

questions.question: Which measure MOST reduces the exposure of the relay-protection drawings during the twelve-week overseas assignment?

options.A: Enable full-disk encryption on the engineers' own laptops before they leave Tampa
options.B: Require engineers to report any device inspection or seizure within twenty-four hours
options.C: Issue single-purpose loaner laptops holding just the project drawings, wiped on return
options.D: Register every itinerary with the embassy and brief the team on the advisory

questions.explanation: The exposure that matters is a machine crossing a border and then sitting in a hotel room, and the control that fits it is minimizing what is on the machine at all. A device built for one project holds one project's files; whatever happens to it, the loss is bounded, and re-imaging on return closes the tail risk of what traveled home with it. A protects a laptop that is switched off and lost. It does nothing for a device handed over unlocked at a checkpoint or imaged while the engineer is at dinner, which is the realistic form of this threat. B is the reporting rule that makes credential revocation possible, and the program needs it, but reporting begins after the drawings have been read. D is the traveler-safety half of the same objective and it should be done, yet an embassy registration protects the engineer rather than the drawing set. Bound the data before defending the device.
questions.recallLine: Engineers are taking proprietary substation drawings to a country under a Level 3 advisory for twelve weeks. Which measure MOST reduces the data exposure?

optionsShort.A: Full-disk encryption on the engineers' own laptops
optionsShort.B: Report device inspection or seizure within a day
optionsShort.C: Loaner laptops holding just the project files
optionsShort.D: Embassy itinerary registration and a travel briefing

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which control protects the drawings if an engineer's powered-down laptop is stolen from a hotel safe or left in a taxi?

B.label: detective when preventive is asked
B.wouldAnswer: How does the firm learn that a border inspection may have copied a device, in time to revoke its credentials?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which measure most improves the firm's ability to locate and evacuate its engineers if the advisory is raised mid-assignment?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-19 Access Control for Mobile Devices
NIST SP 800-124 Rev 2 | Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise
ISC2 CISSP Detailed Content Outline 2024 | 7.15.1 Travel

domains.title: Software Development Security
domains.caseStudy:
Domain 8 covers security in the software lifecycle: development methodologies, secure coding, code repositories and build pipelines, application testing, and the risks in software you buy or integrate rather than write.

Case Study: The "GitHub" API Key Leak

### Context

Global Bank built a "Cardless Cash" feature: the mobile app authenticates to a backend API and the ATM dispenses without a card. The right design used OAuth and short-lived tokens. During a hackathon, to save time, the developers hardcoded a master API key into the source. One developer pushed the code to a public GitHub repository to keep working from home.

### What went wrong

Bots that scan GitHub for strings like API_KEY found it within seconds. With the key, attackers authenticated to the backend as an administrator, skipping user authentication entirely. The API did not check whether the caller owned the records it asked for, so any account was readable; one endpoint was vulnerable to injection; and the same access could initiate transfers.

Cardless transactions are, in the white paper's terms, one of the strongest answers to skimming, shimming and card trapping, because there is no card at the fascia to attack. What that trade does is move the trust from the card reader to the mobile app and the API behind it. The paper's section on software vulnerabilities lists the failure modes that then matter: application flaws, insecure configuration, default credentials. It also observes that attack tooling is a commodity now, sold on darknet forums with manuals; scraping bots are the same economics applied to leaked secrets.

### What a practitioner does differently

Secrets never live in code. They live in a vault, are issued to services as short-lived tokens through OAuth 2.0 client credentials, and rotate on a schedule and instantly on suspicion. Secret scanning runs as a pre-commit hook and as a pre-receive hook on the server, so a key cannot reach a repository, public or private.

Authorization is checked per object: every API call verifies the caller owns the record. Queries are parameterized. Both are OWASP Top 10 items (broken access control, injection), and both are found by static analysis and code review before a hackathon branch is anywhere near production. Which is the larger point: hackathon code is a prototype. It enters the normal lifecycle, with threat modelling at design and testing before release, or it does not ship.

Repository policy closes the door the developer walked through: no public repositories for bank code, branch protection, and mandatory review before merge. Monitoring on the API catches an administrator identity doing what no administrator does at 2 AM.

### Outcome

The key was rotated as soon as the leak was found and the public repository taken down. The bank's postmortem added secret scanning to every pipeline, per-object authorization to the API, and a rule that prototype code re-enters the lifecycle at the requirements stage.

### What the exam tests

Expect questions on where security sits in each SDLC phase, on secure coding and the OWASP Top 10 categories this scenario touches (broken access control, injection, identification and authentication failures, cryptographic failures), on secrets management and repository security, on the difference between authentication and authorization, and on why a prototype needs the same gates as production code before it is deployed.

### Related reading

The bank in this scenario is a composite. The trade-off and the controls are documented in:

- [Technical Risks and Attack Vectors Targeting ATMs](https://portfolio.atmavailability.com/atm-technical-risks-white-paper.pdf), the sections on contactless and cardless transactions, on software, OS and firmware vulnerabilities, and on secure development practices for ATM applications.
- [ATM Security Capability Maturity Worksheet](https://portfolio.atmavailability.com/atm-capability-maturity-worksheet.pdf), Domain 2, logical and cybersecurity controls.

stimuli.title: Global Bank: the pipeline rebuild
stimuli.text: Global Bank is rebuilding the build pipeline for Cardless Cash, its cardless ATM withdrawal service, after a master key committed to source reached a public repository. The new design keeps the same three teams and the same weekly release. Secrets move to a managed vault. Builds run on shared runners any team can queue work on, and the repository is private, but every developer can push to the main branch. Nobody can currently say which build produced the artefact running in production. The bank's examiner has asked for evidence that the pipeline enforces the bank's own rules, not merely that the rules exist somewhere.

profile.organization: Global Bank · Cardless Cash mobile app and API
profile.environment: Private repository · shared build runners · weekly release · managed secret vault
profile.state: Pipeline rebuild after a hardcoded key reached a public repository

stimuli.title: A key in a public repository
stimuli.text: A monitoring service tells Global Bank that a production API key for its Cardless Cash service, the mobile app that lets customers withdraw at an ATM without a card, is sitting in a public repository. A developer pushed it there three days ago while working from home during a hackathon, and scanning bots reach new repositories within seconds. The key grants administrative access to the transaction backend. It is also compiled into the Android and iOS clients already in the app stores. The bank bought a managed secret vault last year and never wired it into anything, and nothing in its process would stop a credential being committed.

profile.organization: Global Bank · Cardless Cash mobile app and API
profile.environment: Hackathon build · public repository · clients already in the app stores
profile.state: Key public for three days, still valid

stimuli.title: Walking a payment API endpoint by endpoint
stimuli.text: Coastal Savings processes card transactions for its own customers and for eight hundred merchants. An administrator credential has been found reaching its backend from outside the company, and the security team is now walking the customer API endpoint by endpoint. Statements are served from a path carrying the account number in the query string. The login endpoint builds its database query by concatenating the values submitted to it. Nothing in the API records which caller owns which record. Forensic work has been slow: the servers keep seven days of logs, application logins were never recorded at all, and log review is a manual quarterly task.

profile.environment: REST API · mobile and web clients · seven-day log retention
profile.state: Administrator credential found reaching the backend from outside

stimuli.title: A penetration test of the customer portal
stimuli.text: Global Bank commissioned a penetration test of its customer web portal, the browser front end customers use for statements and transfers. The testers were given one customer login and nothing else. Every finding sits in a part of the portal that renders or fetches content on a user's behalf: a review board that stores and redisplays what customers type, the funds-transfer form, a document download endpoint that takes a filename, and a link-preview feature that fetches whatever URL a user supplies. The portal runs inside the bank's cloud account, on instances that can reach the cloud provider's own metadata service.

profile.environment: Browser front end for statements and transfers · runs in the bank's cloud account
profile.state: Test complete, four findings reported

stimuli.title: The oldest code in the estate
stimuli.text: Northbridge Clearing settles interbank payments and takes files and messages from card processors and correspondent banks all day. Its partner integration service is the oldest code it runs: a C daemon that parses binary payment messages, a Java component that accepts serialized objects from partner systems over the internet and rebuilds them in memory, and an XML invoice upload used by three suppliers. A destination-account field feeds several downstream systems, and the team maintains an ever-growing filter of known malicious strings against it. None of the service has ever been fuzzed, and a settlement transfer crashed the daemon last week.

profile.environment: C payment daemon · Java object stream · XML invoice upload
profile.state: Never fuzzed; the daemon crashed last week

stimuli.title: How a portal holds a session
stimuli.text: Kestrel Mutual, a general insurer, has commissioned a review of how its policyholder portal handles a session once someone has signed in. The login page is served over HTTPS and every page after it over plain HTTP. The session cookie can be read by any script running in the page, and is transmitted whenever a user follows a link over an unencrypted connection. Version control shows a URL one developer added during testing to save time and never removed. The application server underneath was deployed straight from the vendor's installer and has never been hardened.

profile.environment: HTTPS login, HTTP thereafter · application server from the vendor's installer
profile.state: Review of session handling only

stimuli.title: Global Bank: four programs, four models
stimuli.text: Global Bank's program office is starting four builds in one quarter and must pick a delivery model for each. A regulatory reporting system is fixed by contract: every requirement is agreed up front, formal documentation with approval gates at every stage is mandated, and scope cannot change without a contract modification. A new consumer feature enters a market whose customer needs are poorly understood and expected to shift every few weeks. A multi-year biometric authentication program depends on technology nobody has proved. And a claims-processing interface has produced two contradictory requirements documents from stakeholders who cannot say what they need.

profile.regime: Banking examination · fixed-price supplier contract on one program
profile.environment: Four builds starting in the same quarter
profile.state: Delivery model not yet chosen for any of them

stimuli.title: Two squads, two cadences
stimuli.text: Global Bank's payments squad has moved to two-week sprints and ships a product increment at the end of each one. Defects keep reaching production anyway. The regulator has told the bank that no change to the payment module may be written and merged by a single unreviewed developer, and expects that review to happen as early in development as possible. Marketing has separately put another squad on a hard launch date using time-boxed cycles, heavy prototyping and minimal up-front design, and the CISO has been asked what that approach costs in security terms.

profile.organization: Global Bank · payments and marketing squads
profile.regime: Banking examination · regulator directive on the payment module
profile.environment: Two-week sprints, an increment each sprint · a second squad on a hard launch date
profile.state: Defects still reaching production

stimuli.title: A firm that cannot show how it builds
stimuli.text: Ardent Systems writes software for payment terminals. It lost a government bid because it could not demonstrate the maturity of its development processes: internally, project success still depends on individual heroics and no two teams work alike. An improvement program has been funded and the team wants to start rewriting development procedures immediately. Its terminal firmware is separately certified, and the certifier demands evidence that defects are prevented during development rather than found and patched afterwards, with failure rates certified statistically. Two shortcuts taken to hit a deadline a year ago, a hardcoded credential and skipped input validation, still have open tickets and a tripled estimate.

profile.environment: No two teams work alike · terminal firmware certified separately
profile.state: Improvement program funded after a lost bid

stimuli.title: Twenty deploys a day
stimuli.text: Vantage Retail deploys to production twenty times a day through an automated pipeline. Security review is manual, performed by a separate team in the week before each quarterly compliance audit, so findings routinely reach developers months after the code shipped. A rewritten authentication service has passed every test and is ready to ship, but leadership fears an unforeseen defect could lock out the entire customer base at once. The company is in an acrimonious layoff period and a database administrator due to leave still holds commit access. The product manager has begun showing a redesigned login page to half of all users.

profile.environment: Automated pipeline, twenty production deploys a day · manual security review before each audit
profile.state: Rewritten authentication service ready to ship

stimuli.title: A flaw in a library everybody uses
stimuli.text: A critical flaw is announced in a widely used open-source logging library, and exploitation is already being reported. Global Bank runs four hundred applications and cannot say within hours which of them embed a vulnerable version, including the dependencies pulled in automatically during builds. In the same week a network-management vendor discloses that its customers were breached through a signed, official product update: investigators found the vendor's build server had been compromised months before. And the bank's own VPN appliance carries an actively exploited flaw for which the manufacturer says no patch will exist for several weeks.

profile.environment: Open-source logging library in unknown numbers of builds · vendor-supplied VPN appliance
profile.state: Flaw announced, exploitation already reported

stimuli.title: Two hundred services, no shared plumbing
stimuli.text: Trellis Pay is moving its payments backend off self-managed virtual machines. Two hundred microservices call each other directly, and security now requires mutual TLS and per-call authorization between every pair; modifying two hundred codebases has been ruled out as infeasible. A review of the container platform finds application containers running as root, built from unscanned images pulled from public registries, on shared hosts. A document-processing workload is moving to a serverless functions platform. The architects want the new payment API's threats enumerated before code is written, and the API it replaces is already taking millions of requests enumerating sequential customer identifiers, with stolen credential lists replayed against its login.

profile.environment: Two hundred microservices · container platform on shared hosts · serverless functions
profile.state: Moving off self-managed virtual machines

stimuli.title: A first application security lead
stimuli.text: Global Bank has hired its first application security lead into a company with no existing program, a small training budget and no secure-coding standard, and the lead must choose a starting point for developer training. A threat-modeling workshop for the trading platform has just produced forty distinct threats, far more than the team can address this quarter, and the lead needs a repeatable way to decide which ones get remediation effort first. A separate review is examining an episode in which a master API key became readable by anyone browsing a public repository, and is classifying each event in it.

profile.organization: Global Bank · new application security function
profile.environment: No existing program · small training budget · trading platform under review
profile.state: Lead in post four weeks

stimuli.title: Three incidents on the store estate
stimuli.text: Vantage Retail's in-store machines run a fixed, unchanging set of approved applications and staff cannot administer them. The security team is reviewing three incidents from the quarter. On one server, firewall logs show connections that no local tool reports: process listings, file searches and the installed antivirus all show nothing unusual. Antivirus quarantines one variant of a malware family, yet new infections keep appearing, each sample carrying a different hash and byte pattern while behaving identically on the host. And help-desk tickets reveal that several employees installed a free PDF converter which works as advertised and also opens a remote-control channel.

profile.environment: Fixed set of approved applications · staff cannot administer their machines
profile.state: Quarterly incident review

stimuli.title: An overnight spread, and two peer reports
stimuli.text: Overnight, malware spread to hundreds of Halden Logistics servers across a flat internal network while no user was logged in anywhere: each infected host scanned for neighbors exposing the same vulnerable file-sharing service and infected them directly. Through the sector information-sharing group it belongs to, the company received two reports the same week. A university network team traced abuse complaints to two hundred campus workstations making identical periodic connections to one overseas domain from which they fetch commands. A hospital paid attackers to recover encrypted patient records. An analyst is separately classifying code that appends itself to spreadsheet macro files.

profile.environment: Hundreds of servers on one flat segment · two peer reports received the same week
profile.state: Spread contained, committee prioritizing

stimuli.title: Global Bank: the reporting warehouse
stimuli.text: Global Bank's reporting warehouse serves branch operations, fraud analytics and its cash-in-transit contractor from one database. A customer's mailing address differs across three tables: an update routine changed one copy and missed the others, and refunds are being posted to an outdated address. The fraud reporting view hides individual case records but permits statistical queries. The contractor holds access to three datasets each rated non-sensitive on its own: vehicle maintenance schedules, fuel purchases and crew duty rosters. Nobody has reviewed what those three together would tell a reader, because each was approved on its own rating.

profile.environment: One database serving branch operations, fraud analytics and a logistics contractor
profile.state: Data-quality review after misdirected refunds

questions.question: The examiner wants evidence that the pipeline enforces the bank's rules rather than merely documenting them. Which approach BEST produces that evidence?

options.A: A quarterly audit sampling merged changes against the written development standard.
options.B: A checklist each team lead signs before a release is promoted into production.
options.C: Policy expressed as machine-checked pipeline rules that fail the build and record the result.
options.D: A dashboard showing how many findings each team closed in the most recent release.

questions.explanation: An examiner asking for enforcement is asking for something that cannot have been skipped, and a rule that runs is the only artefact on this list with that property. It also produces its own evidence as a by-product, which is the second half of what was asked. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-50 Software-Enforced Separation and Policy Enforcement is the nearest control in the catalog, and it is new in Revision 5; CM-6 Configuration Settings governs the settings the rules assert. NIST SP 800-218 PO.3.3 requires the toolchain to be configured to generate artifacts that support the security checks. Worth being precise: the phrase software-defined security appears in no NIST document, so SC-50 is a functional match rather than a name match, and it should be presented that way. A is detective when preventive is asked, sampling a quarter after the fact. B is symptom not cause, capturing a person's assertion rather than an enforced condition. D is the right control for a different problem, measuring remediation throughput. Evidence is what the machine produced, not what the team promised.
questions.recallLine: An examiner wants proof the pipeline enforces the rules rather than documenting them. What produces it?

optionsShort.A: Quarterly audit sampling merges
optionsShort.B: Team lead checklist before promotion
optionsShort.C: Machine-checked rules that fail builds
optionsShort.D: Dashboard of findings closed

A.label: detective when preventive is asked
A.wouldAnswer: How does the bank confirm periodically that enforced rules still match the written standard?

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: How is accountability for a release assigned to a named person?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: How does the bank track whether teams are working through their open findings?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-50 Software-Enforced Separation and Policy Enforcement (new in Rev 5); CM-6 Configuration Settings
NIST SP 800-218 | PO.3.3 toolchain generates supporting artifacts

questions.question: Any team can queue work on the shared build runners. Which risk does that arrangement MOST directly create for the Cardless Cash release?

options.A: One team's build step can read another team's secrets or artefacts.
options.B: Builds will queue behind each other and the weekly release will slip.
options.C: Teams will adopt different build tools and the artefacts will diverge.
options.D: The runners will fall behind on operating-system patches between releases.

questions.explanation: A build runner is a machine that holds every credential its jobs need and every artefact they produce, and a shared runner holds all of them at once. A job is arbitrary code by definition, so the team that queues it inherits whatever the runner can reach, and the vault the bank has just bought does not help once a job can ask the vault on someone else's behalf. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-6 Least Privilege, SC-2 Separation of System and User Functionality, and SC-4 Information in Shared System Resources are the controls that name this class of exposure; note that SC-2's Revision 4 title was Application Partitioning. NIST SP 800-218 PO.5 requires environments involved in software development to be separated and protected. B is the right control for a different problem, a capacity concern rather than a security one. C is wrong scope, a consistency issue between teams rather than a boundary failure inside one runner. D is a correct action but not the first one, a real maintenance gap that shared queueing did not cause. Ask what the runner can reach.
questions.recallLine: Any team can queue jobs on shared build runners. Which risk does that most directly create?

optionsShort.A: Cross-team access to secrets and artefacts
optionsShort.B: Queueing delays the weekly release
optionsShort.C: Divergent build tools between teams
optionsShort.D: Runners fall behind on patching

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: What should the platform team plan for if release throughput is the concern?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: What does a shared toolchain standard fix across three independent teams?

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: What maintenance obligation applies to build infrastructure regardless of who queues on it?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 Least Privilege; SC-2 Separation of System and User Functionality (renamed from Rev 4 Application Partitioning); SC-4 Information in Shared System Resources
NIST SP 800-218 | PO.5 secure development environments

questions.question: The key is still live and the repository is still public. What should the team do FIRST?

options.A: Delete the offending file from the repository and rewrite its commit history to purge the key
options.B: Make the repository private so that no additional external parties can view the key
options.C: Revoke the exposed key immediately and issue a replacement through approved channels
options.D: Interview the developer to establish how the key came to be committed and pushed

questions.explanation: Automated bots scrape public repositories for credential patterns within seconds of a push; after three days, the only safe assumption is that the key has already been copied. Nothing that changes who can see the repository going forward alters that, so the first move is to make the stolen value worthless: revoke it and reissue through a proper channel (C), then hunt for fraudulent use during the exposure window. A treats the visible symptom: history rewriting is worth doing afterward for hygiene, but it cannot recall the copies already harvested, and doing it first leaves an active admin credential in attackers' hands meanwhile. B fails the same way: private visibility stops future viewers, not past ones. D matters for the lessons-learned and for fixing the process, but root-cause interviews come after containment, not before it.
questions.recallLine: A production API key with administrative access has sat in a public repository for three days. What should the team do FIRST?

optionsShort.A: Delete the file and rewrite commit history
optionsShort.B: Make the repository private
optionsShort.C: Revoke the key and reissue it
optionsShort.D: Interview the developer about the commit

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Once the credential is dead, what clears the secret out of stored history so it stops appearing in every fresh clone?

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: What keeps a repository that has never leaked from being read by parties outside the bank?

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: Once the exposure is contained, what establishes why the bank's process let a credential be committed and pushed at all?

questions.question: Commits containing secrets must be blocked before they reach the central repository, in a way an individual developer cannot bypass from their own machine. Which mechanism BEST meets this?

options.A: A server-side pre-receive hook that scans incoming pushes and rejects any containing secrets
options.B: A client-side pre-commit hook on every developer workstation that runs local secret scanning
options.C: A nightly scheduled job that scans the repository contents and alerts on any secrets found
options.D: A mandatory code-review checklist item requiring reviewers to look for embedded credentials

questions.explanation: The requirement has two halves, enforcement before the secret enters the shared repository and enforcement developers cannot switch off, and only a control running on the server itself satisfies both. A pre-receive hook (A) evaluates every push at the moment the server is asked to accept it and refuses the whole push if a secret is detected: nothing to install, nothing to bypass. B is the closest wrong answer: client-side hooks give excellent fast feedback, but they live on machines the developer controls: they can be skipped with a flag, and a fresh clone simply does not have them; they complement the server hook, they cannot replace it. C is wrong on timing: by the nightly run the secret has been in shared history for hours, cloned and mirrored. D is wrong because human review is fallible, and in pull-request workflows the code has already been pushed to the server before anyone reviews it. Guarantees of the form 'never enters the repository' can only be enforced where the repository lives.
questions.recallLine: Commits carrying secrets must be blocked before they reach the bank's central repository, unbypassable from a developer's own machine. Which mechanism BEST meets this?

optionsShort.A: Server-side pre-receive hook rejecting pushes containing secrets
optionsShort.B: Client-side pre-commit hook on each workstation
optionsShort.C: Nightly scan of repository contents, alerting
optionsShort.D: Code-review checklist item for embedded credentials

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Which control gives a developer the fastest possible warning about a secret, before a commit is even created locally?

C.label: detective when preventive is asked
C.wouldAnswer: Which check surfaces secrets committed before any blocking control existed and still sitting in the repository today?

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Which practice catches design and logic mistakes in a proposed change that no automated scanner can recognize?

questions.question: Investigators establish the attackers were active for five months and no alert ever fired. Which improvement should the security program prioritize?

options.A: Deploying stronger encryption for stored data so future intrusions yield nothing readable
options.B: Centralized log collection with longer retention and automated alerting on suspicious activity
options.C: Commissioning an annual external penetration test to uncover exploitable weaknesses
options.D: Adopting a stricter rotation schedule for all privileged administrator account passwords

questions.explanation: Five months of undetected activity is a visibility failure, and the stem lists its three ingredients: logs that expire in a week, security-relevant events never captured, and review too infrequent and manual to notice anything. The remedy attacks all three (B): collect logs centrally where intruders cannot quietly erase them, retain them well beyond realistic dwell times so investigations have evidence, and let automation watch continuously so detection happens in hours, not quarters. A is wrong because encryption protects confidentiality against stolen media and eavesdroppers; attackers operating through compromised applications and accounts read data exactly as legitimate users do, and encryption restores no visibility. C is a point-in-time probe for ways in; this organization's demonstrated failure is not knowing when someone is already inside. D is wrong because nothing ties the intrusion to stale passwords, and rotation would not have surfaced the five-month presence. Fix the control family the incident actually indicts. Long dwell times indict detection, so build logging and monitoring before buying more prevention.
questions.recallLine: Attackers worked inside Coastal Savings' payment API for five months and no alert ever fired. Which improvement should the security program prioritize?

optionsShort.A: Stronger encryption for stored data
optionsShort.B: Central logs, longer retention, automated alerting
optionsShort.C: An annual external penetration test
optionsShort.D: Stricter rotation of privileged account passwords

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which control keeps payment data unreadable to someone who walks off with a backup tape or a decommissioned disk?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Which exercise gives the bank an independent measure, once a year, of how hard its API is to break into?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which control limits how long a compromised administrator password stays usable after it has leaked?

questions.question: Simply viewing a certain product review causes browsers to send their session cookies to an unknown domain; script tags stored in the review text are rendered verbatim to every visitor. Which remediation MOST directly addresses this?

options.A: Add anti-forgery tokens to every state-changing form so requests from other sites are rejected
options.B: Move all pages to HTTPS so session cookies are protected from network eavesdropping
options.C: Use parameterized queries so review text is treated as data, not command structure
options.D: Encode user-supplied content on output so browsers render it as text rather than script

questions.explanation: This is stored cross-site scripting: attacker-supplied markup was saved and later delivered into victims' pages, where the browser executed it. The defect is at the rendering step, so the direct fix is contextual output encoding (D): the stored text is displayed as inert characters, never parsed as script; a Content Security Policy and HttpOnly cookies add depth. A is wrong because anti-forgery tokens counter CSRF, where an attacker forges requests using the victim's session; here the attacker injected script, a different mechanism. B is wrong because TLS protects cookies in transit; these cookies are being read and exfiltrated by script running inside the page itself, over any transport. C is wrong because parameterized queries stop SQL injection; the review was stored through a legitimate write, and the database behaved correctly throughout.
questions.recallLine: Script tags stored in a product review render verbatim and send every viewer's session cookie to an unknown domain. Which remediation MOST directly addresses this?

optionsShort.A: Anti-forgery tokens on state-changing forms
optionsShort.B: Move all portal pages to HTTPS
optionsShort.C: Parameterized queries for stored review text
optionsShort.D: Encode user content on output as text

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which control stops a malicious site from making a signed-in customer's browser submit a transfer they never intended?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which change keeps a session cookie from being read by anyone watching the network between customer and bank?

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Which fix stops submitted text from altering the structure of the database command that stores it?

questions.question: A crash dump shows an oversized message-length field overwriting the C daemon's return address, after which the service executed attacker-supplied instructions. Which change BEST addresses the root cause?

options.A: Validate length fields and use bounds-checked memory operations for every buffer write
options.B: Enable address space layout randomization so injected code lands at unpredictable locations
options.C: Filter inbound packets at the network firewall to drop traffic from untrusted address ranges
options.D: Raise the service's logging level so malformed packets are recorded for later investigation

questions.explanation: A buffer overflow happens when code writes more data into a buffer than was allocated, corrupting adjacent memory, in this case the saved return address. The root cause is the unchecked write, so the fix is in the code: validate untrusted length fields and use bounds-checked operations so an oversized value can no longer spill past the buffer (A); migrating hot paths to a memory-safe language is the same idea taken further. B is wrong as the answer here because ASLR is an exploit mitigation: it makes a successful overflow harder to weaponize but leaves the memory-corruption defect in place; it is the right answer for hardening a platform in depth. C fails because the service must accept client packets to function, and any permitted source can send the malformed field; that is scope, not cause. D is wrong because logging is detective; it records the compromise without preventing it. Mitigations raise attacker cost, but only correct code removes the vulnerability.
questions.recallLine: An oversized message-length field overwrote the C daemon's return address and the service then ran attacker instructions. Which change BEST addresses the root cause?

optionsShort.A: Validate lengths and bounds-check every buffer write
optionsShort.B: Enable ASLR so injected code lands unpredictably
optionsShort.C: Drop untrusted address ranges at the firewall
optionsShort.D: Raise logging so malformed packets are recorded

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: Which platform hardening measure makes a memory-corruption bug harder to weaponise while the defective code still runs?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Which measure keeps address ranges with no business reason to talk to the settlement daemon from reaching it?

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: What gives investigators the malformed messages they need to reconstruct how the daemon crashed?

questions.question: An uploaded invoice whose DOCTYPE declaration defines an external entity pointing at /etc/passwd returns that file's contents. Which change BEST fixes this flaw at its source?

options.A: Validate that uploaded invoices are well-formed XML before passing them to the parser
options.B: Configure the XML parser to disable document type definitions and external entity resolution
options.C: Run the upload service in a container so its file reads are confined to the container image
options.D: Scan uploaded files with antivirus to reject those containing known malicious markup

questions.explanation: XML external entity injection is unusual among injection flaws: the vulnerability is a feature, not a bug. The parser is doing exactly what DTD processing specifies, resolving an entity that happens to point at a local file, so the source-level fix is configuration: turn off DTDs and external entity resolution in the parser (B), and the attack ceases to be expressible. A is wrong because the tester's exploit file is perfectly well-formed XML; well-formedness checks syntax, and this attack is syntactically impeccable. C is wrong because containment shrinks the blast radius without fixing the flaw: everything inside the container, including its own credentials and configuration secrets, remains readable, and SSRF-style entity fetches still reach the network. It is reasonable defense in depth. D is wrong because antivirus recognizes known malware, and a three-line DOCTYPE crafted for this one application matches nothing in a signature set. When a parser's features are the attack surface, hardening its configuration is the fix, a lesson that generalizes to any dangerous default.
questions.recallLine: An uploaded invoice whose DOCTYPE points at /etc/passwd returns that file's contents to the supplier. Which change BEST fixes the flaw at its source?

optionsShort.A: Check uploads are well-formed XML first
optionsShort.B: Disable DTDs and entity resolution
optionsShort.C: Run the upload service in a container
optionsShort.D: Antivirus-scan uploads for malicious markup

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Which check rejects a supplier upload that is truncated or malformed before the parser chokes on it?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Which measure limits what an attacker can read once a parser flaw is already being exploited?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Which check catches a supplier upload carrying a known malware sample rather than crafted markup?

questions.question: Which pair of cookie attributes MOST directly closes the script-access and unencrypted-transport exposures together?

options.A: Domain and Path, which limit the hosts and URL prefixes to which the cookie is sent
options.B: HttpOnly and Secure, which deny script access and restrict the cookie to encrypted transport
options.C: Max-Age and Expires, which bound how long the browser retains the session cookie
options.D: SameSite and Path, which control whether cross-site navigation includes the cookie

questions.explanation: Map each finding to the attribute built for it: script access to the cookie is removed by HttpOnly, which hides the cookie from the page's JavaScript so even a successful XSS payload cannot read it; cleartext transmission is removed by Secure, which forbids the browser from sending the cookie over anything but an encrypted connection (B). A is wrong because Domain and Path only scope which requests include the cookie; within that scope, scripts can still read it and HTTP links still carry it. D is wrong for the same reason at a different boundary: SameSite governs whether cross-site requests attach the cookie, which is a CSRF defense, and neither finding involves cross-site requests. C is wrong because lifetime limits shrink the window of misuse without closing either exposure: a cookie can be stolen by script or sniffed off the wire in its first minute.
questions.recallLine: Kestrel Mutual's session cookie is readable by page scripts and travels over plain HTTP. Which pair of cookie attributes MOST directly closes both exposures?

optionsShort.A: Domain and Path, scoping hosts and prefixes
optionsShort.B: HttpOnly and Secure, denying scripts and cleartext
optionsShort.C: Max-Age and Expires, bounding cookie lifetime
optionsShort.D: SameSite and Path, governing cross-site navigation

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Which attributes keep a session cookie from being sent to unrelated subdomains or unrelated paths on the same site?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Which attributes bound how long a stolen session cookie stays usable in the thief's browser?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which attribute keeps the browser from attaching the session cookie to a request that originated on another site?

questions.question: Leadership wants working software delivered early and refined continuously from real user feedback. Which approach BEST fits the consumer feature?

options.A: Waterfall, since completing the full design before coding avoids expensive rework later
options.B: Cleanroom, since formally verified increments give the highest confidence in each release
options.C: Agile, since short iterations and continuous customer feedback absorb changing requirements
options.D: The V-model, since pairing every build phase with a matching test phase catches defects early

questions.explanation: Rapidly shifting requirements plus a demand for early, continuously refined releases are the exact conditions iterative Agile methods were created for: each short cycle delivers working software and folds user feedback into the next. A is wrong because Waterfall assumes requirements can be fixed before design begins — here they cannot, so the finished design would describe the wrong product; it is the right answer when requirements are stable and change is prohibited. B is wrong because Cleanroom's formal specification and verification are slow and assume a precise spec exists; it suits safety-critical software, not a moving target. D is wrong because the V-model is still a sequential, plan-driven shape; its paired test phases verify a fixed specification and cannot absorb change.
questions.recallLine: Leadership wants the new consumer feature delivered early and refined continuously from real user feedback in a market that shifts every few weeks. Which approach fits BEST?

optionsShort.A: Waterfall, full design completed before coding
optionsShort.B: Cleanroom, formally verified increments each release
optionsShort.C: Agile, short iterations absorbing changing requirements
optionsShort.D: V-model, each build phase paired with testing

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: Which model suits the regulatory reporting build, whose requirements are agreed up front and cannot move without a contract change?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which method suits software whose certifier demands formal verification and statistically certified failure rates?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which model suits a stable specification that must be verified stage by stage, with a test level answering every design level?

questions.question: The delivery lead wants claims-processing stakeholders to react to something concrete before the team commits to full development. Which approach BEST serves this goal?

options.A: Completing a comprehensive requirements specification and having every stakeholder sign it
options.B: Adopting cleanroom methods so that defects are formally prevented from the earliest phase
options.C: Proceeding directly to full construction so users can react to the finished system itself
options.D: Building a limited working model of the interface for stakeholders to evaluate and refine

questions.explanation: When stakeholders cannot say what they want, showing beats asking: a prototype (D) gives them something concrete to react to, converts vague or contradictory wishes into specific corrections, and costs little enough to throw away and iterate, which is the entire reason prototyping exists as a development approach. A doubles down on the technique that has already failed twice; signatures on an ambiguous document create commitment, not clarity, and the conflicts will resurface as change requests during build. B is wrong because cleanroom's formal rigor prevents implementation defects; it verifies the software against its specification, and here the specification itself is the problem: a formally verified wrong product is still wrong. C is wrong because it takes the largest possible bet on the least information; feedback arrives only after the full cost is sunk, when rework is most expensive. Prototype when requirements are the risk; formalize when correctness against known requirements is the risk.
questions.recallLine: Claims-processing stakeholders have produced two contradictory requirements documents. Which approach BEST gives them something concrete to react to before the team commits?

optionsShort.A: A comprehensive specification, signed by every stakeholder
optionsShort.B: Cleanroom methods preventing defects formally
optionsShort.C: Proceed directly to full construction
optionsShort.D: A limited working model for stakeholders to evaluate

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Which step is right once stakeholders genuinely agree, giving the build a baseline that scope changes must be measured against?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which method suits a build whose specification is trusted and whose implementation defects must be prevented rather than found later?

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: Which course is defensible when requirements are stable, well understood, and the team has built the same interface before?

questions.question: Which pairing of Extreme Programming practices MOST directly catches defects at the moment the code is being written?

options.A: The planning game and small releases, which shorten the feedback loop with customers
options.B: Collective code ownership and coding standards, which keep the code base uniform
options.C: On-site customer and system metaphor, which keep development aligned with business intent
options.D: Pair programming and test-driven development, which review and test code as it is typed

questions.explanation: The discriminator is at the moment the code is being written, and two XP practices operate at exactly that instant (D): in test-driven development the failing test exists before the code, so the first run verifies the new logic immediately; in pair programming a second developer is reviewing each line as it appears, catching slips that the author is blind to. Together they are XP's tightest defect-feedback loop. A operates at the wrong range: the planning game and small releases work at release granularity; they surface wrong priorities and integration surprises in days or weeks, not keystrokes. B is wrong because shared ownership and standards improve maintainability and consistency, which prevents some future defects but examines nothing as it is created. C is wrong because the on-site customer and metaphor align the product with business intent: they catch building the wrong thing, not building the thing wrong.
questions.recallLine: Which pairing of Extreme Programming practices MOST directly catches defects at the moment payment code is being typed?

optionsShort.A: Planning game and small releases
optionsShort.B: Collective ownership and coding standards
optionsShort.C: On-site customer and system metaphor
optionsShort.D: Pair programming and test-driven development

A.wouldAnswer: Which XP practices surface wrong priorities and integration surprises within days, by putting small releases in front of the customer?

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: Which XP practices let any developer safely change any part of a codebase months later without it fragmenting in style?

questions.question: The certifier wants defects prevented during development rather than found and patched afterwards, with failure rates certified statistically. Which software engineering approach aligns BEST?

options.A: Extreme Programming, relying on test-driven development and continuous pair review
options.B: Cleanroom engineering, using formal specification, verification, and statistical quality control
options.C: Rapid application development, iterating prototypes quickly until users accept the behavior
options.D: Scrum, delivering the firmware in sprints with a defect backlog groomed by the product owner

questions.explanation: The regulator's two demands are the two pillars of cleanroom software engineering (B): defects are prevented before test through formal specification and mathematically based verification of the code, and quality is then demonstrated through statistical usage testing that supports certified reliability claims, precisely the evidence sought. A is the strongest wrong answer: TDD and pair programming are powerful, but they find defects moments after they are written; that is still detect-and-fix, not formal prevention, and XP offers no statistical certification of failure rates. It is the right choice for quality-focused commercial teams without a certification burden. C is wrong because RAD optimizes speed and user acceptance; its tolerance for rough prototypes is the opposite of certifiable rigor. D is wrong because Scrum is a management wrapper that explicitly routes defects into a backlog for later resolution; it prescribes no engineering rigor at all.
questions.recallLine: The firmware certifier wants defects prevented during development rather than patched afterwards, with failure rates certified statistically. Which engineering approach aligns BEST?

optionsShort.A: Extreme Programming, test-driven development and pair review
optionsShort.B: Cleanroom, formal specification, verification, statistical quality control
optionsShort.C: RAD, iterating prototypes until users accept
optionsShort.D: Scrum, sprints with a groomed defect backlog

A.wouldAnswer: Which approach suits a commercial team that wants defects caught within minutes of being written, without a certification burden?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which approach fits a project whose requirements must be discovered from user reaction against a hard deadline?

questions.question: The administrator inserts code that will delete the payroll tables if his employee ID ever disappears from the HR system. Which safeguard would MOST likely catch this insertion before it reaches production?

options.A: Antivirus scanning on the database server to detect malicious executable files
options.B: Full-disk encryption of the storage volumes holding the payroll tables
options.C: An annual disaster-recovery exercise proving that payroll can be restored intact from backup tapes
options.D: Mandatory peer review of every code change before it can be merged and deployed

questions.explanation: This is a logic bomb: legitimate-looking code carrying a malicious trigger. Because it is written by an authorized insider and contains no malware signature, the control most likely to catch it is another human reading the change. Mandatory peer review (D) puts a second set of eyes on a deletion routine conditioned on an HR lookup, an obvious red flag, and its mere existence deters the attempt. A fails because the bomb is source code committed through normal channels, not a foreign binary; antivirus is the right answer for commodity malware dropped onto the host. B is wrong because encryption protects confidentiality of data at rest, and the bomb will delete data through fully authorized paths that decrypt transparently. C is wrong for this question because recovery exercises are corrective; they limit the damage after detonation, which makes them the right answer to reducing impact, not to catching the insertion beforehand. Insider code threats are defeated by process controls on the change pipeline, not by malware tooling.
questions.recallLine: A departing administrator inserts code that deletes the payroll tables if his employee ID leaves the HR system. Which safeguard would MOST likely catch it beforehand?

optionsShort.A: Antivirus scanning on the database server
optionsShort.B: Full-disk encryption of the payroll volumes
optionsShort.C: An annual disaster-recovery restore exercise
optionsShort.D: Mandatory peer review of every code change

A.wouldAnswer: Which control catches a known malware binary dropped onto the database server by an outside attacker?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which control keeps payroll records unreadable if the storage volumes are stolen or disposed of carelessly?
