C.wouldAnswer: Which exercise proves payroll can actually be brought back once the data has already been destroyed?

questions.question: Every customer who applied the vendor's legitimate update received the implant. Which term BEST describes this attack?

options.A: A watering-hole attack, since victims were compromised at a resource they habitually trust
options.B: Spear phishing, since the malicious payload reached a specifically chosen set of targets
options.C: A supply chain attack, since the vendor's build pipeline was subverted to reach its customers
options.D: An insider threat, since the compromise originated within the vendor's own build systems

questions.explanation: The attackers never touched the victims directly: they compromised a supplier's build pipeline so that the trusted product itself became the delivery vehicle, arriving with a valid signature through the official update channel, which is the definition of a supply chain attack (C) and the SolarWinds pattern precisely. The signature is what makes it devastating: the victims' verification checks passed, because the code was signed after the implant was inserted. A is the closest wrong answer: a watering hole also exploits a trusted habit, but it poisons a website the targets visit and exploits their browsers there; here the poison traveled inside a purchased product's update, not a webpage. B is wrong because spear phishing works by deceiving chosen individuals into opening a lure; no human at any customer was deceived; administrators applied a legitimate update correctly. D is wrong because an insider threat is an authorized person misusing their own access; the build server was breached by external attackers, and location inside the vendor does not make them insiders. When upstream trust is the vector, defenses shift to vendor assurance, build integrity, and monitoring what updates actually do.
questions.recallLine: Every customer that applied a network vendor's signed, official update received an implant planted months earlier on the vendor's build server. Which term BEST describes this?

optionsShort.A: A watering-hole attack on a trusted resource
optionsShort.B: Spear phishing aimed at chosen targets
optionsShort.C: A supply chain attack through the build pipeline
optionsShort.D: An insider threat within the vendor's systems

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: Which term fits attackers poisoning an industry website that target employees visit daily, to exploit their browsers there?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which term fits a crafted message sent to a named finance clerk to trick them into opening an attachment?

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: Which term fits an authorized employee of the vendor deliberately misusing the access their own job grants them?

questions.question: Which security responsibilities does the team retain once the document-processing workload runs serverless?

options.A: Securing the function code, its dependencies, its secrets, and its least-privilege IAM roles
options.B: Patching the operating system kernels of the servers on which the functions execute
options.C: Hardening the hypervisor layer that isolates the provider's tenants from one another
options.D: Managing host firewalls and antivirus on the machines running the function runtime

questions.explanation: Serverless shifts the shared-responsibility line sharply toward the provider, but never past the customer's own workload. What remains is everything the team writes or configures (A): the function code and its input handling, the third-party dependencies bundled with it (composition analysis still applies), the secrets it uses, and above all the IAM role it executes under, since over-permissioned functions are the signature serverless failure. B and D are wrong for the same reason: in a functions platform the customer cannot even reach the operating system, hosts, or runtime; the provider owns their patching and protection; both answers describe responsibilities the team held on its old self-managed VMs and would still hold under IaaS. C is wrong one layer deeper still: hypervisor isolation between tenants is the provider's responsibility in every cloud service model, and no customer ever hardens it.
questions.recallLine: The document-processing workload now runs on a serverless functions platform. Which security responsibilities does the Trellis Pay team retain?

optionsShort.A: Function code, dependencies, secrets and IAM roles
optionsShort.B: Patching the kernels of the executing servers
optionsShort.C: Hardening the tenant-isolating hypervisor layer
optionsShort.D: Host firewalls and antivirus on runtime machines

B.wouldAnswer: Which duty does the team keep when it runs the same workload on virtual machines it rents and manages itself?

C.label: not the decision-maker's
C.wouldAnswer: Who is accountable for keeping one cloud tenant's workloads isolated from another's on shared physical hardware?

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: Which protections did the team own on the self-managed machines this workload has just moved off?

questions.question: How should the lead BEST use the OWASP Top 10 in building the program?

options.A: Adopt it as the complete set of security requirements the finished application must satisfy
options.B: Treat it as a substitute for penetration testing, since it already lists the likely findings
options.C: Use it as an awareness baseline that focuses training on the most common web risk categories
options.D: Apply it as a hardening checklist for the servers that will host the company's applications

questions.explanation: The OWASP Top 10 is an awareness document: a consensus ranking of the most prevalent categories of web application risk. That makes it an ideal seed for a first training curriculum and coding standard: maximum coverage of common failure classes for minimal budget (C). A is wrong because OWASP itself warns the Top 10 is a starting point, not a complete requirements set; when the lead needs verification-grade requirements, the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) is the right artifact. B is wrong because a list of risk categories cannot examine an actual implementation; testing finds the specific instances a list can only name. D is wrong because the Top 10 addresses application-layer risks; server hardening belongs to configuration baselines such as CIS Benchmarks.
questions.recallLine: The new application security lead has a small training budget and no secure-coding standard. How should the lead BEST use the OWASP Top 10?

optionsShort.A: The complete set of requirements the application must satisfy
optionsShort.B: A substitute for penetration testing
optionsShort.C: An awareness baseline focusing training on common risks
optionsShort.D: A hardening checklist for the hosting servers

A.wouldAnswer: Which OWASP artifact provides verification-grade requirements that an application can be formally tested against?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: Which reference tells the team how to harden the operating system and web server underneath the application?

questions.question: The team suspects kernel-level malware is concealing its presence on that server. What is the MOST reliable way to restore trust in the system?

options.A: Rebuild the system from known-good installation media and restore data from clean backups
options.B: Run a full scan with the installed antivirus using its most aggressive detection settings
options.C: Delete the executables owning the suspicious connections and then reboot the server
options.D: Patch the operating system to the current level so the malware can no longer operate

questions.explanation: A rootkit subverts the operating system itself, so every answer that system gives, from process lists to scan results, is suspect; the firewall seeing traffic the host denies is the classic symptom. Once the kernel is untrusted, the only way to re-establish a trusted computing base is to rebuild from media you trust and restore data verified clean (A). B is wrong because the antivirus runs on, and asks questions of, the compromised OS; the rootkit filters what it is allowed to see; aggressive settings do not fix a lying oracle. B is reasonable when the suspected malware is ordinary user-mode code. C is wrong twice over: the hiding means you cannot reliably find the owning executables, and deleting visible components leaves whatever the kernel implant protects. D is wrong because patching closes entry vectors for the future; it does not evict malware already resident below the tools that would remove it.
questions.recallLine: Firewall logs show connections that no tool on the server reports, and kernel-level malware is suspected. What is the MOST reliable way to restore trust?

optionsShort.A: Rebuild from known-good media, restore clean backups
optionsShort.B: Full antivirus scan at aggressive detection settings
optionsShort.C: Delete the suspicious executables and reboot
optionsShort.D: Patch the operating system to current level

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which response fits ordinary user-mode malware on a host whose operating system can still be believed?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Which step removes a straightforward malicious process once it has been positively identified on a trustworthy host?

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: Which measure keeps the server from being reinfected through the same vulnerability after it has been rebuilt?

questions.question: Each infected server infected its neighbors directly, with no user action anywhere. Which combination of controls BEST limits this class of attack in future?

options.A: Phishing simulations and awareness training so employees stop opening malicious attachments
options.B: Timely patching of exposed network services plus segmentation to contain lateral movement
options.C: Stronger password complexity requirements and lockout thresholds across all accounts
options.D: Full backups of every server retained for ninety days at a separate offsite location

questions.explanation: Self-propagation through a vulnerable network service with zero user involvement is the signature of a worm, and the stem hands you both contributing causes: an unpatched exposed service, and a flat network where every host can reach every other. Patching removes the exploitable flaw; segmentation shrinks the population each infected host can even reach; together (B) they attack propagation at both ends. A guards the human vector, and the defining clue is that no human acted; training is the right answer when malware arrives by phishing or Trojanized downloads. C is wrong because the worm exploited a service flaw, not credentials; hardening passwords is the right answer when spread rides password spraying or credential reuse. D is wrong for this question because backups are corrective; they rebuild servers after the damage and do nothing to limit the spread itself. Read the propagation mechanism first; it tells you which control family is even in play.
questions.recallLine: Malware spread overnight across Halden Logistics' flat network with nobody logged in, each host infecting neighbors through the same service. Which controls BEST limit this?

optionsShort.A: Phishing simulations and awareness training
optionsShort.B: Timely patching plus network segmentation
optionsShort.C: Stronger password complexity and lockout thresholds
optionsShort.D: Offsite full backups retained ninety days

A.wouldAnswer: Which control matters most when malware arrives as an attachment or download that a user has to open?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: Which controls limit malware that spreads by guessing or reusing account credentials across servers?

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: What lets Halden rebuild the infected servers once an outbreak has already destroyed the data on them?

questions.question: By correlating the three datasets the contractor reconstructs the timing and routes of cash-in-transit runs. Which security concern does this BEST illustrate?

options.A: Inference, since the contractor deduced one hidden value from a permitted statistical result
options.B: Collusion, since several parties pooled their separate accesses to reach protected data
options.C: Data remanence, since sensitive residue persisted inside systems rated non-sensitive
options.D: Aggregation, since individually non-sensitive data sets combined into sensitive knowledge

questions.explanation: Every source the contractor touched was legitimately non-sensitive; the classified picture emerged only when the sources were correlated. That is aggregation (D): the combination carries a higher sensitivity than any of its parts, which is why access decisions must consider what a subject can assemble in total: need-to-know evaluated across holdings, not per database. A is the closest wrong answer: inference is the sibling concern where someone reasons a specific withheld fact out of permitted answers, as with statistical queries; here nothing was individually withheld or deduced; the sensitivity arose from assembly. B is wrong because collusion requires multiple actors combining their separate privileges; this was one contractor acting within one set of grants. C is wrong because remanence is data physically surviving on media after deletion or reuse; nothing here was residual; the databases were serving their intended content.
questions.recallLine: The cash-in-transit contractor correlates maintenance schedules, fuel purchases and duty rosters to reconstruct run timings and routes. Which security concern does this BEST illustrate?

optionsShort.A: Inference, deducing a hidden value from statistics
optionsShort.B: Collusion, parties pooling their separate accesses
optionsShort.C: Data remanence, residue persisting in non-sensitive systems
optionsShort.D: Aggregation, non-sensitive sets combining into sensitive knowledge

B.label: wrong scope
